abstract: How can artificial neural nets generalize better from fewer examples? In order to generalize successfully, neural network learning methods typically require large training data sets. We introduce a neural network learning method that generalizes rationally from many fewer data points, relying instead on prior knowledge encoded in previously learned neural networks. For example, in robot control learning tasks reported here, previously learned networks that model the effects of robot actions are used to guide subsequent learning of robot control functions. For each observed training example of the target function (e.g. the robot control policy), the learner explains the observed example in terms of its prior knowledge, then analyzes this explanation to infer additional information about the shape, or slope, of the target function. This shape knowledge is used to bias generalization when learning the target function. Results are presented applying this approach to a simulated robot task based on reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper proposes a way for neural networks to generalize from fewer training examples by drawing on knowledge stored in previously learned networks. In the robot-control setting, that prior knowledge consists of models of the effects of robot actions. These models guide the learning of a new control function.

For each observed example of the target function, the learner explains the example using its existing knowledge. It then analyzes that explanation to infer information about the target function's shape or slope. A training example thus contributes more than a single observed input-output relationship: the prior model helps constrain how the function should behave around that observation.

The inferred shape information biases generalization during learning. The paper presents results on a simulated robot task based on reinforcement learning and describes learning from many fewer data points. The approach matters because it makes previously learned action models a source of additional constraints on control learning. Its mechanism depends on having relevant prior knowledge available in neural-network form.
summary.tldr: Previously learned models of robot actions help infer control-function slopes, enabling generalization from fewer examples.

title: Explanation-Based Neural Network Learning for Robot Control

abstract: MacKay's Bayesian framework for backpropagation is conceptually appealing as well as practical. It automatically adjusts the weight decay parameters during training, and computes the evidence for each trained network. The evidence is proportional to our belief in the model. The networks with highest evidence turn out to generalise well. In this paper, the framework is extended to pruned nets, leading to an Ockham Factor for "tuning the architecture to the data". A committee of networks, selected by their high evidence, is a natural Bayesian construction. The evidence of a committee is computed. The framework is illustrated on real-world data from a near infrared spectrometer used to determine the fat content in minced meat. Error bars are computed, including the contribution from the dissent of the committee members. 1 THE OCKHAM FACTOR William of Ockham's (1285-1349) principle of economy in explanations, can be formulated as follows: If several theories account for a phenomenon we should prefer the simplest which describes the data sufficiently well.

paragraphs: The paper develops a Bayesian approach to training and selecting neural networks. The underlying framework adjusts weight decay during training and computes model evidence, a quantity used to assess support for each network. The abstract reports that networks with high evidence generalize well, connecting this probabilistic assessment to predictions beyond the training examples.

The authors extend the framework to networks whose connections have been pruned. An Ockham factor accounts for tuning the architecture to the data, bringing structural choices into the Bayesian assessment. They also form committees from networks with high evidence and compute evidence for the committee itself, treating the combined predictor as another model to evaluate.

The application estimates the fat content of minced meat from near infrared spectroscopy measurements. Alongside predictions, the method computes error bars that include disagreement among committee members. This makes uncertainty across plausible networks part of the reported result. The contribution joins regularization, architecture selection, model combination, and uncertainty estimation within the same probabilistic framework.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian backpropagation framework connects pruning, network committees, and prediction error bars in a spectroscopy application.

title: Bayesian Backprop in Action: Pruning, Committees, Error Bars and an Application to Spectroscopy

abstract: Visual occlusion events constitute a major source of depth information. This paper presents a self-organizing neural network that learns to detect, represent, and predict the visibility and invisibility relationships that arise during occlusion events, after a period of exposure to motion sequences containing occlusion and disocclusion events. The network develops two parallel opponent channels or "chains" of lateral excitatory connections for every resolvable motion trajectory. One channel, the "On" chain or "visible" chain, is activated when a moving stimulus is visible. The other channel, the "Off" chain or "invisible" chain, carries a persistent, amodal representation that predicts the motion of a formerly visible stimulus that becomes invisible due to occlusion. The learning rule uses disinhibition from the On chain to trigger learning in the Off chain. The On and Off chain neurons can learn separate associations with object depth ordering. The results are closely related to the recent discovery (Assad & Maunsell, 1995) of neurons in macaque monkey posterior parietal cortex that respond selectively to inferred motion of invisible stimuli.

paragraphs: A moving object can disappear behind another object while continuing along its path. This paper presents a self-organizing network that learns visibility relationships from motion sequences containing disappearance and reappearance. The aim is to represent both what is currently visible and the inferred motion of something temporarily hidden.

For each resolvable motion trajectory, the network develops two parallel chains of excitatory connections. The On chain responds to visible motion. The Off chain maintains a persistent representation of a previously visible stimulus during occlusion. Learning in the Off chain is triggered through disinhibition from the On chain, linking the hidden-motion representation to visible experience.

The two chains can separately learn associations with the depth ordering of objects. This connects prediction through occlusion with information about which object lies in front. The results are related to reported parietal neurons that respond to inferred motion of invisible stimuli. The model offers a learning mechanism through which experience with visibility changes can produce persistent representations of hidden motion.
summary.tldr: A self-organizing network learns paired pathways for visible motion and the predicted motion of objects hidden by occlusion.

title: Learning to Predict Visibility and Invisibility from Occlusion Events

abstract: Severe contamination of electroencephalographic (EEG) activity by eye movements, blinks, muscle, heart and line noise is a serious problem for EEG interpretation and analysis. Rejecting contami(cid:173) nated EEG segments results in a considerable loss of information and may be impractical for clinical data. Many methods have been proposed to remove eye movement and blink artifacts from EEG recordings. Often regression in the time or frequency domain is performed on simultaneous EEG and electrooculographic (EOG) recordings to derive parameters characterizing the appearance and spread of EOG artifacts in the EEG channels. However, EOG records also contain brain signals [1, 2], so regressing out EOG ac(cid:173) tivity inevitably involves subtracting a portion of the relevant EEG signal from each recording as well. Regression cannot be used to remove muscle noise or line noise, since these have no reference channels. Here , we propose a new and generally applicable method for removing a wide variety of artifacts from EEG records. The method is based on an extended version of a previous Indepen(cid:173) dent Component Analysis (lCA) algorithm [3, 4] for performing blind source separation on linear mixtures of independent source signals with either sub-Gaussian or super-Gaussian distributions. Our results show that ICA can effectively detect, separate and re(cid:173) move activity in EEG records from a wide variety of artifactual sources, with results comparing favorably to those obtained using regression-based methods. Extended leA Removes Artifacts from EEG Recordings

paragraphs: EEG recordings mix brain activity with interference from eye movements, blinking, muscles, the heart, and electrical line noise. Discarding contaminated segments loses information. Removing an eye-recording reference through regression also poses a problem: that reference contains some brain activity, so subtracting its contribution removes relevant signal along with interference.

The paper proposes an extended independent component analysis method to separate these contributions. Its model treats the recordings as linear mixtures of independent sources. The extension accommodates both sub-Gaussian and super-Gaussian source distributions, broadening the kinds of statistical patterns the separation algorithm can handle. This provides a common approach to several artifact types rather than requiring an eye-activity reference for each one.

The reported results show effective detection, separation, and removal of varied artifacts, with favorable comparisons to regression methods. The significance is the possibility of cleaning recordings without rejecting every affected segment. The linear-mixture and independent-source assumptions are central to the approach: they specify how the method interprets the recorded channels and separates their contributions.
summary.tldr: Extended independent component analysis separates varied EEG artifacts by modeling recordings as linear mixtures of independent sources.

title: Extended ICA Removes Artifacts from Electroencephalographic Recordings

abstract: We present a method for the analysis of nonstationary time se(cid:173) ries with multiple operating modes. In particular, it is possible to detect and to model both a switching of the dynamics and a less abrupt, time consuming drift from one mode to another. This is achieved in two steps. First, an unsupervised training method pro(cid:173) vides prediction experts for the inherent dynamical modes. Then, the trained experts are used in a hidden Markov model that allows to model drifts. An application to physiological wake/sleep data demonstrates that analysis and modeling of real-world time series can be improved when the drift paradigm is taken into account.

paragraphs: The paper studies time series whose behavior changes between multiple operating modes. Such changes can be abrupt, but they can also unfold gradually as the system drifts from one mode toward another. The proposed method explicitly represents both possibilities, making the transition itself part of the analysis rather than assuming every change happens immediately.

Training proceeds in two stages. An unsupervised method first learns prediction experts for the different dynamics present in the data. These trained experts are then incorporated into a hidden Markov model that can represent drift. The experts describe how the system behaves within its modes, while the combined model accounts for how behavior evolves between them.

An application to physiological wake and sleep recordings demonstrates the value of including gradual transitions. The authors report improved analysis and modeling when drift is taken into account. The significance is that identifying operating modes alone may not capture the full temporal structure: the path between modes can also be useful information.
summary.tldr: Prediction experts combined with a hidden Markov model capture both abrupt switches and gradual drift in changing time series.

title: Analysis of Drifting Dynamics with Neural Network Hidden Markov Models

paragraphs: The paper asks how difficult it is to train a neural network whose fit is close to the best possible fit within a chosen network class. The data consist of input vectors paired with real-valued outputs. Performance is assessed through the square root of the average squared prediction error.

The quantity studied is the gap between a candidate network's error and the smallest error achievable in its class. This distinction matters because the target is proximity to the best available network, even when that best network cannot fit the data perfectly. The paper examines whether training can reliably make this gap smaller than a fixed positive threshold.

For several classes of neural networks, achieving such a gap is proved NP-hard. The threshold does not depend on the number of data points, so the result concerns even a fixed level of approximation to the optimum. It establishes a computational obstacle to general guarantees of near-best training performance, with the claim applying to the network classes covered by the proofs.
summary.tldr: For several neural-network classes, finding a fit within a fixed error gap of the optimum is NP-hard.

title: On the Infeasibility of Training Neural Networks with Small Squared Errors

abstract: We present test results from spike-timing correlation learning ex- periments carried out with silicon neurons with STDP (Spike Tim- ing Dependent Plasticity) synapses. The weight change scheme of the STDP synapses can be set to either weight-independent or weight-dependent mode. We present results that characterise the learning window implemented for both modes of operation. When presented with spike trains with di(cid:11)erent types of synchronisation the neurons develop bimodal weight distributions. We also show that a 2-layered network of silicon spiking neurons with STDP synapses can perform hierarchical synchrony detection.

We present results that characterise the learning window implemented for both modes of operation. paragraphs: The paper reports learning experiments with silicon spiking neurons whose synapses change according to spike timing. The aim is to examine how this hardware responds to temporal correlations in its inputs and whether it can learn to detect synchrony across spike trains.

The synaptic update scheme supports two modes: weight-independent and weight-dependent changes. The authors characterize the implemented learning window in each mode, describing how the timing relationship between spikes affects learning. When the neurons receive spike trains with different types of synchronization, their synaptic weights develop bimodal distributions, with weights concentrated around two modes.

The authors also demonstrate hierarchical synchrony detection in a two-layer network of these silicon neurons. This extends the evidence from synaptic learning behavior to a network-level computation performed across layers. Together, the results connect the measured timing-dependent learning mechanism, the weight distributions it produces, and the ability of a small hardware network to detect temporal structure hierarchically.
summary.tldr: Silicon neurons with timing-dependent synapses develop bimodal weights and demonstrate hierarchical synchrony detection in a two-layer network.

title: Synchrony Detection by Analogue VLSI Neurons with Bimodal STDP Synapses

abstract: The problem of extracting the relevant aspects of data was ad- dressed through the information bottleneck (IB) method, by (soft) clustering one variable while preserving information about another - relevance - variable. An interesting question addressed in the current work is the extension of these ideas to obtain continuous representations that preserve relevant information, rather than dis- crete clusters. We give a formal deﬂnition of the general continuous IB problem and obtain an analytic solution for the optimal repre- sentation for the important case of multivariate Gaussian variables. The obtained optimal representation is a noisy linear projection to eigenvectors of the normalized correlation matrix §xjy§¡1 x , which is also the basis obtained in Canonical Correlation Analysis. How- ever, in Gaussian IB, the compression tradeoﬁ parameter uniquely determines the dimension, as well as the scale of each eigenvector. This introduces a novel interpretation where solutions of diﬁerent ranks lie on a continuum parametrized by the compression level. Our analysis also provides an analytic expression for the optimal tradeoﬁ - the information curve - in terms of the eigenvalue spec- trum.

paragraphs: The information bottleneck method compresses one variable while retaining information about another variable that defines relevance. This paper extends that idea from discrete clusters to continuous representations. It formally defines the continuous problem and derives an analytical optimal representation for the specific case of multivariate Gaussian variables.

The optimal representation is a linear projection with added noise, using eigenvector directions of a normalized correlation matrix. These directions also appear in canonical correlation analysis. The distinctive feature is how the compression tradeoff controls the representation: it uniquely determines both how many directions are retained and the scale assigned to each direction.

This creates a continuous view of representations with different dimensions. As the compression level changes, the solution’s rank and scaling are governed by the same tradeoff rather than treated as unrelated choices. The analysis also gives an exact expression for the optimal information curve in terms of the eigenvalues, making the balance between compression and retained relevance analytically explicit in the Gaussian setting.
summary.tldr: For Gaussian variables, the optimal continuous information bottleneck is a noisy linear projection whose dimension and scaling follow the compression tradeoff.

title: Information Bottleneck for Gaussian Variables

abstract: This paper proposes a new approach to feature selection based on a sta- tistical feature mining technique for sequence and tree kernels. Since natural language data take discrete structures, convolution kernels, such as sequence and tree kernels, are advantageous for both the concept and accuracy of many natural language processing tasks. However, experi- ments have shown that the best results can only be achieved when lim- ited small sub-structures are dealt with by these kernels. This paper dis- cusses this issue of convolution kernels and then proposes a statistical feature selection that enable us to use larger sub-structures effectively. The proposed method, in order to execute efﬁciently, can be embedded into an original kernel calculation process by using sub-structure min- ing algorithms. Experiments on real NLP tasks conﬁrm the problem in the conventional method and compare the performance of a conventional method to that of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Sequence and tree kernels let learning algorithms work with the discrete structures found in language. The paper addresses a practical difficulty with these methods: experiments had shown the best results when kernels were restricted to small substructures. Simply including larger structures did not automatically make their extra information useful.

The authors propose statistical feature selection based on mining substructures. Its purpose is to make larger substructures usable by selecting features rather than indiscriminately including them. To keep the procedure efficient, the mining algorithms can be incorporated into the original kernel calculation. Feature selection is therefore connected directly to how structural similarities are computed.

Experiments on real natural-language-processing tasks confirm the problem with conventional kernels and compare the proposed method against a conventional approach. The abstract presents the selection method as enabling effective use of larger substructures, without specifying numerical gains. The contribution is a way to control which structural features enter the kernel while integrating that control into its computation.
summary.tldr: Statistical substructure mining adds feature selection to sequence and tree kernels so larger language structures can be used effectively.

title: Sequence and Tree Kernels with Statistical Feature Mining

abstract: We propose an extended probabilistic model for human perception. We argue that in many circumstances, human observers simultaneously evaluate sensory evidence under different hypotheses regarding the underlying physical process that might have generated the sensory information. Within this context, inference can be optimal if the observer weighs each hypothesis according to the correct belief in that hypothesis. But if the observer commits to a particular hypothesis, the belief in that hypothesis is converted into subjective certainty, and subsequent perceptual behavior is suboptimal, conditioned only on the chosen hypothesis. We demonstrate that this framework can explain psychophysical data of a recently reported decision-estimation experiment. The model well accounts for the data, predicting the same estimation bias as a consequence of the preceding decision step. The power of the framework is that it has no free parameters except the degree of the observer's uncertainty about its internal sensory representation. All other parameters are defined by the particular experiment which allows us to make quantitative predictions of human perception to two modifications of the original experiment.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a probabilistic explanation for how making a decision can influence what someone subsequently perceives. Its starting point is that observers may consider several hypotheses about the physical process behind a sensory signal. Perception can be optimal when each hypothesis contributes according to the observer’s correct belief in it.

The key change occurs when an observer commits to one hypothesis. In the model, that commitment turns a tentative belief into subjective certainty. Subsequent estimation then uses only the selected explanation, rather than continuing to account for alternatives. This provides a mechanism through which an earlier decision can bias a later perceptual estimate.

The authors show that the model accounts well for data from a decision-followed-by-estimation experiment, including the direction of the estimation bias. Its only free parameter describes uncertainty in the observer’s internal sensory representation; the experiment determines the remaining parameters. This constrained setup also supports quantitative predictions for two modifications of the experiment. Those predictions extend the framework’s reach without requiring additional adjustable parameters.
summary.tldr: A Bayesian model explains how committing to a perceptual decision can bias subsequent estimates by treating one hypothesis as certain.

title: A Bayesian Model of Conditioned Perception

abstract: Maximum entropy models have become popular statistical models in neuroscience and other areas in biology, and can be useful tools for obtaining estimates of mu- tual information in biological systems. However, maximum entropy models fit to small data sets can be subject to sampling bias; i.e. the true entropy of the data can be severely underestimated. Here we study the sampling properties of estimates of the entropy obtained from maximum entropy models. We show that if the data is generated by a distribution that lies in the model class, the bias is equal to the number of parameters divided by twice the number of observations. However, in practice, the true distribution is usually outside the model class, and we show here that this misspecification can lead to much larger bias. We provide a perturba- tive approximation of the maximally expected bias when the true model is out of model class, and we illustrate our results using numerical simulations of an Ising model; i.e. the second-order maximum entropy distribution on binary data.

paragraphs: Maximum entropy models can be used to estimate entropy and, in turn, mutual information in biological systems. When fitted to small datasets, however, their entropy estimates can be biased downward. This paper examines that sampling bias and asks how it depends on whether the chosen model class can represent the true data distribution.

When the data-generating distribution belongs to the model class, the authors show that the bias equals the number of parameters divided by twice the number of observations. This gives a direct relationship between model size, sample size, and bias under the stated modeling condition. The condition is essential to interpreting that expression.

The paper then studies misspecification, where the true distribution falls outside the model class, and shows that bias can be much larger. It provides a perturbative approximation to the maximally expected bias in that setting and illustrates the analysis with Ising-model simulations. The findings show why a bias calculation based only on parameter and observation counts may be inadequate when the model cannot represent the underlying distribution.
summary.tldr: Entropy estimates from maximum entropy models can have substantially greater sampling bias when the true distribution lies outside the model class.

title: How biased are maximum entropy models?

abstract: In this paper we investigate the computational complexity of learning the graph structure underlying a discrete undirected graphical model from i.i.d. samples. Our first result is an unconditional computational lower bound of $\Omega (p^{d/2})$ for learning general graphical models on $p$ nodes of maximum degree $d$, for the class of statistical algorithms recently introduced by Feldman et al. The construction is related to the notoriously difficult learning parities with noise problem in computational learning theory. Our lower bound shows that the $\widetilde O(p^{d+2})$ runtime required by Bresler, Mossel, and Sly's exhaustive-search algorithm cannot be significantly improved without restricting the class of models. Aside from structural assumptions on the graph such as it being a tree, hypertree, tree-like, etc., most recent papers on structure learning assume that the model has the correlation decay property. Indeed, focusing on ferromagnetic Ising models, Bento and Montanari showed that all known low-complexity algorithms fail to learn simple graphs when the interaction strength exceeds a number related to the correlation decay threshold. Our second set of results gives a class of repelling (antiferromagnetic) models that have the \emph{opposite} behavior: very strong repelling allows efficient learning in time $\widetilde O(p^2)$. We provide an algorithm whose performance interpolates between $\widetilde O(p^2)$ and $\widetilde O(p^{d+2})$ depending on the strength of the repulsion.

We provide an algorithm whose performance interpolates between $\widetilde O(p^2)$ and $\widetilde O(p^{d+2})$ depending on the strength of the repulsion.

paragraphs: The paper asks how difficult it is to recover the graph underlying a discrete undirected graphical model from independent samples. For general models with p nodes and maximum degree d, it establishes an unconditional Ω(p^(d/2)) computational lower bound for a specified class of statistical algorithms. The construction connects this difficulty to learning parities with noise.

This lower bound shows that substantial improvements over exhaustive search require restrictions on the model class within the scope of the result. The paper then investigates antiferromagnetic models, where interactions are repelling. Its findings reveal a setting in which strong interactions can make structure learning computationally easier.

For a class of these models, sufficiently strong repulsion permits learning in approximately quadratic time, expressed as Õ(p²). The proposed algorithm's performance ranges between Õ(p²) and Õ(p^(d+2)), depending on repulsion strength. The two contributions together distinguish general computational hardness from the favorable behavior available in a particular model family, showing that interaction type and strength can be central to learning complexity.
summary.tldr: General graphical-model learning has a strong computational lower bound, while strong repulsion enables efficient learning for a class of antiferromagnetic models.

title: Structure learning of antiferromagnetic Ising models

abstract: In many learning problems, ranging from clustering to ranking through metric learning, empirical estimates of the risk functional consist of an average over tuples (e.g., pairs or triplets) of observations, rather than over individual observations. In this paper, we focus on how to best implement a stochastic approximation approach to solve such risk minimization problems. We argue that in the large-scale setting, gradient estimates should be obtained by sampling tuples of data points with replacement (incomplete U-statistics) instead of sampling data points without replacement (complete U-statistics based on subsamples). We develop a theoretical framework accounting for the substantial impact of this strategy on the generalization ability of the prediction model returned by the Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) algorithm. It reveals that the method we promote achieves a much better trade-off between statistical accuracy and computational cost. Beyond the rate bound analysis, experiments on AUC maximization and metric learning provide strong empirical evidence of the superiority of the proposed approach.

paragraphs: Some learning objectives average losses over pairs or triplets of observations rather than individual examples. This occurs in tasks such as ranking, clustering, and metric learning. The paper asks how stochastic gradient descent should sample data when estimating gradients for these tuple-based objectives at large scale.

The authors advocate sampling tuples directly with replacement, producing incomplete U-statistics. They contrast this with selecting individual data points without replacement and computing complete U-statistics over that subsample. The distinction changes which combinations contribute to a gradient estimate and how computational effort is allocated across the full tuple-based objective.

A theoretical framework connects this sampling choice to the generalization performance of the model returned by stochastic gradient descent. The analysis finds a substantially better balance between statistical accuracy and computational cost for the proposed approach. Experiments on AUC maximization and metric learning provide strong supporting evidence. The contribution makes tuple sampling itself an important design choice in efficient learning, with consequences beyond the cost of a single gradient update.
summary.tldr: Directly sampling tuples with replacement improves the analyzed accuracy–computation tradeoff for SGD on tuple-based learning objectives.

title: SGD Algorithms based on Incomplete U-statistics: Large-Scale Minimization of Empirical Risk

abstract: This work aims to address the problem of image-based question-answering (QA) with new models and datasets. In our work, we propose to use neural networks and visual semantic embeddings, without intermediate stages such as object detection and image segmentation, to predict answers to simple questions about images. Our model performs 1.8 times better than the only published results on an existing image QA dataset. We also present a question generation algorithm that converts image descriptions, which are widely available, into QA form. We used this algorithm to produce an order-of-magnitude larger dataset, with more evenly distributed answers. A suite of baseline results on this new dataset are also presented.

It does so without intermediate object-detection or image-segmentation stages, bringing visual and language information into the answer-prediction process directly.

This is a comparison within the stated evaluation, rather than a claim about all visual reasoning tasks. It supports the usefulness of the proposed modeling approach for the simple image questions studied.

The second contribution is an algorithm that converts image descriptions into question-answer pairs. Because descriptions are widely available, this provides a route to expanding the data used for the task. The resulting dataset is an order of magnitude larger and has more evenly distributed answers. The authors also provide baseline results, establishing reference performance for evaluating models on the new collection.
summary.tldr: The paper introduces a neural image question-answering model and generates a larger, more answer-balanced dataset from image descriptions.

title: Exploring Models and Data for Image Question Answering

abstract: We unify slice sampling and Hamiltonian Monte Carlo (HMC) sampling, demonstrating their connection via the Hamiltonian-Jacobi equation from Hamiltonian mechanics. This insight enables extension of HMC and slice sampling to a broader family of samplers, called Monomial Gamma Samplers (MGS). We provide a theoretical analysis of the mixing performance of such samplers, proving that in the limit of a single parameter, the MGS draws decorrelated samples from the desired target distribution. We further show that as this parameter tends toward this limit, performance gains are achieved at a cost of increasing numerical difficulty and some practical convergence issues. Our theoretical results are validated with synthetic data and real-world applications.

The authors analyze how these samplers mix, meaning how effectively their draws move through the target distribution rather than remaining strongly related. They prove that, in a limit of one parameter, Monomial Gamma Samplers produce decorrelated samples from the desired distribution. This identifies an appealing theoretical regime within the larger family.

The practical message is that the limiting decorrelation result must be considered alongside the numerical behavior of samplers operating near that limit.
summary.tldr: Monomial Gamma Samplers unify HMC and slice sampling, with limiting decorrelation gains accompanied by increasing numerical difficulty.

title: Towards Unifying Hamiltonian Monte Carlo and Slice Sampling

abstract: Neural networks augmented with external memory have the ability to learn algorithmic solutions to complex tasks. These models appear promising for applications such as language modeling and machine translation. However, they scale poorly in both space and time as the amount of memory grows --- limiting their applicability to real-world domains. Here, we present an end-to-end differentiable memory access scheme, which we call Sparse Access Memory (SAM), that retains the representational power of the original approaches whilst training efficiently with very large memories. We show that SAM achieves asymptotic lower bounds in space and time complexity, and find that an implementation runs $1,\!000\times$ faster and with $3,\!000\times$ less physical memory than non-sparse models. SAM learns with comparable data efficiency to existing models on a range of synthetic tasks and one-shot Omniglot character recognition, and can scale to tasks requiring $100,\!000$s of time steps and memories. As well, we show how our approach can be adapted for models that maintain temporal associations between memories, as with the recently introduced Differentiable Neural Computer.

They also report an implementation running 1,000 times faster and using 3,000 times less physical memory than nonsparse models. These implementation results demonstrate substantial savings in the reported comparison, alongside the separate theoretical claim about computational scaling.

The contribution makes large external memories more computationally accessible while maintaining demonstrated learning capability.
summary.tldr: Sparse Access Memory enables differentiable neural memory to scale with major reported reductions in runtime and physical memory use.

title: Scaling Memory-Augmented Neural Networks with Sparse Reads and Writes

abstract: We study the cost function for hierarchical clusterings introduced by [Dasgupta, 2015] where hierarchies are treated as first-class objects rather than deriving their cost from projections into flat clusters. It was also shown in [Dasgupta, 2015] that a top-down algorithm returns a hierarchical clustering of cost at most (O\left(\alpha n \log n\right)) times the cost of the optimal hierarchical clustering, where (\alpha n) is the approximation ratio of the Sparsest Cut subroutine used. Thus using the best known approximation algorithm for Sparsest Cut due to Arora-Rao-Vazirani, the top down algorithm returns a hierarchical clustering of cost at most (O\left(\log^{3/2} n\right)) times the cost of the optimal solution. We improve this by giving an (O(\log{n}))-approximation algorithm for this problem. Our main technical ingredients are a combinatorial characterization of ultrametrics induced by this cost function, deriving an Integer Linear Programming (ILP) formulation for this family of ultrametrics, and showing how to iteratively round an LP relaxation of this formulation by using the idea of \emph{sphere growing} which has been extensively used in the context of graph partitioning. We also prove that our algorithm returns an (O(\log{n}))-approximate hierarchical clustering for a generalization of this cost function also studied in [Dasgupta, 2015]. Experiments show that the hierarchies found by using the ILP formulation as well as our rounding algorithm often have better projections into flat clusters than the standard linkage based algorithms. We conclude with an inapproximability result for this problem, namely that no polynomial sized LP or SDP can be used to obtain a constant factor approximation for this problem.

paragraphs: Hierarchical clustering produces a nested organization of data, but evaluating only individual flat partitions can miss the quality of the hierarchy itself. This paper studies a cost function that directly scores the full hierarchy. It improves the approximation guarantee from O(log^(3/2) n) to O(log n), where n is the number of objects.

The method characterizes the ultrametrics associated with the objective and expresses them through an integer linear program. It then relaxes that formulation to a linear program and rounds the solution iteratively using sphere growing, an idea from graph partitioning. The same approximation order also holds for a generalization of the cost function.

Experiments show that hierarchies obtained from the integer formulation and the rounding algorithm often produce better flat partitions than standard linkage methods. That empirical advantage is qualified by 'often.' The paper also establishes a specific theoretical barrier: polynomial-sized linear or semidefinite programs cannot provide a constant-factor approximation for this problem. This limits those formulation families, rather than ruling out every conceivable approximation approach.
summary.tldr: An optimization-and-rounding approach improves the hierarchical clustering approximation guarantee to O(log n) and establishes a barrier for polynomial-sized LP and SDP formulations.

title: Hierarchical Clustering via Spreading Metrics

abstract: This paper studies the trade-off between two different kinds of pure exploration: breadth versus depth. We focus on the most biased coin problem, asking how many total coin flips are required to identify a ``heavy'' coin from an infinite bag containing both ``heavy'' coins with mean $\theta_1 \in (0,1)$, and ``light" coins with mean $\theta_0 \in (0,\theta_1)$, where heavy coins are drawn from the bag with proportion $\alpha \in (0,1/2)$. When $\alpha,\theta_0,\theta_1$ are unknown, the key difficulty of this problem lies in distinguishing whether the two kinds of coins have very similar means, or whether heavy coins are just extremely rare. While existing solutions to this problem require some prior knowledge of the parameters $\theta_0,\theta_1,\alpha$, we propose an adaptive algorithm that requires no such knowledge yet still obtains near-optimal sample complexity guarantees. In contrast, we provide a lower bound showing that non-adaptive strategies require at least quadratically more samples. In characterizing this gap between adaptive and nonadaptive strategies, we make connections to anomaly detection and prove lower bounds on the sample complexity of differentiating between a single parametric distribution and a mixture of two such distributions.

paragraphs: The paper examines a search problem involving an unlimited supply of coins of two types. Heavy coins have a higher probability of heads, but they are less common. The learner wants to identify a heavy coin using few flips, balancing inspection of new coins against further testing of already selected ones.

Neither type's probability of heads nor the proportion of heavy coins is known. This creates an ambiguity: difficulty finding a heavy coin could mean that heavy coins are rare or that the two types behave very similarly. The authors propose an adaptive algorithm that needs no prior knowledge of those parameters and still achieves near-optimal sample complexity.

The paper also connects the problem to anomaly detection and establishes sample-complexity lower bounds for distinguishing one parametric distribution from a mixture of two, extending the breadth-versus-depth question to statistical testing.
summary.tldr: An adaptive heavy-coin search needs no parameter knowledge and achieves near-optimal sampling, while non-adaptive strategies face a quadratic disadvantage.

title: The Power of Adaptivity in Identifying Statistical Alternatives

abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), one of the key components is policy evaluation, which aims to estimate the value function (i.e., expected long-term accumulated reward) of a policy. With a good policy evaluation method, the RL algorithms will estimate the value function more accurately and find a better policy. When the state space is large or continuous \emph{Gradient-based Temporal Difference(GTD)} policy evaluation algorithms with linear function approximation are widely used. Considering that the collection of the evaluation data is both time and reward consuming, a clear understanding of the finite sample performance of the policy evaluation algorithms is very important to reinforcement learning. Under the assumption that data are i.i.d. generated, previous work provided the finite sample analysis of the GTD algorithms with constant step size by converting them into convex-concave saddle point problems. However, it is well-known that, the data are generated from Markov processes rather than i.i.d in RL problems.. In this paper, in the realistic Markov setting, we derive the finite sample bounds for the general convex-concave saddle point problems, and hence for the GTD algorithms. We have the following discussions based on our bounds. (1) With variants of step size, GTD algorithms converge. (2) The convergence rate is determined by the step size, with the mixing time of the Markov process as the coefficient. The faster the Markov processes mix, the faster the convergence. (3) We explain that the experience replay trick is effective by improving the mixing property of the Markov process. To the best of our knowledge, our analysis is the first to provide finite sample bounds for the GTD algorithms in Markov setting.

summary.tldr: The paper gives finite-sample guarantees for GTD policy evaluation with Markov data, showing how step size and mixing time govern convergence.

title: Finite Sample Analysis of the GTD Policy Evaluation Algorithms in Markov Setting

abstract: We consider model-free reinforcement learning for infinite-horizon discounted Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) with a continuous state space and unknown transition kernel, when only a single sample path under an arbitrary policy of the system is available. We consider the Nearest Neighbor Q-Learning (NNQL) algorithm to learn the optimal Q function using nearest neighbor regression method. As the main contribution, we provide tight finite sample analysis of the convergence rate. In particular, for MDPs with a $d$-dimensional state space and the discounted factor $\gamma \in (0,1)$, given an arbitrary sample path with ``covering time'' $L$, we establish that the algorithm is guaranteed to output an $\varepsilon$-accurate estimate of the optimal Q-function using $\Ot(L/(\varepsilon^3(1-\gamma)^7))$ samples. For instance, for a well-behaved MDP, the covering time of the sample path under the purely random policy scales as $\Ot(1/\varepsilon^d),$ so the sample complexity scales as $\Ot(1/\varepsilon^{d+3}).$ Indeed, we establish a lower bound that argues that the dependence of $ \Omegat(1/\varepsilon^{d+2})$ is necessary.

As the main contribution, we provide tight finite sample analysis of the convergence rate. paragraphs: The paper studies learning optimal action values in a continuous-state Markov decision process with unknown transitions. The learner has only one sample trajectory, generated by an arbitrary policy, and values rewards over an infinite horizon with discounting. Nearest Neighbor Q-Learning uses nearby observed states to estimate the optimal Q-function without learning a transition model.

The main contribution is a finite-sample convergence analysis. For a trajectory with covering time L and discount factor gamma, the required sample count scales as L divided by epsilon cubed and (1 − gamma) to the seventh power, up to logarithmic factors, to achieve epsilon accuracy. Coverage of the state space therefore directly affects the guarantee.

For a well-behaved process explored by a purely random policy, covering time scales approximately as epsilon to the power −d, where d is the state dimension. This yields an upper bound with exponent d + 3, while the paper establishes a necessary lower-bound dependence with exponent d + 2, again suppressing logarithmic factors. These results quantify both the algorithm's learning requirements and the substantial difficulty introduced by continuous-state dimension.
summary.tldr: Finite-sample bounds characterize how nearest-neighbor Q-learning from one trajectory depends on state coverage, accuracy, discounting, and dimension.

title: Q-learning with Nearest Neighbors

abstract: Realistic music generation is a challenging task. When building generative models of music that are learnt from data, typically high-level representations such as scores or MIDI are used that abstract away the idiosyncrasies of a particular performance. But these nuances are very important for our perception of musicality and realism, so in this work we embark on modelling music in the raw audio domain. It has been shown that autoregressive models excel at generating raw audio waveforms of speech, but when applied to music, we find them biased towards capturing local signal structure at the expense of modelling long-range correlations. This is problematic because music exhibits structure at many different timescales. In this work, we explore autoregressive discrete autoencoders (ADAs) as a means to enable autoregressive models to capture long-range correlations in waveforms. We find that they allow us to unconditionally generate piano music directly in the raw audio domain, which shows stylistic consistency across tens of seconds.

paragraphs: Music generation often uses scores or MIDI, which capture musical events while abstracting away details of an individual performance. This paper works directly with raw audio to retain nuances that matter for perceived realism and musicality. Doing so requires a model to handle both the immediate waveform and musical relationships extending over much longer periods.

The authors find that autoregressive models, despite their success with speech waveforms, favor local signal structure when applied to music. That emphasis comes at the expense of long-range correlations. Since music contains organization at many timescales, accurately modeling nearby audio samples alone does not address the full generation problem.

The paper explores autoregressive discrete autoencoders as a way to help autoregressive models capture those longer relationships. The resulting system generates piano music unconditionally in the raw audio domain, with reported stylistic consistency lasting tens of seconds. This finding supports the proposed representation as a way to extend coherence beyond short waveform patterns, while preserving the paper's focus on the demonstrated piano-generation setting.
summary.tldr: Autoregressive discrete autoencoders enable raw-audio piano generation with reported stylistic consistency across tens of seconds.

title: The challenge of realistic music generation: modelling raw audio at scale

abstract: The high-dimensional convolution is widely used in various disciplines but has a serious performance problem due to its high computational complexity. Over the decades, people took a handmade approach to design fast algorithms for the Gaussian convolution. Recently, requirements for various non-Gaussian convolutions have emerged and are continuously getting higher. However, the handmade acceleration approach is no longer feasible for so many different convolutions since it is a time-consuming and painstaking job. Instead, we propose an Acceleration Network (AccNet) which turns the work of designing new fast algorithms to training the AccNet. This is done by: 1, interpreting splatting, blurring, slicing operations as convolutions; 2, turning these convolutions to $g$CP layers to build AccNet. After training, the activation function $g$ together with AccNet weights automatically define the new splatting, blurring and slicing operations. Experiments demonstrate AccNet is able to design acceleration algorithms for a ton of convolutions including Gaussian/non-Gaussian convolutions and produce state-of-the-art results.

paragraphs: High-dimensional convolution is computationally expensive, and designing a fast algorithm by hand can require substantial effort. The paper focuses on the growing need to accelerate many different convolutions, including non-Gaussian ones. Its proposed Acceleration Network, or AccNet, turns the task of constructing an acceleration algorithm into a training problem.

The approach begins with splatting, blurring, and slicing operations and interprets them as convolutions. Those convolutions become gCP layers that form AccNet. After training, the activation function g and learned weights define new versions of the underlying operations. The network therefore supplies a way to determine the operations used by an acceleration algorithm through learning.

Experiments show that AccNet can design acceleration algorithms for a broad range of Gaussian and non-Gaussian convolutions, with results the authors describe as state of the art. The significance is the reuse of a training-based design procedure across different convolution requirements. This addresses the effort involved in crafting a separate fast method for each new convolution.
summary.tldr: AccNet learns operations that define fast high-dimensional convolution algorithms, with reported strong results across Gaussian and non-Gaussian convolutions.

title: Designing by Training: Acceleration Neural Network for Fast High-Dimensional Convolution

abstract: We propose DecaProp (Densely Connected Attention Propagation), a new densely connected neural architecture for reading comprehension (RC). There are two distinct characteristics of our model. Firstly, our model densely connects all pairwise layers of the network, modeling relationships between passage and query across all hierarchical levels. Secondly, the dense connectors in our network are learned via attention instead of standard residual skip-connectors. To this end, we propose novel Bidirectional Attention Connectors (BAC) for efficiently forging connections throughout the network. We conduct extensive experiments on four challenging RC benchmarks. Our proposed approach achieves state-of-the-art results on all four, outperforming existing baselines by up to 2.6% to 14.2% in absolute F1 score.

paragraphs: DecaProp is a neural architecture for reading comprehension, where a model must relate a question to a passage. Its main idea is to connect passage and question representations across all hierarchical levels of the network. This allows the architecture to model relationships between representations formed at different depths, giving those relationships a central role in processing.

The connections themselves are learned through attention. Instead of using standard residual skip connections, the model introduces Bidirectional Attention Connectors to build dense links throughout the network efficiently. Attention therefore serves two purposes in the design: relating the passage to the query and determining how information connects across layers.

The authors evaluate DecaProp on four challenging reading comprehension benchmarks and report state-of-the-art results on all four. Reported absolute F1 improvements over existing baselines range from 2.6% to 14.2%. These experiments support the value of combining dense connectivity with learned attention connectors, showing gains across several tested comprehension settings rather than on a single benchmark alone.
summary.tldr: DecaProp connects passage and question representations across network depths using attention, achieving leading results on four reading comprehension benchmarks.

title: Densely Connected Attention Propagation for Reading Comprehension

abstract: Model-free reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms directly parameterize and update value functions or policies, bypassing the modeling of the environment. They are typically simpler, more flexible to use, and thus more prevalent in modern deep RL than model-based approaches. However, empirical work has suggested that they require large numbers of samples to learn. The theoretical question of whether not model-free algorithms are in fact \emph{sample efficient} is one of the most fundamental questions in RL. The problem is unsolved even in the basic scenario with finitely many states and actions. We prove that, in an episodic MDP setting, Q-learning with UCB exploration achieves regret $\tlO(\sqrt{H^3 SAT})$ where $S$ and $A$ are the numbers of states and actions, $H$ is the number of steps per episode, and $T$ is the total number of steps. Our regret matches the optimal regret up to a single $\sqrt{H}$ factor. Thus we establish the sample efficiency of a classical model-free approach. Moreover, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first model-free analysis to establish $\sqrt{T}$ regret \emph{without} requiring access to a ``simulator.''

paragraphs: This paper asks whether model-free reinforcement learning can learn efficiently from interactions, even in the basic setting of finitely many states and actions. Model-free methods update values or policies directly rather than constructing an environment model. Their practical popularity makes it important to understand whether their apparent demand for many samples is unavoidable.

The authors analyze Q-learning equipped with upper-confidence-bound exploration in an episodic Markov decision process. They prove a regret bound of approximately sqrt(H³SAT), suppressing logarithmic factors. Here S and A count states and actions, H is the episode length, and T is the total number of interaction steps. The bound is within a factor of sqrt(H) of optimal regret.

This result establishes sample efficiency for the analyzed classical model-free approach. Its square-root dependence on T means cumulative regret grows sublinearly with experience. The analysis does not require a simulator, and the authors identify it as the first model-free square-root-T regret result with that property. The guarantee specifically concerns the stated episodic setting and exploration-equipped Q-learning algorithm.
summary.tldr: Q-learning with UCB exploration achieves near-optimal regret in finite episodic environments without requiring a simulator.

title: Is Q-Learning Provably Efficient?

abstract: Hyperbolic spaces have recently gained momentum in the context of machine learning due to their high capacity and tree-likeliness properties. However, the representational power of hyperbolic geometry is not yet on par with Euclidean geometry, firstly because of the absence of corresponding hyperbolic neural network layers. Here, we bridge this gap in a principled manner by combining the formalism of Möbius gyrovector spaces with the Riemannian geometry of the Poincaré model of hyperbolic spaces. As a result, we derive hyperbolic versions of important deep learning tools: multinomial logistic regression, feed-forward and recurrent neural networks. This allows to embed sequential data and perform classification in the hyperbolic space. Empirically, we show that, even if hyperbolic optimization tools are limited, hyperbolic sentence embeddings either outperform or are on par with their Euclidean variants on textual entailment and noisy-prefix recognition tasks.

paragraphs: Hyperbolic spaces offer representational capacity and a geometry suited to tree-like structure. Using that geometry in learning requires more than placing data points in a curved space: neural networks also need compatible layers and operations. This paper addresses the lack of hyperbolic counterparts to several standard deep learning tools.

The authors combine Möbius gyrovector algebra with the Riemannian geometry of the Poincaré model. From this foundation, they derive hyperbolic versions of multinomial logistic regression, feed-forward networks, and recurrent networks. These constructions allow sequential data to be embedded and classified within hyperbolic space, extending the range of computations available beyond the embeddings themselves.

Experiments compare hyperbolic sentence embeddings with their Euclidean counterparts on textual entailment and noisy-prefix recognition. Despite limited hyperbolic optimization tools, the hyperbolic versions either outperform or match the Euclidean alternatives on those tasks. The contribution is thus both a principled collection of neural building blocks and empirical evidence that the resulting geometry can be useful for the evaluated sequence problems.
summary.tldr: The paper derives neural-network layers for hyperbolic space and shows competitive or better sentence-embedding performance on two text tasks.

title: Hyperbolic Neural Networks

abstract: Protein modeling is an increasingly popular area of machine learning research. Semi-supervised learning has emerged as an important paradigm in protein modeling due to the high cost of acquiring supervised protein labels, but the current literature is fragmented when it comes to datasets and standardized evaluation techniques. To facilitate progress in this field, we introduce the Tasks Assessing Protein Embeddings (TAPE), a set of five biologically relevant semi-supervised learning tasks spread across different domains of protein biology. We curate tasks into specific training, validation, and test splits to ensure that each task tests biologically relevant generalization that transfers to real-life scenarios. We benchmark a range of approaches to semi-supervised protein representation learning, which span recent work as well as canonical sequence learning techniques. We find that self-supervised pretraining is helpful for almost all models on all tasks, more than doubling performance in some cases. Despite this increase, in several cases features learned by self-supervised pretraining still lag behind features extracted by state-of-the-art non-neural techniques. This gap in performance suggests a huge opportunity for innovative architecture design and improved modeling paradigms that better capture the signal in biological sequences. TAPE will help the machine learning community focus effort on scientifically relevant problems. Toward this end, all data and code used to run these experiments is available at https://github.com/songlab-cal/tape

paragraphs: Protein learning faces expensive supervised labels and inconsistent evaluation across studies. TAPE addresses the evaluation problem with five biologically relevant tasks spanning different areas of protein biology. The authors construct training, validation, and test splits intended to assess generalization that matters for real biological applications.

The benchmark compares several approaches to semi-supervised protein representation learning, including recent methods and established sequence-learning techniques. Its shared tasks and evaluation structure make it possible to examine whether learned representations transfer usefully across different biological problems. This places emphasis on what a representation supports after pretraining, rather than treating pretraining itself as sufficient evidence of usefulness.

Self-supervised pretraining helps almost all evaluated models across all tasks, with performance more than doubling in some cases. Nevertheless, pretrained features remain behind leading non-neural features in several comparisons. These findings show both the value of pretraining and room for better biological representations. The released data and code provide a common basis for investigating that gap.
summary.tldr: TAPE standardizes protein transfer-learning evaluation and finds broad benefits from pretraining alongside persistent gaps against non-neural features.

title: Evaluating Protein Transfer Learning with TAPE

abstract: Gradient Boosting (\GB) is a popular and very successful ensemble method for binary trees. While various types of regularization of the base predictors are used with this algorithm, the theory that connects such regularizations with generalization guarantees is poorly understood. We fill this gap by deriving data-dependent learning guarantees for \GB\ used with \emph{regularization}, expressed in terms of the Rademacher complexities of the constrained families of base predictors. We introduce a new algorithm, called \rgb\, that directly benefits from these generalization bounds and that, at every boosting round, applies the \emph{Structural Risk Minimization} principle to search for a base predictor with the best empirical fit versus complexity trade-off. Inspired by \emph{Randomized Coordinate Descent} we provide a scalable implementation of our algorithm, able to search over large families of base predictors. Finally, we provide experimental results, demonstrating that our algorithm achieves significantly better out-of-sample performance on multiple datasets than the standard \GB\ algorithm used with its regularization.

paragraphs: Gradient boosting builds an ensemble by adding base predictors over successive rounds. Although practitioners regularize those predictors, the paper identifies a gap in the theory linking such choices to generalization. It develops data-dependent learning guarantees expressed through Rademacher complexities, quantities that measure the capacity of the constrained families from which base predictors are selected.

The authors use these bounds to design Regularized Gradient Boosting. At each round, the algorithm applies Structural Risk Minimization to balance how well a candidate fits the training data against the complexity of its predictor family. Regularization therefore directly informs the search for the next ensemble component through the trade-off described by the theory.

A scalable implementation draws inspiration from randomized coordinate descent and can search large families of base predictors. Experiments on multiple datasets report significantly better out-of-sample performance than standard gradient boosting with its regularization. The contribution connects a generalization analysis, a round-by-round selection rule, and a practical search procedure, with empirical support for that combination on the evaluated datasets.
summary.tldr: Regularized Gradient Boosting uses generalization bounds to balance fit and predictor complexity at each boosting round.

title: Regularized Gradient Boosting

abstract: We present a method to incrementally generate complete 2D or 3D scenes with the following properties: (a) it is globally consistent at each step according to a learned scene prior, (b) real observations of a scene can be incorporated while observing global consistency, (c) unobserved regions can be hallucinated locally in consistence with previous observations, hallucinations and global priors, and (d) hallucinations are statistical in nature, i.e., different scenes can be generated from the same observations. To achieve this, we model the virtual scene, where an active agent at each step can either perceive an observed part of the scene or generate a local hallucination. The latter can be interpreted as the agent's expectation at this step through the scene and can be applied to autonomous navigation. In the limit of observing real data at each point, our method converges to solving the SLAM problem. It can otherwise sample entirely imagined scenes from prior distributions. Besides autonomous agents, applications include problems where large data is required for building robust real-world applications, but few samples are available. We demonstrate efficacy on various 2D as well as 3D data.

paragraphs: Building a scene from partial observations requires deciding what might exist beyond what has been seen. This paper presents a method that constructs complete 2D or 3D scenes incrementally. Each addition remains globally consistent according to a learned scene prior, while accommodating both real observations and previously generated content.

The method models an active agent moving through a virtual scene. At each step, the agent either perceives an observed region or generates a plausible local completion. Such generated regions represent expectations about unseen surroundings. Because generation is statistical, the same observed evidence can support multiple imagined scenes rather than one fixed reconstruction.

The framework connects two endpoints: when real data is observed everywhere, it converges to solving simultaneous localization and mapping; when observations are absent, it can sample entirely imagined scenes from prior distributions. Experiments demonstrate effectiveness on several 2D and 3D datasets. The authors identify autonomous navigation and data generation for sample-limited applications as uses for this combination of observation, expectation, and incremental consistency.
summary.tldr: An incremental scene generator combines observations with varied plausible completions while maintaining consistency with a learned global scene model.

title: Incremental Scene Synthesis

abstract: Model-free deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have been widely used for a range of complex control tasks. However, slow convergence and sample inefficiency remain challenging problems in RL, especially when handling continuous and high-dimensional state spaces. To tackle this problem, we propose a general acceleration method for model-free, off-policy deep RL algorithms by drawing the idea underlying regularized Anderson acceleration (RAA), which is an effective approach to accelerating the solving of fixed point problems with perturbations. Specifically, we first explain how policy iteration can be applied directly with Anderson acceleration. Then we extend RAA to the case of deep RL by introducing a regularization term to control the impact of perturbation induced by function approximation errors. We further propose two strategies, i.e., progressive update and adaptive restart, to enhance the performance. The effectiveness of our method is evaluated on a variety of benchmark tasks, including Atari 2600 and MuJoCo. Experimental results show that our approach substantially improves both the learning speed and final performance of state-of-the-art deep RL algorithms.

paragraphs: Deep reinforcement learning can require many interactions and converge slowly, especially with continuous or high-dimensional states. This paper develops a general acceleration method for model-free, off-policy algorithms. It draws on regularized Anderson acceleration, an approach for speeding up the solution of fixed-point problems in the presence of perturbations.

The authors first explain how Anderson acceleration applies directly to policy iteration. They then adapt regularized acceleration to deep reinforcement learning, where approximating functions with neural networks introduces errors. A regularization term controls the influence of these perturbations. Progressive updates and adaptive restarts provide two additional strategies for improving the method's behavior.

The approach is evaluated on benchmark tasks including Atari 2600 and MuJoCo. The reported experiments show substantial improvements in both learning speed and final performance for state-of-the-art deep reinforcement-learning algorithms. The contribution connects an established acceleration idea to policy learning while explicitly accounting for approximation error. Its reported benefits concern both how quickly learning progresses and the eventual performance reached in the tested tasks.
summary.tldr: Regularized Anderson acceleration improves tested off-policy deep reinforcement-learning algorithms by speeding learning and increasing final performance.

title: Regularized Anderson Acceleration for Off-Policy Deep Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Combinatorial optimization problems are typically tackled by the branch-and-bound paradigm. We propose a new graph convolutional neural network model for learning branch-and-bound variable selection policies, which leverages the natural variable-constraint bipartite graph representation of mixed-integer linear programs. We train our model via imitation learning from the strong branching expert rule, and demonstrate on a series of hard problems that our approach produces policies that improve upon state-of-the-art machine-learning methods for branching and generalize to instances significantly larger than seen during training. Moreover, we improve for the first time over expert-designed branching rules implemented in a state-of-the-art solver on large problems. Code for reproducing all the experiments can be found at https://github.com/ds4dm/learn2branch.

paragraphs: Branch-and-bound solves combinatorial optimization problems by repeatedly dividing them into smaller search problems. Choosing which variable to branch on influences how that search proceeds. This paper learns that choice for mixed-integer linear programs, placing a neural decision policy inside the established optimization framework.

The model uses a graph with two kinds of nodes: variables and constraints. Their connections expose the problem's natural structure to a graph convolutional neural network. Training follows imitation learning, with the strong branching rule providing expert decisions. The network thus learns branching choices from an existing expert while using the relationships between variables and constraints as its representation.

Across a series of hard problems, the learned policies outperform previous machine-learning approaches to branching and transfer to instances substantially larger than those used for training. On large problems, the authors also report the first improvement over expert-designed branching rules in a state-of-the-art solver. These findings show that learned variable selection can improve an exact solver's search while generalizing beyond training-instance sizes.
summary.tldr: A graph neural network trained to imitate strong branching improves variable selection in an exact optimization solver and generalizes to larger instances.

title: Exact Combinatorial Optimization with Graph Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: We study gradient compression methods to alleviate the communication bottleneck in data-parallel distributed optimization. Despite the significant attention received, current compression schemes either do not scale well, or fail to achieve the target test accuracy. We propose a low-rank gradient compressor that can i) compress gradients rapidly, ii) efficiently aggregate the compressed gradients using all-reduce, and iii) achieve test performance on par with SGD. The proposed algorithm is the only method evaluated that achieves consistent wall-clock speedups when benchmarked against regular SGD with an optimized communication backend. We demonstrate reduced training times for convolutional networks as well as LSTMs on common datasets.

We propose a low-rank gradient compressor that can i) compress gradients rapidly, ii) efficiently aggregate the compressed gradients using all-reduce, and iii) achieve test performance on par with SGD. paragraphs: PowerSGD addresses communication costs in data-parallel training, where workers need to combine gradient information. Reducing the amount of communicated data can help, but compression must also be fast and preserve test performance. The paper focuses on meeting these requirements together so that compression translates into shorter actual training time.

The proposed method represents gradients through a low-rank compressor. Its design supports rapid compression and efficient aggregation using all-reduce, the collective communication operation used to combine information across workers. Compatibility with this aggregation mechanism matters because a compact representation is useful only if the distributed system can combine it efficiently.

In the reported evaluations, PowerSGD achieves test performance comparable to SGD and reduces training times for convolutional networks and LSTMs on common datasets. It is the only evaluated compression method to deliver consistent wall-clock speedups against regular SGD using an optimized communication backend. This comparison supports a practical efficiency claim within the tested methods and workloads, rather than merely a reduction in communication volume.
summary.tldr: PowerSGD combines fast low-rank gradient compression with efficient all-reduce to shorten tested training runs while matching SGD's test performance.

title: PowerSGD: Practical Low-Rank Gradient Compression for Distributed Optimization

abstract: Local differential privacy is a strong notion of privacy in which the provider of the data guarantees privacy by perturbing the data with random noise. In the standard application of local differential differential privacy the distribution of the noise is constant and known by the learner. In this paper we generalize this approach by allowing the provider of the data to choose the distribution of the noise without disclosing any parameters of the distribution to the learner, under the constraint that the distribution is symmetrical. We consider this problem in the unconstrained Online Convex Optimization setting with noisy feedback. In this setting the learner receives the subgradient of a loss function, perturbed by noise, and aims to achieve sublinear regret with respect to some competitor, without constraints on the norm of the competitor. We derive the first algorithms that have adaptive regret bounds in this setting, i.e. our algorithms adapt to the unknown competitor norm, unknown noise, and unknown sum of the norms of the subgradients, matching state of the art bounds in all cases.

In this paper we generalize this approach by allowing the provider of the data to choose the distribution of the noise without disclosing any parameters of the distribution to the learner, under the constraint that the distribution is symmetrical. We consider this problem in the unconstrained Online Convex Optimization setting with noisy feedback. In this setting the learner receives the subgradient of a loss function, perturbed by noise, and aims to achieve sublinear regret with respect to some competitor, without constraints on the norm of the competitor. paragraphs: Local differential privacy lets a data provider protect information by adding random noise before sharing it. Standard treatments assume that the learner knows a fixed noise distribution. This paper allows providers to choose that distribution without revealing its parameters, subject to the requirement that the distribution is symmetric.

The learning problem is unconstrained online convex optimization with noisy feedback. At each step, the learner receives a loss subgradient corrupted by noise and aims for sublinear regret relative to a competitor. The competitor's norm is unrestricted, so the learner must handle uncertainty about both the feedback and the scale of the comparison.

The authors derive algorithms with regret bounds that adapt simultaneously to the unknown competitor norm, unknown noise, and unknown accumulated subgradient norms. They report matching state-of-the-art bounds across the cases considered. The contribution combines provider control over privacy noise with theoretical learning guarantees, while retaining the explicit symmetry condition that makes this noise model part of the studied setting.
summary.tldr: Adaptive online-learning algorithms handle provider-chosen symmetric privacy noise without knowing its parameters or the competitor's norm.

title: User-Specified Local Differential Privacy in Unconstrained Adaptive Online Learning

abstract: People can learn a new concept and use it compositionally, understanding how to "blicket twice" after learning how to "blicket." In contrast, powerful sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) neural networks fail such tests of compositionality, especially when composing new concepts together with existing concepts. In this paper, I show how memory-augmented neural networks can be trained to generalize compositionally through meta seq2seq learning. In this approach, models train on a series of seq2seq problems to acquire the compositional skills needed to solve new seq2seq problems. Meta se2seq learning solves several of the SCAN tests for compositional learning and can learn to apply implicit rules to variables.
