In contrast, powerful sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) neural networks fail such tests of compositionality, especially when composing new concepts together with existing concepts. In this paper, I show how memory-augmented neural networks can be trained to generalize compositionally through meta seq2seq learning. In this approach, models train on a series of seq2seq problems to acquire the compositional skills needed to solve new seq2seq problems. Meta se2seq learning solves several of the SCAN tests for compositional learning and can learn to apply implicit rules to variables.

paragraphs: Compositional generalization means using familiar pieces of knowledge in new combinations. Learning a new action, for example, should make it possible to understand a request to repeat that action. The paper addresses the difficulty sequence-to-sequence neural networks have with this ability, particularly when combining newly learned concepts with concepts they already know.

The proposed method trains memory-augmented networks through meta sequence-to-sequence learning. Models encounter a series of sequence-to-sequence problems and learn compositional skills that can support solving new problems. This makes the training experience itself span multiple problems, so that learning how to handle new combinations becomes part of what the model acquires.

The reported results show that this approach solves several SCAN tests of compositional learning and can learn to apply implicit rules to variables. These findings support the possibility of learning reusable compositional behavior through this training setup. The stated success concerns several tests and rule-application capabilities, rather than a claim that all forms of compositional generalization have been solved.
summary.tldr: Training memory-augmented networks across sequence-to-sequence problems enables success on several tests of compositional generalization.

title: Compositional generalization through meta sequence-to-sequence learning

abstract: A conventional camera often suffers from over- or under-exposure when recording a real-world scene with a very high dynamic range (HDR). In contrast, a modulo camera with a Markov random field (MRF) based unwrapping algorithm can theoretically accomplish unbounded dynamic range but shows degenerate performances when there are modulus-intensity ambiguity, strong local contrast, and color misalignment. In this paper, we reformulate the modulo image unwrapping problem into a series of binary labeling problems and propose a modulo edge-aware model, named as UnModNet, to iteratively estimate the binary rollover masks of the modulo image for unwrapping. Experimental results show that our approach can generate 12-bit HDR images from 8-bit modulo images reliably, and runs much faster than the previous MRF-based algorithm thanks to the GPU acceleration.
originalAbstract: A conventional camera often suffers from over- or under-exposure when recording a real-world scene with a very high dynamic range (HDR). In contrast, a modulo camera with a Markov random field (MRF) based unwrapping algorithm can theoretically accomplish unbounded dynamic range but shows degenerate performances when there are modulus-intensity ambiguity, strong local contrast, and color misalignment. In this paper, we reformulate the modulo image unwrapping problem into a series of binary labeling problems and propose a modulo edge-aware model, named as UnModNet, to iteratively estimate the binary rollover masks of the modulo image for unwrapping. Experimental results show that our approach can generate 12-bit HDR images from 8-bit modulo images reliably, and runs much faster than the previous MRF-based algorithm thanks to the GPU acceleration.

paragraphs: Scenes with a wide range of brightness can produce overexposed or underexposed regions in conventional cameras. Modulo cameras offer a different route to high dynamic range, but their images must be unwrapped to recover brightness information. Earlier unwrapping based on Markov random fields degrades under intensity ambiguity, strong local contrast, and color misalignment.

UnModNet reformulates this reconstruction problem as a sequence of binary labeling tasks. Its modulo edge-aware model repeatedly estimates binary rollover masks, which guide the unwrapping of the recorded image. This breaks the reconstruction into successive decisions about rollovers while using edge information in the estimation process.

Experiments show that the approach can reliably reconstruct 12-bit high-dynamic-range images from 8-bit modulo images. It also runs substantially faster than the previous Markov-random-field method, with the speed advantage attributed to GPU acceleration. The contribution is both a reformulation of modulo unwrapping and a learned model for carrying it out, demonstrating practical reconstruction at the reported bit depths despite difficulties associated with earlier unwrapping methods.
summary.tldr: UnModNet iteratively predicts rollover masks to reconstruct 12-bit HDR images from 8-bit modulo images faster than the previous MRF-based approach.

title: UnModNet: Learning to Unwrap a Modulo Image for High Dynamic Range Imaging

abstract: We consider ReLU networks with random weights, in which the dimension decreases at each layer. We show that for most such networks, most examples $x$ admit an adversarial perturbation at an Euclidean distance of $O\left(\frac{\|x\|}{\sqrt{d}}\right)$, where $d$ is the input dimension. Moreover, this perturbation can be found via gradient flow, as well as gradient descent with sufficiently small steps. This result can be seen as an explanation to the abundance of adversarial examples, and to the fact that they are found via gradient descent.

paragraphs: This paper gives a theoretical account of adversarial perturbations in a particular family of ReLU networks. The networks have random weights, and their dimensions decrease from one layer to the next. Within that setting, the authors show that most networks have adversarial perturbations near most inputs. Both qualifications are part of the result.

The distance bound is proportional, in big-O terms, to the input's Euclidean norm divided by the square root of input dimension. Relative to the size of the input, the bound therefore shrinks as dimension grows. This formalizes how a perturbation can be small in Euclidean distance while still being adversarial for the network.

The authors also show that such perturbations can be found using gradient flow or gradient descent with sufficiently small steps. The contribution thus covers both existence and a way to locate the perturbations. Under the stated network assumptions, it offers an explanation for the prevalence of adversarial examples and the effectiveness of gradient-based searches.
summary.tldr: For most random ReLU networks with shrinking layer dimensions, most inputs admit small adversarial perturbations discoverable by gradient-based methods.

title: Most ReLU Networks Suffer from $\ell^2$ Adversarial Perturbations

abstract: Supervised learning requires a large amount of training data, limiting its application where labeled data is scarce. To compensate for data scarcity, one possible method is to utilize auxiliary tasks to provide additional supervision for the main task. Assigning and optimizing the importance weights for different auxiliary tasks remains an crucial and largely understudied research question. In this work, we propose a method to automatically reweight auxiliary tasks in order to reduce the data requirement on the main task. Specifically, we formulate the weighted likelihood function of auxiliary tasks as a surrogate prior for the main task. By adjusting the auxiliary task weights to minimize the divergence between the surrogate prior and the true prior of the main task, we obtain a more accurate prior estimation, achieving the goal of minimizing the required amount of training data for the main task and avoiding a costly grid search. In multiple experimental settings (e.g. semi-supervised learning, multi-label classification), we demonstrate that our algorithm can effectively utilize limited labeled data of the main task with the benefit of auxiliary tasks compared with previous task reweighting methods. We also show that under extreme cases with only a few extra examples (e.g. few-shot domain adaptation), our algorithm results in significant improvement over the baseline. Our code and video is available at https://sites.google.com/view/auxiliary-task-reweighting.

This paper proposes an automatic weighting method intended to reduce the amount of labeled data required for the main task.

The method interprets the weighted likelihoods of auxiliary tasks as a surrogate prior: a mathematical representation of information about the main task supplied by those tasks. It adjusts their weights to reduce divergence between this surrogate and the main task's true prior. This formulation gives task weighting a statistical objective and avoids a costly grid search over possible weight combinations.

The authors report that the method uses limited main-task labels more effectively than previous task reweighting approaches. They also report substantial improvement over a baseline in few-shot domain adaptation with only a few extra examples. These findings support automatic weighting as a practical way to make auxiliary supervision more useful under data scarcity.
summary.tldr: Automatically weighting auxiliary tasks through a surrogate-prior objective improves learning when labels for the main task are scarce.

title: Auxiliary Task Reweighting for Minimum-data Learning

abstract: Learning from indirect supervision signals is important in real-world AI applications when, often, gold labels are missing or too costly. In this paper, we develop a unified theoretical framework for multi-class classification when the supervision is provided by a variable that contains nonzero mutual information with the gold label. The nature of this problem is determined by (i) the transition probability from the gold labels to the indirect supervision variables and (ii) the learner's prior knowledge about the transition. Our framework relaxes assumptions made in the literature, and supports learning with unknown, non-invertible and instance-dependent transitions. Our theory introduces a novel concept called \emph{separation}, which characterizes the learnability and generalization bounds. We also demonstrate the application of our framework via concrete novel results in a variety of learning scenarios such as learning with superset annotations and joint supervision signals.

paragraphs: This paper asks when a classifier can learn from signals that are informative about the correct label without directly revealing it. Such supervision matters when reliable labels are unavailable or costly. The framework studies multiclass classification with an observed supervision variable that has nonzero mutual information with the true label.

Two ingredients determine the learning problem: the probabilistic relationship from true labels to observed signals, and what the learner already knows about that relationship. The framework permits transitions that are unknown, cannot be inverted, or depend on the individual example. This broadens the set of indirect supervision mechanisms that its theory can address.

The authors introduce a concept called separation to characterize learnability and generalization bounds. Thus, the analysis goes beyond asking whether an observed signal contains some label information to studying the structure relevant to learning. Applications include new results for superset annotations and joint supervision signals, placing different forms of indirect labeling within one theoretical framework.
summary.tldr: A unified theory characterizes learning from indirect label signals through their transition structure, prior knowledge, and a concept called separation.

title: Learnability with Indirect Supervision Signals

abstract: Active inference is a Bayesian framework for understanding biological intelligence. The underlying theory brings together perception and action under one single imperative: minimizing free energy. However, despite its theoretical utility in explaining intelligence, computational implementations have been restricted to low-dimensional and idealized situations. In this paper, we present a neural architecture for building deep active inference agents operating in complex, continuous state-spaces using multiple forms of Monte-Carlo (MC) sampling. For this, we introduce a number of techniques, novel to active inference. These include: i) selecting free-energy-optimal policies via MC tree search, ii) approximating this optimal policy distribution via a feed-forward `habitual' network, iii) predicting future parameter belief updates using MC dropouts and, finally, iv) optimizing state transition precision (a high-end form of attention). Our approach enables agents to learn environmental dynamics efficiently, while maintaining task performance, in relation to reward-based counterparts. We illustrate this in a new toy environment, based on the dSprites data-set, and demonstrate that active inference agents automatically create disentangled representations that are apt for modeling state transitions. In a more complex Animal-AI environment, our agents (using the same neural architecture) are able to simulate future state transitions and actions (i.e., plan), to evince reward-directed navigation - despite temporary suspension of visual input. These results show that deep active inference - equipped with MC methods - provides a flexible framework to develop biologically-inspired intelligent agents, with applications in both machine learning and cognitive science.

These demonstrations suggest that sampling-based deep active inference can support both internal models of environmental change and useful behavior in more demanding environments.
summary.tldr: Monte Carlo methods extend deep active inference to continuous environments, enabling learned dynamics, planning, and navigation during temporary loss of vision.

title: Deep active inference agents using Monte-Carlo methods

abstract: The goal of this work is to shed light on the remarkable phenomenon of "transition to linearity" of certain neural networks as their width approaches infinity. We show that the "transition to linearity'' of the model and, equivalently, constancy of the (neural) tangent kernel (NTK) result from the scaling properties of the norm of the Hessian matrix of the network as a function of the network width. We present a general framework for understanding the constancy of the tangent kernel via Hessian scaling applicable to the standard classes of neural networks. Our analysis provides a new perspective on the phenomenon of constant tangent kernel, which is different from the widely accepted "lazy training''. Furthermore, we show that the "transition to linearity" is not a general property of wide neural networks and does not hold when the last layer of the network is non-linear. It is also not necessary for successful optimization by gradient descent.

paragraphs: Some neural networks become effectively linear in their parameters as their width tends to infinity, even though their construction uses nonlinear components. This behavior is associated with a constant neural tangent kernel. The paper investigates what causes that transition and which aspects of network architecture determine whether it occurs.

The explanation centers on how the norm of the network's Hessian changes with width. The Hessian describes curvature with respect to parameters, so its scaling provides a way to understand the disappearance of nonlinear parameter dependence. The authors develop a general framework based on this relationship for standard network classes, offering a perspective distinct from the usual explanation through lazy training.

The analysis also establishes boundaries on the phenomenon. Increasing width does not make every network enter this linear regime; the transition fails when the last layer is nonlinear. Moreover, the transition is not necessary for gradient descent to optimize successfully. These findings separate network width, parameter-space linearity, and optimization success, showing why they should not automatically be treated as equivalent.
summary.tldr: Hessian scaling explains constant tangent kernels in certain wide networks, while showing that linearization is neither universal nor required for successful gradient descent.

title: On the linearity of large non-linear models: when and why the tangent kernel is constant

abstract: We study the question of obtaining last-iterate convergence rates for no-regret learning algorithms in multi-player games. We show that the optimistic gradient (OG) algorithm with a constant step-size, which is no-regret, achieves a last-iterate rate of O(1/√T) with respect to the gap function in smooth monotone games. This result addresses a question of Mertikopoulos & Zhou (2018), who asked whether extra-gradient approaches (such as OG) can be applied to achieve improved guarantees in the multi-agent learning setting. The proof of our upper bound uses a new technique centered around an adaptive choice of potential function at each iteration. We also show that the O(1/√T) rate is tight for all p-SCLI algorithms, which includes OG as a special case. As a byproduct of our lower bound analysis we additionally present a proof of a conjecture of Arjevani et al. (2015) which is more direct than previous approaches.

paragraphs: When several players learn simultaneously, guarantees about accumulated regret do not directly describe the quality of their latest decisions. This paper studies last-iterate convergence, asking how quickly the current output of a learning algorithm approaches a solution. It considers smooth monotone games and measures progress using a gap function.

The authors show that optimistic gradient with a constant step size achieves an O(1/√T) last-iterate rate, while also being a no-regret algorithm. Here T is the number of iterations. Their proof introduces an adaptive potential function chosen at each iteration, providing a way to analyze the evolving learning process and establish the rate.

A matching lower bound shows that this rate is tight for the class of p-SCLI algorithms, which includes optimistic gradient. The optimality statement therefore applies within that algorithm class and the stated game setting. The lower-bound analysis also gives a more direct proof of an existing conjecture. Together, the results clarify both the attainable last-iterate guarantee and a boundary on improving it within the considered class.
summary.tldr: Optimistic gradient achieves an O(1/√T) last-iterate rate in smooth monotone games, matching a lower bound for its broader algorithm class.

title: Tight last-iterate convergence rates for no-regret learning in multi-player games

abstract: A growing body of work has begun to study intervention design for efficient structure learning of causal directed acyclic graphs (DAGs). A typical setting is a \emph{causally sufficient} setting, i.e. a system with no latent confounders, selection bias, or feedback, when the essential graph of the observational equivalence class (EC) is given as an input and interventions are assumed to be noiseless. Most existing works focus on \textit{worst-case} or \textit{average-case} lower bounds for the number of interventions required to orient a DAG. These worst-case lower bounds only establish that the largest clique in the essential graph \textit{could} make it difficult to learn the true DAG. In this work, we develop a \textit{universal} lower bound for single-node interventions that establishes that the largest clique is \textit{always} a fundamental impediment to structure learning. Specifically, we present a decomposition of a DAG into independently orientable components through \emph{directed clique trees} and use it to prove that the number of single-node interventions necessary to orient any DAG in an EC is at least the sum of half the size of the largest cliques in each chain component of the essential graph. Moreover, we present a two-phase intervention design algorithm that, under certain conditions on the chordal skeleton, matches the optimal number of interventions up to a multiplicative logarithmic factor in the number of maximal cliques. We show via synthetic experiments that our algorithm can scale to much larger graphs than most of the related work and achieves better worst-case performance than other scalable approaches. A code base to recreate these results can be found at \url{https://github.com/csquires/dct-policy}.

This paper studies intervention design when the observational equivalence class is already supplied. summary.tldr: Directed clique trees reveal a universal intervention lower bound and support an efficient, conditionally near-optimal causal discovery strategy.

title: Active Structure Learning of Causal DAGs via Directed Clique Trees

abstract: This paper presents a new algorithm for domain generalization (DG), \textit{test-time template adjuster (T3A)}, aiming to robustify a model to unknown distribution shift. Unlike existing methods that focus on \textit{training phase}, our method focuses \textit{test phase}, i.e., correcting its prediction by itself during test time. Specifically, T3A adjusts a trained linear classifier (the last layer of deep neural networks) with the following procedure: (1) compute a pseudo-prototype representation for each class using online unlabeled data augmented by the base classifier trained in the source domains, (2) and then classify each sample based on its distance to the pseudo-prototypes. T3A is back-propagation-free and modifies only the linear layer; therefore, the increase in computational cost during inference is negligible and avoids the catastrophic failure might caused by stochastic optimization. Despite its simplicity, T3A can leverage knowledge about the target domain by using off-the-shelf test-time data and improve performance. We tested our method on four domain generalization benchmarks, namely PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, and TerraIncognita, along with various backbone networks including ResNet18, ResNet50, Big Transfer (BiT), Vision Transformers (ViT), and MLP-Mixer. The results show T3A stably improves performance on unseen domains across choices of backbone networks, and outperforms existing domain generalization methods.

paragraphs: A trained classifier may encounter images whose distribution differs from its training domains. This paper introduces the test-time template adjuster, T3A, to use incoming unlabeled data when making predictions under such shifts. It operates on the trained model's final linear classifier, providing a test-time mechanism for adjusting classification.

T3A constructs a pseudo-prototype representation for each class using online unlabeled examples together with information from the source-trained classifier. It then classifies each sample according to its distance from those prototypes. The procedure requires no backpropagation and modifies only the linear layer, giving negligible additional inference cost according to the authors. It also avoids the potential catastrophic failures associated with stochastic optimization during adaptation.

Experiments span PACS, VLCS, OfficeHome, and TerraIncognita and include convolutional, Transformer, and MLP-Mixer backbones. T3A consistently improves performance on unseen domains across the evaluated backbone choices and outperforms existing domain-generalization methods in these tests. The results support lightweight classifier adjustment as a useful way to exploit information available at deployment.
summary.tldr: T3A uses unlabeled test data to adjust class prototypes without backpropagation, improving unseen-domain classification across the evaluated models.

title: Test-Time Classifier Adjustment Module for Model-Agnostic Domain Generalization

abstract: We consider an online prediction problem in the context of network caching. Assume that multiple users are connected to several caches via a bipartite network. At any time slot, each user may request an arbitrary file chosen from a large catalog. A user's request at a slot is met if the requested file is cached in at least one of the caches connected to the user. Our objective is to predict, prefetch, and optimally distribute the files on the caches at each slot to maximize the total number of cache hits. The problem is non-trivial due to the non-convex and non-smooth nature of the objective function. In this paper, we propose $\texttt{LeadCache}$ - an efficient online caching policy based on the Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader paradigm. We show that $\texttt{LeadCache}$ is regret-optimal up to a factor of $\tilde{O}(n^{3/8}),$ where $n$ is the number of users. We design two efficient implementations of the $\texttt{LeadCache}$ policy, one based on Pipage rounding and the other based on Madow's sampling, each of which makes precisely one call to an LP-solver per iteration. Furthermore, with a Strong-Law-type assumption, we show that the total number of file fetches under $\texttt{LeadCache}$ remains almost surely finite over an infinite horizon. Finally, we derive an approximately tight regret lower bound using results from graph coloring. We conclude that the learning-based $\texttt{LeadCache}$ policy decisively outperforms the state-of-the-art caching policies both theoretically and empirically.

paragraphs: In the network studied here, users connect to several caches and can request arbitrary files from a large catalog. A request succeeds when at least one connected cache holds the file. The challenge is to predict requests and coordinate file placement across caches to maximize hits despite a nonsmooth, nonconvex objective.

LeadCache uses the Follow-the-Perturbed-Leader approach to make these online placement decisions. The authors establish regret optimality up to a factor of roughly n^(3/8), with logarithmic factors suppressed, where n is the number of users. Two efficient implementations use different rounding or sampling procedures, each requiring exactly one linear-programming solver call per iteration.

Under an additional Strong-Law-type assumption, the total number of file fetches is almost surely finite even over an infinite horizon. The paper also derives an approximately tight regret lower bound using graph coloring and reports theoretical and empirical advantages over prior caching policies. The finite-fetch result specifically depends on the stated assumption, while the broader framework addresses online caching with arbitrary requests.
summary.tldr: LeadCache coordinates online file placement with efficient implementations and regret guarantees close to optimal up to a user-dependent factor.

title: $\texttt{LeadCache}$: Regret-Optimal Caching in Networks

abstract: Tree Search (TS) is crucial to some of the most influential successes in reinforcement learning. Here, we tackle two major challenges with TS that limit its usability: \textit{distribution shift} and \textit{scalability}. We first discover and analyze a counter-intuitive phenomenon: action selection through TS and a pre-trained value function often leads to lower performance compared to the original pre-trained agent, even when having access to the exact state and reward in future steps. We show this is due to a distribution shift to areas where value estimates are highly inaccurate and analyze this effect using Extreme Value theory. To overcome this problem, we introduce a novel off-policy correction term that accounts for the mismatch between the pre-trained value and its corresponding TS policy by penalizing under-sampled trajectories. We prove that our correction eliminates the above mismatch and bound the probability of sub-optimal action selection. Our correction significantly improves pre-trained Rainbow agents without any further training, often more than doubling their scores on Atari games. Next, we address the scalability issue given by the computational complexity of exhaustive TS that scales exponentially with the tree depth. We introduce Batch-BFS: a GPU breadth-first search that advances all nodes in each depth of the tree simultaneously. Batch-BFS reduces runtime by two orders of magnitude and, beyond inference, enables also training with TS of depths that were not feasible before. We train DQN agents from scratch using TS and show improvement in several Atari games compared to both the original DQN and the more advanced Rainbow. We will share the code upon publication.

We train DQN agents from scratch using TS and show improvement in several Atari games compared to both the original DQN and the more advanced Rainbow. We will share the code upon publication.

paragraphs: Adding tree search to a trained reinforcement learning agent can unexpectedly reduce performance, even with exact future states and rewards. The authors trace this to distribution shift: search reaches regions where the pretrained value function is inaccurate. They analyze the phenomenon using Extreme Value theory, explaining why additional search can expose harmful estimation errors.

Their remedy is an off-policy correction that penalizes undersampled trajectories and accounts for the mismatch between the pretrained value function and the search policy. They prove that it removes this mismatch and bound the probability of selecting a suboptimal action. On Atari, the correction substantially improves pretrained Rainbow agents without retraining, often more than doubling their scores.

The paper also introduces Batch-BFS, which uses a GPU to advance all tree nodes at the same depth together. It reduces runtime by two orders of magnitude, making previously infeasible search depths usable for training. DQN agents trained with tree search improve on several Atari games compared with both original DQN and Rainbow.
summary.tldr: An off-policy correction makes tree search improve pretrained agents, while GPU breadth-first search greatly reduces its runtime.

title: Improve Agents without Retraining: Parallel Tree Search with Off-Policy Correction

abstract: Numerical solutions to high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) based on neural networks have seen exciting developments. This paper derives complexity estimates of the solutions of $d$-dimensional second-order elliptic PDEs in the Barron space, that is a set of functions admitting the integral of certain parametric ridge function against a probability measure on the parameters. We prove under some appropriate assumptions that if the coefficients and the source term of the elliptic PDE lie in Barron spaces, then the solution of the PDE is $\epsilon$-close with respect to the $H^1$ norm to a Barron function. Moreover, we prove dimension-explicit bounds for the Barron norm of this approximate solution, depending at most polynomially on the dimension $d$ of the PDE. As a direct consequence of the complexity estimates, the solution of the PDE can be approximated on any bounded domain by a two-layer neural network with respect to the $H^1$ norm with a dimension-explicit convergence rate.

paragraphs: The paper studies how complex a neural representation must be to approximate solutions of high-dimensional elliptic partial differential equations. It works with Barron spaces, whose functions admit integral representations built from parameterized ridge functions. This setting connects properties of the equation’s ingredients to the representational complexity of its solution.

Under appropriate assumptions, the authors prove that when the equation’s coefficients and source term belong to Barron spaces, its solution can be approximated arbitrarily closely by a Barron function in the H1 norm. They also bound the Barron norm of that approximating function, making the dependence on the equation’s dimension explicit and at most polynomial.

These estimates imply that a two-layer neural network can approximate the solution on any bounded domain with an explicit dimension-dependent convergence rate in H1. The contribution provides a conditional theoretical foundation for neural approximation of these equations. It establishes representational possibility and complexity bounds under the stated structural assumptions, rather than making a claim about all high-dimensional PDEs.
summary.tldr: Under suitable Barron-space assumptions, elliptic PDE solutions admit controlled Barron approximations and two-layer neural approximations with explicit dimension-dependent rates.

title: On the Representation of Solutions to Elliptic PDEs in Barron Spaces

abstract: Work in deep clustering focuses on finding a single partition of data. However, high-dimensional data, such as images, typically feature multiple interesting characteristics one could cluster over. For example, images of objects against a background could be clustered over the shape of the object and separately by the colour of the background. In this paper, we introduce Multi-Facet Clustering Variational Autoencoders (MFCVAE), a novel class of variational autoencoders with a hierarchy of latent variables, each with a Mixture-of-Gaussians prior, that learns multiple clusterings simultaneously, and is trained fully unsupervised and end-to-end. MFCVAE uses a progressively-trained ladder architecture which leads to highly stable performance. We provide novel theoretical results for optimising the ELBO analytically with respect to the categorical variational posterior distribution, correcting earlier influential theoretical work. On image benchmarks, we demonstrate that our approach separates out and clusters over different aspects of the data in a disentangled manner. We also show other advantages of our model: the compositionality of its latent space and that it provides controlled generation of samples.

paragraphs: A collection of images can support several meaningful groupings at once, such as object shape and background color. A clustering method that produces only one partition may overlook this multiplicity. Multi-Facet Clustering Variational Autoencoders are designed to learn several clusterings simultaneously from the same data without supervision.

The model uses a hierarchy of latent variables, each governed by a mixture-of-Gaussians prior. A progressively trained ladder architecture supports stable performance while the system is trained end to end. The paper also develops theoretical results for analytically optimizing the variational training objective with respect to the categorical posterior, correcting earlier influential theoretical work.

On image benchmarks, the authors show that the model separates and clusters different aspects of the data in a disentangled way. They also demonstrate a compositional latent space and controlled sample generation. These findings connect multiple clusterings to a generative representation: the learned internal organization supports both grouping observations along different aspects and controlling aspects of generated samples.
summary.tldr: MFCVAE learns multiple unsupervised clusterings within a hierarchical generative model, separating image aspects and supporting controlled generation.

title: Multi-Facet Clustering Variational Autoencoders

abstract: Adversarial imitation learning has become a popular framework for imitation in continuous control. Over the years, several variations of its components were proposed to enhance the performance of the learned policies as well as the sample complexity of the algorithm. In practice, these choices are rarely tested all together in rigorous empirical studies.It is therefore difficult to discuss and understand what choices, among the high-level algorithmic options as well as low-level implementation details, matter. To tackle this issue, we implement more than 50 of these choices in a generic adversarial imitation learning frameworkand investigate their impacts in a large-scale study (>500k trained agents) with both synthetic and human-generated demonstrations. We analyze the key results and highlight the most surprising findings.

paragraphs: Adversarial imitation learning is widely used to learn continuous-control behavior from demonstrations. Many proposed variations aim to improve policy performance or reduce the amount of experience required for learning. Yet these choices are rarely examined together, making it difficult to understand which algorithmic components and implementation details drive the results.

This paper builds a generic framework containing more than fifty such choices and studies their effects at large scale. The investigation includes more than half a million trained agents and uses both synthetic and human-generated demonstrations. Bringing these options into one framework enables a broad empirical examination of choices that are otherwise often evaluated in separate implementations.

The authors analyze the main results and emphasize surprising findings from the study. The contribution described in the abstract is the breadth and systematic nature of this investigation, covering both high-level algorithm design and lower-level implementation decisions. It provides an empirical basis for assessing what matters in adversarial imitation learning, with attention to both learned behavior and sample efficiency.
summary.tldr: A study of over fifty design choices and half a million trained agents systematically examines what affects adversarial imitation learning.

title: What Matters for Adversarial Imitation Learning?

abstract: Deep neural networks are known to have security issues. One particular threat is the Trojan attack. It occurs when the attackers stealthily manipulate the model's behavior through Trojaned training samples, which can later be exploited. Guided by basic neuroscientific principles, we discover subtle -- yet critical -- structural deviation characterizing Trojaned models. In our analysis we use topological tools. They allow us to model high-order dependencies in the networks, robustly compare different networks, and localize structural abnormalities. One interesting observation is that Trojaned models develop short-cuts from shallow to deep layers. Inspired by these observations, we devise a strategy for robust detection of Trojaned models. Compared to standard baselines it displays better performance on multiple benchmarks.

paragraphs: A Trojan attack manipulates training samples so that a neural network acquires behavior an attacker can exploit later. This paper investigates whether such manipulation leaves detectable structural traces inside the trained model. Guided by neuroscientific principles, the authors identify subtle differences that characterize the Trojaned networks they analyze.

Their analysis uses topological tools to represent higher-order dependencies, compare networks robustly, and locate structural abnormalities. One notable observation is the development of shortcuts between shallow and deep layers in Trojaned models. This gives the detection approach a concrete structural motivation: maliciously altered training can be associated with changes in how dependencies connect different network depths.

The authors turn these observations into a strategy for detecting Trojaned models. Across multiple benchmarks, it performs better than the standard baselines included in the comparison. The findings support internal network structure as useful evidence for detecting compromised models, with topology providing both a way to compare networks and a means of locating the abnormalities behind the decision.
summary.tldr: Topological analysis detects structural abnormalities in Trojaned networks and motivates a detector that outperforms tested baselines.

title: Topological Detection of Trojaned Neural Networks

abstract: Neural ordinary differential equations describe how values change in time. This is the reason why they gained importance in modeling sequential data, especially when the observations are made at irregular intervals. In this paper we propose an alternative by directly modeling the solution curves - the flow of an ODE - with a neural network. This immediately eliminates the need for expensive numerical solvers while still maintaining the modeling capability of neural ODEs. We propose several flow architectures suitable for different applications by establishing precise conditions on when a function defines a valid flow. Apart from computational efficiency, we also provide empirical evidence of favorable generalization performance via applications in time series modeling, forecasting, and density estimation.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations describe how a system changes over time, making them useful for sequential data with irregular observation intervals. Obtaining their trajectories requires numerical solution of the differential equation, which can be expensive. This paper proposes representing the solution curves directly with a neural network, removing that numerical-solver requirement.

The authors call these direct representations neural flows. They establish precise conditions under which a function defines a valid flow and use those conditions to construct several architectures suited to different applications. The mathematical conditions connect the proposed networks to the behavior of ODE solutions, supporting the aim of preserving neural ODE modeling capabilities.

The paper evaluates the approach through time-series modeling, forecasting, and density estimation. Alongside computational efficiency, it reports empirical evidence of favorable generalization. The findings support direct flow modeling as an alternative route to learning continuous-time behavior: the network represents the evolution itself, and the architectures are designed to satisfy the conditions needed for that representation.
summary.tldr: Neural flows directly model ODE solution curves, avoiding numerical solvers while retaining continuous-time modeling capabilities.

title: Neural Flows: Efficient Alternative to Neural ODEs

abstract: Contrastive learning (CL) can learn generalizable feature representations and achieve state-of-the-art performance of downstream tasks by finetuning a linear classifier on top of it. However, as adversarial robustness becomes vital in image classification, it remains unclear whether or not CL is able to preserve robustness to downstream tasks. The main challenge is that in the self-supervised pretraining + supervised finetuning paradigm, adversarial robustness is easily forgotten due to a learning task mismatch from pretraining to finetuning. We call such challenge 'cross-task robustness transferability'. To address the above problem, in this paper we revisit and advance CL principles through the lens of robustness enhancement. We show that (1) the design of contrastive views matters: High-frequency components of images are beneficial to improving model robustness; (2) Augmenting CL with pseudo-supervision stimulus (e.g., resorting to feature clustering) helps preserve robustness without forgetting. Equipped with our new designs, we propose AdvCL, a novel adversarial contrastive pretraining framework. We show that AdvCL is able to enhance cross-task robustness transferability without loss of model accuracy and finetuning efficiency. With a thorough experimental study, we demonstrate that AdvCL outperforms the state-of-the-art self-supervised robust learning methods across multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and STL-10) and finetuning schemes (linear evaluation and full model finetuning).

paragraphs: A representation learned through self-supervised contrastive training may lose adversarial robustness when adapted to a supervised task. The paper attributes this difficulty to the mismatch between pretraining and finetuning objectives and studies how robustness can transfer across that change. Its proposed framework, AdvCL, modifies adversarial contrastive pretraining to address the problem.

The findings support coordinating pretraining design with the later supervised task, rather than assuming robustness will automatically survive the transition.
summary.tldr: AdvCL uses high-frequency image information and pseudo-supervision to improve adversarial robustness transfer from contrastive pretraining to finetuning.

title: When does Contrastive Learning Preserve Adversarial Robustness from Pretraining to Finetuning?

abstract: Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are popular tools for studying computational dynamics in neurobiological circuits. However, due to the dizzying array of design choices, it is unclear if computational dynamics unearthed from RNNs provide reliable neurobiological inferences. Understanding the effects of design choices on RNN computation is valuable in two ways. First, invariant properties that persist in RNNs across a wide range of design choices are more likely to be candidate neurobiological mechanisms. Second, understanding what design choices lead to similar dynamical solutions reduces the burden of imposing that all design choices be totally faithful replications of biology. We focus our investigation on how RNN learning rule and task design affect RNN computation. We trained large populations of RNNs with different, but commonly used, learning rules on decision-making tasks inspired by neuroscience literature. For relatively complex tasks, we find that attractor topology is invariant to the choice of learning rule, but representational geometry is not. For simple tasks, we find that attractor topology depends on task input noise. However, when a task becomes increasingly complex, RNN attractor topology becomes invariant to input noise. Together, our results suggest that RNN dynamics are robust across learning rules but can be sensitive to the training task design, especially for simpler tasks.

They also identify simpler tasks as particularly sensitive to the input-noise choice.
summary.tldr: In the studied decision tasks, learning rules alter RNN representations while attractor topology is more stable, especially for complex tasks.

title: Learning rule influences recurrent network representations but not attractor structure in decision-making tasks

abstract: Most existing methods for conditional average treatment effect estimation are designed to estimate the effect of a single cause - only one variable can be intervened on at one time. However, many applications involve simultaneous intervention on multiple variables, which leads to multi-cause treatment effect problems. The multi-cause problem is challenging because one needs to overcome the confounding bias for a large number of treatment groups, each with a different cause combination. The combinatorial nature of the problem also leads to severe data scarcity - we only observe one factual outcome out of many potential outcomes. In this work, we propose Single-cause Perturbation (SCP), a novel two-step procedure to estimate the multi-cause treatment effect. SCP starts by augmenting the observational dataset with the estimated potential outcomes under single-cause interventions. It then performs covariate adjustment on the augmented dataset to obtain the estimator. SCP is agnostic to the exact choice of algorithm in either step. We show formally that the procedure is valid under standard assumptions in causal inference. We demonstrate the performance gain of SCP on extensive synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments.

paragraphs: Estimating the effect of changing several variables together is harder than estimating a single intervention. Each combination defines a different treatment group, creating many groups with limited observations. Confounding must also be addressed across those combinations, while each observed case reveals only its factual outcome rather than the alternatives.

Single-cause Perturbation tackles this problem in two stages. It first estimates outcomes under interventions that change one cause at a time and uses those estimates to augment the observational dataset. It then performs covariate adjustment on that augmented dataset to estimate effects involving multiple causes. Neither stage is tied to one particular estimation algorithm.

The authors formally establish the procedure’s validity under standard causal-inference assumptions and demonstrate performance gains in synthetic and semi-synthetic experiments. The assumption-dependent guarantee matters because the added outcomes are estimates, not newly observed interventions. The contribution is a flexible route from simpler single-cause estimation to a more complex multi-cause problem, using augmentation and adjustment together to address the scarcity of observations across treatment combinations.
summary.tldr: Single-cause Perturbation combines estimated single-intervention outcomes with covariate adjustment to estimate multi-cause treatment effects under causal assumptions.

title: Estimating Multi-cause Treatment Effects via Single-cause Perturbation

abstract: Reinforcement learning has achieved great success in many applications. However, sample efficiency remains a key challenge, with prominent methods requiring millions (or even billions) of environment steps to train. Recently, there has been significant progress in sample efficient image-based RL algorithms; however, consistent human-level performance on the Atari game benchmark remains an elusive goal. We propose a sample efficient model-based visual RL algorithm built on MuZero, which we name EfficientZero. Our method achieves 194.3% mean human performance and 109.0% median performance on the Atari 100k benchmark with only two hours of real-time game experience and outperforms the state SAC in some tasks on the DMControl 100k benchmark. This is the first time an algorithm achieves super-human performance on Atari games with such little data. EfficientZero's performance is also close to DQN's performance at 200 million frames while we consume 500 times less data. EfficientZero's low sample complexity and high performance can bring RL closer to real-world applicability. We implement our algorithm in an easy-to-understand manner and it is available at https://github.com/YeWR/EfficientZero. We hope it will accelerate the research of MCTS-based RL algorithms in the wider community.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning can require enormous amounts of interaction before an agent performs well. This paper targets sample efficiency in learning from images, where achieving consistent human-level Atari performance with little experience has been difficult. The authors introduce EfficientZero, a model-based visual reinforcement-learning algorithm built on MuZero.

On the Atari 100k benchmark, EfficientZero achieves mean performance of 194.3% and median performance of 109.0% relative to human performance, using experience corresponding to two hours of real-time play. These aggregate results put both the mean and median above the human reference. The paper describes this as the first superhuman Atari result with such limited data.

EfficientZero also approaches DQN's performance at 200 million frames while using 500 times less data. On some tasks in the DMControl 100k benchmark, it outperforms state SAC. These findings demonstrate substantial interaction efficiency in the evaluated settings, which the authors connect to the prospect of more practical reinforcement learning. They also provide an implementation intended to make research on Monte Carlo tree search-based reinforcement learning more accessible.
summary.tldr: EfficientZero achieves above-human mean and median Atari 100k performance with limited experience, demonstrating strong sample efficiency for model-based visual reinforcement learning.

title: Mastering Atari Games with Limited Data

abstract: Peer review systems such as conference paper review often suffer from the issue of miscalibration. Previous works on peer review calibration usually only use the ordinal information or assume simplistic reviewer scoring functions such as linear functions. In practice, applications like academic conferences often rely on manual methods, such as open discussions, to mitigate miscalibration. It remains an important question to develop algorithms that can handle different types of miscalibrations based on available prior knowledge. In this paper, we propose a flexible framework, namely \emph{least square calibration} (LSC), for selecting top candidates from peer ratings. Our framework provably performs perfect calibration from noiseless linear scoring functions under mild assumptions, yet also provides competitive calibration results when the scoring function is from broader classes beyond linear functions and with arbitrary noise. On our synthetic dataset, we empirically demonstrate that our algorithm consistently outperforms the baseline which select top papers based on the highest average ratings.

paragraphs: Peer-review scores can be miscalibrated because reviewers use rating scales differently. Selecting the highest average scores can therefore be affected by how reviewers score as well as what they think of the candidates. This paper proposes least square calibration, or LSC, as a flexible framework for selecting top candidates while accounting for different forms of miscalibration.

The framework is designed to incorporate available prior knowledge about reviewer scoring behavior. Earlier approaches often rely only on rankings or assume simple scoring functions. LSC establishes a precise guarantee for one important case: under mild assumptions, it achieves perfect calibration when scoring functions are linear and observations contain no noise.

The authors also report competitive calibration for broader classes of scoring functions with arbitrary noise, extending the method’s scope beyond the setting of the perfect-calibration result. On their synthetic dataset, LSC consistently outperforms selection by average rating. The contribution combines a conditional theoretical guarantee with empirical evidence that calibration can improve candidate selection when reviewer scores are not directly comparable.
summary.tldr: Least square calibration adjusts for reviewer scoring differences, with perfect calibration guaranteed for noiseless linear scoring under mild assumptions.

title: Least Square Calibration for Peer Reviews

abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can generate near photo realistic images in narrow domains such as human faces. Yet, modeling complex distributions of datasets such as ImageNet and COCO-Stuff remains challenging in unconditional settings. In this paper, we take inspiration from kernel density estimation techniques and introduce a non-parametric approach to modeling distributions of complex datasets. We partition the data manifold into a mixture of overlapping neighborhoods described by a datapoint and its nearest neighbors, and introduce a model, called instance-conditioned GAN (IC-GAN), which learns the distribution around each datapoint. Experimental results on ImageNet and COCO-Stuff show that IC-GAN significantly improves over unconditional models and unsupervised data partitioning baselines. Moreover, we show that IC-GAN can effortlessly transfer to datasets not seen during training by simply changing the conditioning instances, and still generate realistic images. Finally, we extend IC-GAN to the class-conditional case and show semantically controllable generation and competitive quantitative results on ImageNet; while improving over BigGAN on ImageNet-LT. Code and trained models to reproduce the reported results are available at https://github.com/facebookresearch/ic_gan.

paragraphs: Generating realistic images becomes difficult when a dataset contains many kinds of scenes and objects. Instance-conditioned GAN addresses this complexity by modeling overlapping local neighborhoods of the data. Inspired by kernel density estimation, it describes each neighborhood through an example and its nearest neighbors, then learns to generate images from the distribution around that example.

Conditioning on an individual instance gives the model a local region of the overall distribution to represent. Experiments on ImageNet and COCO-Stuff show substantial improvements over unconditional generation and unsupervised data-partitioning baselines. The results support organizing a complex dataset through overlapping neighborhoods rather than relying only on one unconditional generation setting.

The authors also demonstrate transfer to datasets unseen during training by replacing the conditioning instances, while retaining realistic outputs. An extension that includes class conditioning provides semantic control over generation. It achieves competitive quantitative results on ImageNet and improves over BigGAN on ImageNet-LT, showing that instance-based conditioning can also be combined with class information.
summary.tldr: IC-GAN models overlapping neighborhoods around individual examples to improve complex image generation and enable transfer through new conditioning instances.

title: Instance-Conditioned GAN

abstract: In this paper, we study phase retrieval under model misspecification and generative priors. In particular, we aim to estimate an $n$-dimensional signal $\mathbf{x}$ from $m$ i.i.d.~realizations of the single index model $y = f(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{x})$, where $f$ is an unknown and possibly random nonlinear link function and $\mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^n$ is a standard Gaussian vector. We make the assumption $\mathrm{Cov}[y,(\mathbf{a}^T\mathbf{x})^2] \ne 0$, which corresponds to the misspecified phase retrieval problem. In addition, the underlying signal $\mathbf{x}$ is assumed to lie in the range of an $L$-Lipschitz continuous generative model with bounded $k$-dimensional inputs. We propose a two-step approach, for which the first step plays the role of spectral initialization and the second step refines the estimated vector produced by the first step iteratively. We show that both steps enjoy a statistical rate of order $\sqrt{(k\log L)\cdot (\log m)/m}$ under suitable conditions. Experiments on image datasets are performed to demonstrate that our approach performs on par with or even significantly outperforms several competing methods.

paragraphs: The paper studies signal recovery when measurements pass a Gaussian projection of the signal through an unknown, possibly random nonlinear function. This allows the measurement relationship to be misspecified. The analysis assumes a nonzero covariance between the observed response and the squared projection, giving the observations a particular statistical connection to the signal.

The signal is also assumed to belong to the range of a Lipschitz-continuous generative model whose inputs are bounded and k-dimensional. This prior describes candidate signals through a lower-dimensional input space. The proposed recovery procedure first forms a spectral initialization, then iteratively refines the resulting estimate.

Under suitable conditions, both stages achieve a statistical rate proportional to the square root of k log L times log m divided by m, where L is the generator's Lipschitz constant and m is the measurement count. Image experiments show performance comparable to or substantially better than several competing methods. The contribution links recovery under an unknown measurement function to a structured generative signal model.
summary.tldr: A two-stage method recovers generatively structured signals from misspecified nonlinear measurements with statistical guarantees under stated conditions.

title: Misspecified Phase Retrieval with Generative Priors

abstract: Mean-Field Game (MFG) serves as a crucial mathematical framework in modeling the collective behavior of individual agents interacting stochastically with a large population. In this work, we aim at solving a challenging class of MFGs in which the differentiability of these interacting preferences may not be available to the solver, and the population is urged to converge exactly to some desired distribution. These setups are, despite being well-motivated for practical purposes, complicated enough to paralyze most (deep) numerical solvers. Nevertheless, we show that Schrödinger Bridge — as an entropy-regularized optimal transport model — can be generalized to accepting mean-field structures, hence solving these MFGs. This is achieved via the application of Forward-Backward Stochastic Differential Equations theory, which, intriguingly, leads to a computational framework with a similar structure to Temporal Difference learning. As such, it opens up novel algorithmic connections to Deep Reinforcement Learning that we leverage to facilitate practical training. We show that our proposed objective function provides necessary and sufficient conditions to the mean-field problem. Our method, named Deep Generalized Schrödinger Bridge (DeepGSB), not only outperforms prior methods in solving classical population navigation MFGs, but is also capable of solving 1000-dimensional opinion depolarization, setting a new state-of-the-art numerical solver for high-dimensional MFGs. Our code will be made available at https://github.com/ghliu/DeepGSB.

paragraphs: Mean-field games describe many agents whose individual decisions interact with the behavior of a large population. This paper targets a difficult version of that problem: the solver may lack derivatives of the interaction preferences, and the population must reach a specified final distribution exactly. Together, these requirements challenge many numerical methods.

The authors generalize the Schrödinger bridge, an entropy-regularized model of transporting distributions, to incorporate mean-field interactions. They use forward-backward stochastic differential equations to derive a computational framework resembling temporal-difference learning. That connection allows techniques from deep reinforcement learning to support practical training. They also show that their objective provides necessary and sufficient conditions for the mean-field problem.

The resulting method, DeepGSB, outperforms prior approaches on classical population-navigation problems. It also solves an opinion-depolarization problem with 1,000 dimensions. These findings demonstrate both the method's performance on established examples and its ability to tackle a high-dimensional application. The broader contribution is a bridge between population-level interaction models, distribution transport, and learning procedures that can make demanding mean-field problems computationally accessible.
summary.tldr: DeepGSB extends Schrödinger bridges to difficult mean-field games and demonstrates a solver for a 1,000-dimensional opinion-depolarization problem.

title: Deep Generalized Schrödinger Bridge

abstract: A critical challenge in multi-agent reinforcement learning(MARL) is for multiple agents to efficiently accomplish complex, long-horizon tasks. The agents often have difficulties in cooperating on common goals, dividing complex tasks, and planning through several stages to make progress. We propose to address these challenges by guiding agents with programs designed for parallelization, since programs as a representation contain rich structural and semantic information, and are widely used as abstractions for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, we introduce Efficient Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Parallel Program Guidance(E-MAPP), a novel framework that leverages parallel programs to guide multiple agents to efficiently accomplish goals that require planning over $10+$ stages. E-MAPP integrates the structural information from a parallel program, promotes the cooperative behaviors grounded in program semantics, and improves the time efficiency via a task allocator. We conduct extensive experiments on a series of challenging, long-horizon cooperative tasks in the Overcooked environment. Results show that E-MAPP outperforms strong baselines in terms of the completion rate, time efficiency, and zero-shot generalization ability by a large margin.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents can struggle when a shared goal requires many stages of action. They must divide work, coordinate their behavior, and make progress through a long plan. E-MAPP addresses these difficulties by guiding reinforcement learning with programs designed to express work that can be carried out in parallel.

The framework uses both the structure of a parallel program and the meaning of its operations. Program structure supplies information about the organization of a task, while program semantics guide cooperative behavior. A task allocator improves time efficiency by distributing work among agents. Together, these components support goals requiring planning across more than ten stages.

The authors evaluate E-MAPP on challenging cooperative tasks in the Overcooked environment. They report large improvements over strong baselines in completion rate, time efficiency, and zero-shot generalization. These findings support parallel programs as useful guidance for the tested long-horizon tasks: the program gives agents an explicit organization for cooperation, while reinforcement learning supplies the behaviors needed to carry it out.
summary.tldr: E-MAPP uses parallel programs and task allocation to help multiple reinforcement-learning agents coordinate on long, multistage tasks.

title: E-MAPP: Efficient Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with Parallel Program Guidance

abstract: It is important that consumers and regulators can verify the provenance of large neural models to evaluate their capabilities and risks. We introduce the concept of a "Proof-of-Training-Data": any protocol that allows a model trainer to convince a Verifier of the training data that produced a set of model weights. Such protocols could verify the amount and kind of data and compute used to train the model, including whether it was trained on specific harmful or beneficial data sources. We explore efficient verification strategies for Proof-of-Training-Data that are compatible with most current large-model training procedures. These include a method for the model-trainer to verifiably pre-commit to a random seed used in training, and a method that exploits models' tendency to temporarily overfit to training data in order to detect whether a given data-point was included in training. We show experimentally that our verification procedures can catch a wide variety of attacks, including all known attacks from the Proof-of-Learning literature.

paragraphs: Assessing a neural model's capabilities and risks can require knowing where its training data came from. This paper introduces Proof-of-Training-Data: protocols through which a trainer can convince a verifier which data produced a set of model weights. Such protocols could support checks on the quantity and type of training data and compute, including whether particular harmful or beneficial sources were used.

The authors explore efficient verification methods compatible with most current large-model training procedures. One lets a trainer verifiably commit in advance to a random seed used during training. Another uses the tendency of models to temporarily overfit training examples as evidence for whether a particular example was included. These methods examine aspects of the training process that can help substantiate provenance claims.

Experiments show that the verification procedures catch a wide range of attacks, including all known attacks from the Proof-of-Learning literature considered by the paper. This is evidence of resistance to those attacks, rather than a guarantee against every possible deception. The contribution provides concrete tools toward making training-data claims verifiable.
summary.tldr: Proof-of-Training-Data protocols use training-process evidence to verify data provenance and experimentally detect a wide variety of attacks.

title: Tools for Verifying Neural Models' Training Data

abstract: While diffusion models have demonstrated exceptional image generation capabilities, the iterative noise estimation process required for these models is compute-intensive and their practical implementation is limited by slow sampling speeds. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to speed up the noise estimation network by leveraging the robustness of early-stage diffusion models. Our findings indicate that inaccurate computation during the early-stage of the reverse diffusion process has minimal impact on the quality of generated images, as this stage primarily outlines the image while later stages handle the finer details that require more sensitive information. To improve computational efficiency, we combine our findings with post-training quantization (PTQ) to introduce a method that utilizes low-bit activation for the early reverse diffusion process while maintaining high-bit activation for the later stages. Experimental results show that the proposed method can accelerate the early-stage computation without sacrificing the quality of the generated images.

paragraphs: Diffusion image generation requires repeated noise-estimation computations, making sampling expensive and slow. This paper investigates whether every stage needs the same numerical precision. The authors find that inaccurate computation early in the reverse diffusion process has little effect on generated-image quality. Their explanation is that these early stages establish the image's broad outline, while later stages handle more sensitive fine details.

The proposed method combines this observation with post-training quantization. It uses low-bit activations during early reverse-diffusion steps and keeps higher-bit activations for later steps. Activations are the intermediate values computed inside the network, so changing their precision changes how those computations are represented. The precision schedule follows the reported difference in sensitivity across the generation process.

Experiments show that the approach can accelerate early-stage computation without sacrificing generated-image quality. The stated result concerns exploiting tolerance in that part of sampling, rather than establishing that all diffusion steps are equally tolerant of reduced precision. Its practical significance is a way to allocate computational precision according to when the model needs it most.
summary.tldr: Using lower-precision activations early and higher precision later can speed diffusion sampling's early computations while preserving image quality.

title: Leveraging Early-Stage Robustness in Diffusion Models for Efficient and High-Quality Image Synthesis

abstract: We present an exact Bayesian inference method for discrete statistical models, which can find exact solutions to a large class of discrete inference problems, even with infinite support and continuous priors.To express such models, we introduce a probabilistic programming language that supports discrete and continuous sampling, discrete observations, affine functions, (stochastic) branching, and conditioning on discrete events.Our key tool is *probability generating functions*:they provide a compact closed-form representation of distributions that are definable by programs, thus enabling the exact computation of posterior probabilities, expectation, variance, and higher moments.Our inference method is provably correct and fully automated in a tool called *Genfer*, which uses automatic differentiation (specifically, Taylor polynomials), but does not require computer algebra.Our experiments show that Genfer is often faster than the existing exact inference tools PSI, Dice, and Prodigy.On a range of real-world inference problems that none of these exact tools can solve, Genfer's performance is competitive with approximate Monte Carlo methods, while avoiding approximation errors.

paragraphs: Exact Bayesian inference computes posterior quantities without the approximation error associated with sampling-based estimates. This paper develops an exact method for a large class of discrete statistical models, including supported problems with infinitely many possible outcomes and continuous priors. A probabilistic programming language expresses models using sampling, discrete observations, affine functions, branching, and conditioning on discrete events.

The central representation is a probability generating function, which compactly encodes distributions described by these programs. This representation enables exact calculation of posterior probabilities, means, variances, and higher moments. The authors prove the method correct and automate it in Genfer, a tool using automatic differentiation with Taylor polynomials rather than requiring computer algebra.

Experiments show that Genfer is often faster than the existing exact tools PSI, Dice, and Prodigy. On a range of real-world problems those tools cannot solve, its performance is competitive with approximate Monte Carlo methods while avoiding their approximation errors. The findings demonstrate that exact inference can be computationally practical for the model class handled by this representation.
summary.tldr: Genfer uses probability generating functions to automate exact Bayesian inference for a broad class of discrete models.

title: Exact Bayesian Inference on Discrete Models via Probability Generating Functions: A Probabilistic Programming Approach

abstract: Predicting how different interventions will causally affect a specific individual is important in a variety of domains such as personalized medicine, public policy, and online marketing. There are a large number of methods to predict the effect of an existing intervention based on historical data from individuals who received it. However, in many settings it is important to predict the effects of novel interventions (e.g., a newly invented drug), which these methods do not address.Here, we consider zero-shot causal learning: predicting the personalized effects of a novel intervention. We propose CaML, a causal meta-learning framework which formulates the personalized prediction of each intervention's effect as a task. CaML trains a single meta-model across thousands of tasks, each constructed by sampling an intervention, its recipients, and its nonrecipients. By leveraging both intervention information (e.g., a drug's attributes) and individual features (e.g., a patient's history), CaML is able to predict the personalized effects of novel interventions that do not exist at the time of training. Experimental results on real world datasets in large-scale medical claims and cell-line perturbations demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Most strikingly, CaML's zero-shot predictions outperform even strong baselines trained directly on data from the test interventions.

paragraphs: Predicting an intervention’s effect on a particular individual is difficult when that intervention has no historical recipient data. Conventional methods typically focus on interventions already observed. This paper studies zero-shot causal learning: estimating personalized effects for new interventions, including ones that did not exist when the model was trained.

CaML treats prediction of each intervention’s personalized effect as a separate learning task. It trains one meta-model across thousands of tasks constructed by sampling an intervention, people who received it, and people who did not. The model combines information about interventions with individual features, allowing predictions to draw on patterns learned across earlier tasks.

Experiments use large-scale medical claims and cell-line perturbation datasets. In these evaluations, CaML’s zero-shot predictions outperform strong baselines that were trained directly on data from the test interventions. This is an empirical result for the studied settings. It supports the possibility that shared learning across many interventions can provide useful predictive information even before outcomes from a new intervention are available.
summary.tldr: CaML learns across intervention-specific tasks to predict personalized effects of new interventions without training on their outcomes.

title: Zero-shot causal learning

abstract: Noisy marginals are a common form of confidentiality-protecting data release and are useful for many downstream tasks such as contingency table analysis, construction of Bayesian networks, and even synthetic data generation. Privacy mechanisms that provide unbiased noisy answers to linear queries (such as marginals) are known as matrix mechanisms.We propose ResidualPlanner, a matrix mechanism for marginals with Gaussian noise that is both optimal and scalable. ResidualPlanner can optimize for many loss functions that can be written as a convex function of marginal variances (prior work was restricted to just one predefined objective function). ResidualPlanner can optimize the accuracy of marginals in large scale settings in seconds, even when the previous state of the art (HDMM) runs out of memory. It even runs on datasets with 100 attributes in a couple of minutes. Furthermore ResidualPlanner can efficiently compute variance/covariance values for each marginal (prior methods quickly run out of memory, even for relatively small datasets).
