paragraphs: Aligning a pretrained generative model with human preferences requires changing its outputs while retaining information from its original distribution. This paper focuses on flow matching models and the difficulty of combining efficient adaptation with probabilistically principled preservation of that prior. VGG-Flow approaches the problem through optimal control theory.

A flow model generates samples using a velocity field. The central idea is to match the difference between the adapted and pretrained velocity fields to the gradient of a value function. This turns the desired change in generative behavior into a gradient-matching objective. The method also uses first-order information from the reward model to inform adaptation.

A heuristic initialization of the value function helps the method adapt quickly. Experiments on Stable Diffusion 3 show effective, prior-preserving alignment under limited computational budgets. The empirical result supports the combined design: an optimal-control formulation supplies the relationship between velocity changes and value gradients, while reward information and initialization make adaptation practical. The demonstrated outcome concerns the tested text-to-image model and computational setting.
summary.tldr: VGG-Flow uses value-function gradients to efficiently align flow matching models while preserving information from their pretrained distribution.

title: Value Gradient Guidance for Flow Matching Alignment

abstract: Diffusion Transformers have emerged as the foundation for vision generative models, but their scalability is limited by the high cost of hyperparameter (HP) tuning at large scales. Recently, Maximal Update Parametrization ($\mu$P) was proposed for vanilla Transformers, which enables stable HP transfer from small to large language models, and dramatically reduces tuning costs. However, it remains unclear whether $\mu$P of vanilla Transformers extends to diffusion Transformers, which differ architecturally and objectively. In this work, we generalize $\mu$P to diffusion Transformers and validate its effectiveness through large-scale experiments. First, we rigorously prove that $\mu$P of mainstream diffusion Transformers, including DiT, U-ViT, PixArt-$\alpha$, and MMDiT, aligns with that of the vanilla Transformer, enabling the direct application of existing $\mu$P methodologies. Leveraging this result, we systematically demonstrate that DiT-$\mu$P enjoys robust HP transferability. Notably, DiT-XL-2-$\mu$P with transferred learning rate achieves 2.9$\times$ faster convergence than the original DiT-XL-2. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of $\mu$P on text-to-image generation by scaling PixArt-$\alpha$ from 0.04B to 0.61B and MMDiT from 0.18B to 18B. In both cases, models under $\mu$P outperform their respective baselines while requiring small tuning cost—only 5.5% of one training run for PixArt-$\alpha$ and 3% of consumption by human experts for MMDiT-18B. \textit{These results establish $\mu$P as a principled and efficient framework for scaling diffusion Transformers}.

paragraphs: Scaling diffusion transformers is expensive partly because hyperparameters must be tuned at large model sizes. Maximal Update Parametrization, or μP, enables hyperparameter transfer from smaller language transformers, but diffusion transformers differ in architecture and objective. This paper establishes when the same parameterization principles carry over to those generative models.

The authors prove that μP for DiT, U-ViT, PixArt-α, and MMDiT aligns with the formulation for conventional transformers. Experiments then demonstrate robust hyperparameter transfer for DiT. In one reported comparison, DiT-XL-2 using μP and a transferred learning rate converges 2.9 times faster than the original DiT-XL-2.

The study also scales PixArt-α from 0.04 billion to 0.61 billion parameters and MMDiT from 0.18 billion to 18 billion. Both μP models outperform their respective baselines. Reported tuning costs are 5.5% of one training run for PixArt-α and 3% of the human-expert tuning consumption for MMDiT-18B. These results support small-model tuning as an efficient route to configuring the tested larger diffusion transformers.
summary.tldr: The paper extends μP to major diffusion-transformer architectures, enabling effective small-to-large hyperparameter transfer and substantially cheaper tuning.

title: Scaling Diffusion Transformers Efficiently via $\mu$P

abstract: With the rise of the fine-tuned–pretrained paradigm, storing numerous fine-tuned models for multi-tasking creates significant storage overhead. Delta compression alleviates this by storing only the pretrained model and the highly compressed delta weights (the differences between fine-tuned and pretrained model weights). However, existing methods fail to maintain both high compression and performance, and often rely on data. To address these challenges, we propose UltraDelta, the first data-free delta compression pipeline that achieves both ultra-high compression and strong performance. UltraDelta is designed to minimize redundancy, maximize information, and stabilize performance across inter-layer, intra-layer, and global dimensions, using three key components: (1) Variance-Based Mixed Sparsity Allocation assigns sparsity based on variance, giving lower sparsity to high-variance layers to preserve inter-layer information. (2) Distribution-Aware Compression applies uniform quantization and then groups parameters by value, followed by group-wise pruning, to better preserve intra-layer distribution. (3) Trace-Norm-Guided Rescaling uses the trace norm of delta weights to estimate a global rescaling factor, improving model stability under higher compression. Extensive experiments across (a) large language models (fine-tuned on LLaMA-2 7B and 13B) with up to 50$\times$ compression, (b) general NLP models (RoBERTa-base, T5-base) with up to 224$\times$ compression, (c) vision models (ViT-B/32, ViT-L/14) with up to 132$\times$ compression, and (d) multi-modal models (BEiT-3) with 18$\times$ compression, demonstrate that UltraDelta consistently outperforms existing methods, especially under ultra-high compression. Code is available at https://github.com/xiaohuiwang000/UltraDelta.

paragraphs: Keeping many fine-tuned models can require substantial storage even when they share a pretrained starting point. Delta compression instead stores that shared model plus compressed differences for each fine-tuned version. UltraDelta targets the difficulty of compressing those differences aggressively while preserving performance, using a pipeline that does not require data.

Its three components address different levels of information loss. Variance-based allocation retains more weights in high-variance layers. Distribution-aware compression quantizes values, groups similar parameters, and prunes within those groups to better preserve their distribution. Finally, trace-norm-guided rescaling estimates a global adjustment intended to stabilize the compressed model’s behavior.

Experiments report compression of up to 50 times for the tested LLaMA-2 fine-tunes, 224 times for general NLP models, 132 times for vision models, and 18 times for BEiT-3. UltraDelta consistently outperforms existing methods in these evaluations, particularly at very high compression. These results support coordinating decisions across layers, within layers, and globally when compressing the changes introduced by fine-tuning.
summary.tldr: UltraDelta compresses fine-tuning weight differences without data by coordinating sparsity, quantization, pruning, and global rescaling.

title: Breaking the Compression Ceiling: Data-Free Pipeline for Ultra-Efficient Delta Compression

abstract: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs), as a biologically inspired neural network architecture, have garnered significant attention due to their exceptional energy efficiency and increasing potential for various applications. In this work, we extend the use of SNNs to neural rendering tasks and introduce Spik-NeRF (Spiking Neural Radiance Fields). We observe that the binary spike activation map of traditional SNNs lacks sufficient information capacity, leading to information loss and a subsequent decline in the performance of spiking neural rendering models. To address this limitation, we propose the use of ternary spike neurons, which enhance the information-carrying capacity in the spiking neural rendering model. With ternary spike neurons, Spik-NeRF achieves performance that is on par with, or nearly identical to, traditional ANN-based rendering models. Additionally, we present a re-parameterization technique for inference that allows Spik-NeRF with ternary spike neurons to retain the event-driven, multiplication-free advantages typical of binary spike neurons. Furthermore, to further boost the performance of Spik-NeRF, we employ a distillation method, using an ANN-based NeRF to guide the training of our Spik-NeRF model, which is more compatible with the ternary neurons compared to the standard binary neurons. We evaluate Spik-NeRF on both realistic and synthetic scenes, and the experimental results demonstrate that Spik-NeRF achieves rendering performance comparable to ANN-based NeRF models.

paragraphs: Spik-NeRF applies spiking neural networks to neural rendering. The paper identifies a specific obstacle: traditional binary spike activations carry too little information for this setting, causing information loss and weaker rendering. Its approach increases the expressive capacity of the spike representation while preserving computational properties that make spiking networks attractive.

The model uses ternary spike neurons, giving activations three possible states. An inference-time re-parameterization allows these neurons to retain event-driven, multiplication-free computation. Training also uses distillation from a conventional neural radiance field, which guides the spiking model. The authors find this guidance more compatible with ternary neurons than with standard binary ones.

Evaluations on realistic and synthetic scenes show rendering quality comparable to conventional neural-network-based NeRF models. The findings support ternary spikes as a way to address the information bottleneck in spiking neural rendering. The contribution combines a richer activation representation, an inference transformation, and teacher-guided training; the stated results establish comparable rendering performance while retaining the specified computational advantages of spike-based inference.
summary.tldr: Spik-NeRF uses ternary spikes and distillation to match conventional NeRF rendering quality while retaining event-driven, multiplication-free inference.

title: Spik-NeRF: Spiking Neural Networks for Neural Radiance Fields

abstract: We address the problem of Gaussian Process (GP) optimization in the presence of unknown and potentially varying adversarial perturbations. Unlike traditional robust optimization approaches that focus on maximizing performance under worst-case scenarios, we consider a robust satisficing objective, where the goal is to consistently achieve a predefined performance threshold $\tau$, even under adversarial conditions. We propose two novel algorithms based on distinct formulations of robust satisficing, and show that they are instances of a general robust satisficing framework. Further, each algorithm offers different guarantees depending on the nature of the adversary. Specifically, we derive two regret bounds: one that is sublinear over time, assuming certain conditions on the adversary and the satisficing threshold $\tau$, and another that scales with the perturbation magnitude but requires no assumptions on the adversary. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms the established robust optimization methods in achieving the satisficing objective, particularly when the ambiguity set of the robust optimization framework is inaccurately specified.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization with Gaussian processes when an adversary can introduce unknown and potentially changing perturbations. Its objective is robust satisficing: repeatedly achieving a chosen performance threshold despite those disturbances. This changes the target from maximizing worst-case performance to reliably reaching a level considered sufficient.

The authors propose two algorithms based on different formulations of that objective and place both within a general framework. Their theoretical guarantees reflect different assumptions. One regret bound grows sublinearly with time when conditions on the adversary and the threshold hold. Another scales with the magnitude of the perturbations and requires no assumptions on the adversary.

Experiments show that the proposed approach achieves the satisficing objective more effectively than established robust optimization methods. The advantage is particularly evident when the comparison framework's ambiguity set, which describes the uncertainty it considers, is specified inaccurately. The findings make threshold selection central to the problem and show how different guarantees accommodate different levels of knowledge about adversarial behavior.
summary.tldr: Two Gaussian-process algorithms target reliable threshold attainment under adversarial perturbations, with guarantees that depend on different assumptions about the adversary.

title: Robust Satisficing Gaussian Process Bandits Under Adversarial Attacks

abstract: Scenario-based testing is essential for validating the performance of autonomous driving (AD) systems. However, such testing is limited by the scarcity of long-tailed, safety-critical scenarios in existing datasets collected in the real world. To tackle the data issue, we propose the Adv-BMT framework, which augments real-world scenarios with diverse and realistic adversarial interactions. The core component of Adv-BMT is a bidirectional motion transformer (BMT) model to perform inverse traffic motion predictions, which takes the last frame of the scenario as input and reconstruct the traffic in the inverse of chronological order, till the initial time step. The Adv-BMT framework is a two-stage pipeline: it first conducts adversarial initializations and then inverse motion predictions. Different from previous work, we do not need any collision data for pretraining and are still able to generate realistic and diverse collision interactions. Our experimental results validate the quality of generated collision scenarios by Adv-BMT: training in our augmented dataset would reduce episode collision rates by 20\% compared to previous work. The code will be made available.

paragraphs: Autonomous driving systems need testing on dangerous traffic situations, but real-world datasets contain relatively few of these rare events. Adv-BMT addresses this shortage by augmenting recorded scenarios with realistic, varied adversarial interactions. The goal is to supply challenging situations that can help evaluate and train driving systems.

The framework constructs scenarios in two stages. It first creates adversarial initializations, then uses a bidirectional motion transformer to predict traffic motion backward. Starting from the scenario's final frame, the model reconstructs earlier frames until it reaches the beginning. This reverses the usual chronological prediction direction and provides a way to generate the traffic interactions leading into a challenging final situation.

The authors report that realistic and diverse collision interactions can be generated without collision data for pretraining. In their experiments, training with the augmented dataset reduces episode collision rates by 20% compared with previous work. This result connects scenario generation to a downstream training benefit, suggesting that the generated interactions provide useful experience with situations that ordinary driving datasets rarely capture.
summary.tldr: Adv-BMT generates challenging traffic scenarios backward from final frames, with augmented training reducing episode collision rates by 20% in the reported comparison.

title: Adv-BMT: Bidirectional Motion Transformer for Safety-Critical Traffic Scenario Generation

abstract: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has proven effective for training large language models (LLMs) on complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem solving. A prerequisite for the scalability of RLVR is a high-quality problem set with precise and verifiable answers. However, the scarcity of well-crafted human-labeled math problems and limited-verification answers in existing distillation-oriented synthetic datasets limit their effectiveness in RL. Additionally, most problem synthesis strategies indiscriminately expand the problem set without considering the model’s capabilities, leading to low efficiency in generating useful questions. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a Self-aware Weakness-driven problem Synthesis framework (SwS) that systematically identifies model deficiencies and leverages them for problem augmentation. Specifically, we define weaknesses as questions that the model consistently fails to learn through its iterative sampling during RL training. We then extract the core concepts from these failure cases and synthesize new problems to strengthen the model's weak areas in subsequent augmented training, enabling it to focus on and gradually overcome its weaknesses. Without relying on external knowledge distillation, our framework enables robust generalization by empowering the model to self-identify and address its weaknesses in RL, yielding average performance gains of 10% and 7.7% on 7B and 32B models across eight mainstream reasoning benchmarks. Our code and data are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/SwS-E6F5/

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards needs problems with precise, checkable answers. Simply generating more questions can be inefficient when those questions do not address what a model needs to learn. SwS makes problem synthesis responsive to the model's observed weaknesses during reasoning training.

The framework defines weaknesses as questions the model repeatedly fails to learn through iterative sampling during reinforcement learning. It extracts the core concepts from those persistent failures and generates additional problems focused on them. Subsequent augmented training then targets these weak areas. This creates a feedback process in which training behavior determines what new material is synthesized.

The authors report average performance gains of 10% for 7-billion-parameter models and 7.7% for 32-billion-parameter models across eight reasoning benchmarks, without external knowledge distillation. These results support using a model's own failure history to guide data augmentation. The approach matters because it treats the usefulness of a new question as dependent on the learner's current capabilities, connecting problem generation directly to training needs.
summary.tldr: SwS generates new reasoning problems from persistent training failures to target model weaknesses without external distillation.

title: SwS: Self-aware Weakness-driven Problem Synthesis in Reinforcement Learning for LLM Reasoning

abstract: Advancing code reasoning in large language models (LLMs) is fundamentally limited by the scarcity of high-difficulty datasets, especially those with verifiable input-output test cases necessary for rigorous solution validation at scale. We introduce rStar-Coder, which significantly improves LLM code reasoning capabilities by constructing a large-scale, verified dataset of 418K competition-level code problems, 580K long-reasoning solutions along with rich test cases of varying difficulty. This is achieved through three core contributions: (1) we curate competitive programming code problems and solutions to synthesize new, solvable problems; (2) we introduce a reliable input-output test case synthesis pipeline that decouples the generation into a three-step input generation method and a mutual verification mechanism for effective output labeling; (3) we augment problems with high-quality, test-case-verified long-reasoning solutions. Extensive experiments on Qwen models (1.5B-14B) across various code reasoning benchmarks demonstrate the superiority of rStar-Coder dataset, achieving leading performance comparable to frontier reasoning LLMs with significantly smaller model sizes. On LiveCodeBench, rStar-Coder improves Qwen2.5-7B from 17.4% to an impressive 57.3%, and Qwen2.5-14B from 23.3% to 62.5%, surpassing o3-mini (low) by 3.1%. On the more challenging USA Computing Olympiad, our 7B model achieves an average pass@1 accuracy of 16.15%, outperforming the frontier-level QWQ-32B. rStar-Coder dataset is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/microsoft/rStar-Coder.

paragraphs: Training strong code-reasoning models requires difficult problems and reliable ways to check solutions. rStar-Coder addresses both needs with a dataset of 418,000 competition-level problems and 580,000 long-reasoning solutions, accompanied by test cases of varying difficulty. The emphasis on verification makes checking generated solutions a central part of data construction.

The pipeline starts from curated competitive programming problems and solutions to synthesize new solvable problems. It generates test inputs through a three-step procedure and uses mutual verification to label outputs. Problems are then augmented with long-reasoning solutions verified against test cases, connecting the reasoning examples to executable checks.

Experiments train Qwen models ranging from 1.5 to 14 billion parameters. On LiveCodeBench, the reported scores rise from 17.4% to 57.3% for Qwen2.5-7B and from 23.3% to 62.5% for Qwen2.5-14B. A 7B model also exceeds QWQ-32B on the tested USA Computing Olympiad evaluation. These results show substantial benefits from the verified dataset, including competitive performance against larger reasoning models on the reported benchmarks.
summary.tldr: rStar-Coder pairs large-scale competition problems with verified tests and reasoning solutions, substantially improving Qwen code-reasoning performance.

title: rStar-Coder: Scaling Competitive Code Reasoning with a Large-Scale Verified Dataset

abstract: We introduce a novel framework for differentially private (DP) statistical estimation via data truncation, addressing a key challenge in DP estimation when the data support is unbounded. Traditional approaches rely on problem-specific sensitivity analysis, limiting their applicability. By leveraging techniques from truncated statistics, we develop computationally efficient DP estimators for exponential family distributions, including Gaussian mean and covariance estimation, achieving near-optimal sample complexity. Previous works on exponential families only consider bounded or one-dimensional families. Our approach mitigates sensitivity through truncation while carefully correcting for the introduced bias using maximum likelihood estimation and DP stochastic gradient descent. Along the way, we establish improved uniform convergence guarantees for the log-likelihood function of exponential families, which may be of independent interest. Our results provide a general blueprint for DP algorithm design via truncated statistics.

paragraphs: Differentially private estimation becomes difficult when data values are unbounded, because individual observations can have large effects on the result. Traditional solutions often require sensitivity analyses tailored to each statistical problem. This paper develops a more general framework that uses data truncation to control sensitivity while explicitly accounting for the distortion that truncation introduces.

The method combines tools from truncated statistics with maximum likelihood estimation and differentially private stochastic gradient descent. Truncation helps limit sensitivity, while the estimation procedure corrects the resulting bias. The authors construct computationally efficient estimators for exponential-family distributions, including estimation of Gaussian means and covariances, and obtain near-optimal sample complexity.

The stated scope extends beyond earlier exponential-family work limited to bounded or one-dimensional families. The analysis also establishes improved uniform convergence guarantees for exponential-family log-likelihood functions, a theoretical result that may have uses beyond this framework. Together, the results show how controlling extreme observations and correcting their statistical consequences can support a broader approach to private estimation.
summary.tldr: The paper combines truncation with bias correction to build efficient private estimators for unbounded exponential-family distributions.

title: Private Statistical Estimation via Truncation

abstract: Dynamic graphs exhibit complex temporal dynamics due to the interplay between evolving node features and changing network structures. Recently, Graph Neural Controlled Differential Equations (Graph Neural CDEs) successfully adapted Neural CDEs from paths on Euclidean domains to paths on graph domains. Building on this foundation, we introduce \textit{Permutation Equivariant Graph Neural CDEs}, which project Graph Neural CDEs onto permutation equivariant function spaces. This significantly reduces the model's parameter count without compromising representational power, resulting in more efficient training and improved generalisation. We empirically demonstrate the advantages of our approach through experiments on simulated dynamical systems and real-world tasks, showing improved performance in both interpolation and extrapolation scenarios.

paragraphs: Dynamic graphs change in two interacting ways: the features of their nodes evolve, and connections between nodes can change. Graph Neural Controlled Differential Equations model these temporal paths on graph domains. This paper builds on that approach by incorporating permutation equivariance, a symmetry that makes the model respond consistently when nodes are relabeled.

The proposed method projects Graph Neural CDEs into a space of functions with that symmetry. Relabeling a graph should relabel the corresponding representation in the same way. Restricting the model to this function space substantially reduces its parameter count, while the authors report that it retains representational power. The architectural constraint therefore provides a route to greater efficiency without sacrificing the stated modeling capability.

Experiments cover simulated dynamical systems and real-world tasks. They show more efficient training, improved generalization, and better performance in both interpolation and extrapolation scenarios. The findings support using graph symmetry directly in continuous-time representation learning, especially when the objective includes learning temporal behavior that extends beyond the observed examples.
summary.tldr: Permutation-equivariant Graph Neural CDEs reduce parameter counts while preserving representational power and improving empirical temporal generalization.

title: Permutation Equivariant Neural Controlled Differential Equations for Dynamic Graph Representation Learning

abstract: Although data that can be naturally represented as graphs is widespread in real-world applications across diverse industries, popular graph ML benchmarks for node property prediction only cover a surprisingly narrow set of data domains, and graph neural networks (GNNs) are often evaluated on just a few academic citation networks. This issue is particularly pressing in light of the recent growing interest in designing graph foundation models. These models are supposed to be able to transfer to diverse graph datasets from different domains, and yet the proposed graph foundation models are often evaluated on a very limited set of datasets from narrow applications. To alleviate this issue, we introduce GraphLand: a benchmark of 14 diverse graph datasets for node property prediction from a range of different industrial applications. GraphLand allows evaluating graph ML models on a wide range of graphs with diverse sizes, structural characteristics, and feature sets, all in a unified setting. Further, GraphLand allows investigating such previously underexplored research questions as how realistic temporal distributional shifts under transductive and inductive settings influence graph ML model performance. To mimic realistic industrial settings, we use GraphLand to compare GNNs with gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT) models that are popular in industrial applications and show that GBDTs provided with additional graph-based input features can sometimes be very strong baselines. Further, we evaluate currently available general-purpose graph foundation models and find that they fail to produce competitive results on our proposed datasets.

paragraphs: Graph learning models are often evaluated on a small selection of academic citation networks, despite their intended use across many industries. GraphLand broadens that evaluation with 14 industrial graph datasets for predicting properties of individual nodes. The datasets vary in size, connectivity structure, and available features within a unified benchmark.

The benchmark also supports studying distribution changes over time. It covers both transductive and inductive settings, allowing researchers to examine temporal shifts under different conditions for applying a learned model. This matters especially for graph foundation models, whose proposed value includes transferring across datasets and application domains.

The authors compare graph neural networks with gradient-boosted decision trees, including trees supplied with additional graph-derived features. Those augmented tree models sometimes provide strong baselines. The evaluated general-purpose graph foundation models fail to achieve competitive results on these datasets. Together, the findings show why broader industrial evaluation can change the apparent strength of methods and why established industrial models deserve inclusion in comparisons.
summary.tldr: GraphLand tests graph learning on 14 industrial datasets, revealing strong tree-based baselines and weaknesses in evaluated graph foundation models.

title: GraphLand: Evaluating Graph Machine Learning Models on Diverse Industrial Data

abstract: Finetuning provides a scalable and cost-effective means of customizing language models for specific tasks or response styles, with greater reliability than prompting or in-context learning. In contrast, the conventional wisdom is that injecting knowledge via finetuning results in brittle performance and poor generalization. We argue that the dichotomy of "task customization" (e.g., instruction tuning) and "knowledge injection" (e.g., teaching new facts) is a distinction without a difference. We instead identify concrete factors that explain the heterogeneous effectiveness observed with finetuning. To this end, we conduct a large-scale experimental study of finetuning the frontier Gemini v1.5 model family on a spectrum of datasets that are artificially engineered to interpolate between the strengths and failure modes of finetuning. Our findings indicate that question-answer training data formats provide much stronger knowledge generalization than document/article-style training data, numerical information can be harder for finetuning to retain than categorical information, and models struggle to apply finetuned knowledge during multi-step reasoning even when trained on similar examples---all factors that render ``knowledge injection'' to be especially difficult, even after controlling for considerations like data augmentation and information volume. On the other hand, our findings also indicate that it is not fundamentally more difficult to finetune information about a real-world event than information about writing style.

The authors conduct a large experimental study with the Gemini v1.5 family, using deliberately constructed datasets that span conditions where finetuning works well and conditions where it struggles.

The experiments also indicate that learning information about a real event is not fundamentally harder than learning information about writing style. The practical implication is to evaluate data format, information type, and required reasoning together when assessing what finetuning can accomplish.
summary.tldr: Finetuning outcomes depend on training format, information type, and reasoning demands more concretely than on a simple distinction between style and facts.

title: From Style to Facts: Mapping the Boundaries of Knowledge Injection with Finetuning

abstract: Training large language models (LLMs) from scratch can yield models with unique functionalities and strengths, but it is costly and often leads to redundant capabilities. A more cost-effective alternative is to fuse existing pre-trained LLMs with different architectures into a more powerful model. However, a key challenge in existing model fusion is their dependence on manually predefined vocabulary alignment, which may not generalize well across diverse contexts, leading to performance degradation in several evaluation. To solve this, we draw inspiration from distribution learning and propose the probabilistic token alignment method as a general and soft mapping for alignment, named as PTA-LLM. Our approach innovatively reformulates token alignment into a classic mathematical problem: optimal transport, seamlessly leveraging distribution-aware learning to facilitate more coherent model fusion. Apart from its inherent generality, PTA-LLM exhibits interpretability from a distributional perspective, offering insights into the essence of the token alignment. Empirical results demonstrate that probabilistic token alignment enhances the target model's performance across multiple capabilities.

paragraphs: Combining pretrained language models offers a way to bring together existing capabilities without training another model from scratch. A major obstacle is aligning the vocabularies of models with different architectures. Manually specified token correspondences can work unevenly across contexts, which the paper identifies as a source of degraded fusion performance.

PTA-LLM replaces rigid predefined alignment with a probabilistic, soft mapping. It formulates token alignment as an optimal transport problem, using information about distributions to establish correspondences. The central idea is to make vocabulary alignment sensitive to distributional structure, giving fusion a more general way to relate the tokens used by different models.

The distributional formulation also makes the alignment interpretable from the perspective of how those distributions are matched. Empirical evaluations show that the method improves the target model across multiple capabilities. These findings support token alignment as an important component of successful model fusion: improving the correspondence between vocabularies can help transfer capabilities more coherently, without requiring the abstract’s results to imply universal gains for every possible model combination.
summary.tldr: PTA-LLM uses optimal transport to learn soft vocabulary alignments, improving the evaluated target model across multiple capabilities.

title: Probabilistic Token Alignment for Large Language Model Fusion

abstract: Recent advances in *inverse problem* solving have increasingly adopted flow *priors* over diffusion models due to their ability to construct straight probability paths from noise to data, thereby enhancing efficiency in both training and inference. However, current flow-based inverse solvers face two primary limitations: (i) they operate directly in pixel space, which demands heavy computational resources for training and restricts scalability to high-resolution images, and (ii) they employ guidance strategies with *prior*-agnostic posterior covariances, which can weaken alignment with the generative trajectory and degrade posterior coverage. In this paper, we propose **LFlow** (**L**atent Refinement via **Flow**s), a *training-free* framework for solving linear inverse problems via pretrained latent flow priors. LFlow leverages the efficiency of flow matching to perform ODE sampling in latent space along an optimal path. This latent formulation further allows us to introduce a theoretically grounded posterior covariance, derived from the optimal vector field, enabling effective flow guidance. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art latent diffusion solvers in reconstruction quality across most tasks.

paragraphs: Linear inverse problems involve reconstructing an underlying signal or image from measurements linked to it by a linear process. Generative priors help guide that reconstruction. The paper identifies two difficulties in existing flow-based solvers: expensive operation directly in pixel space and guidance that uses posterior covariance estimates without accounting for the generative prior.

LFlow uses pretrained latent flow priors to solve these problems without additional training. It performs sampling by following an ordinary differential equation in latent space, taking advantage of the efficient paths provided by flow matching. Working in this representation also supports a theoretically grounded posterior covariance derived from the optimal vector field, giving the guidance information tied to the flow itself.

Experiments show better reconstruction quality than state-of-the-art latent diffusion solvers across most evaluated tasks. The qualification matters: the reported advantage is broad within the evaluation but is not stated for every task. The method combines a more scalable representation with guidance designed to align better with the generative trajectory and its posterior structure.
summary.tldr: LFlow solves linear inverse problems without additional training by combining pretrained latent flows with guidance derived from their vector field.

title: Latent Refinement via Flow Matching for Training-free Linear Inverse Problem Solving

abstract: In this paper, we develop a novel algorithm for constructing time-uniform, asymptotic confidence sequences for quantiles under local differential privacy (LDP). The procedure combines dynamically chained parallel stochastic gradient descent (P-SGD) with a randomized response mechanism, thereby guaranteeing privacy protection while simultaneously estimating the target quantile and its variance. A strong Gaussian approximation for the proposed estimator yields asymptotically anytime-valid confidence sequences whose widths obey the law of the iterated logarithm (LIL). Moreover, the method is fully online, offering high computational efficiency and requiring only $\mathcal{O}(\kappa)$ memory, where $\kappa$ denotes the number of chains and is much smaller than the sample size. Rigorous mathematical proofs and extensive numerical experiments demonstrate the theoretical soundness and practical effectiveness of the algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate a quantile while protecting individual data through local differential privacy and tracking uncertainty as observations arrive. Its target is a confidence sequence: a succession of uncertainty intervals designed for monitoring over time. The stated validity is asymptotic, an important qualification to its anytime interpretation.

The algorithm combines dynamically chained parallel stochastic gradient descent with randomized response. The privacy mechanism protects the data, while the online procedure jointly estimates the target quantile and the variance of its estimator. Estimating both quantities allows the method to produce an uncertainty assessment alongside its changing quantile estimate.

A strong Gaussian approximation supports the asymptotically anytime-valid confidence sequences, whose widths follow law-of-the-iterated-logarithm behavior. The method requires only O(κ) memory, where κ is the number of chains and is much smaller than the sample size. Mathematical proofs and numerical experiments support the procedure, connecting privacy protection, ongoing statistical inference, and efficient processing in a single online algorithm.
summary.tldr: The paper develops a memory-efficient online quantile estimator with local privacy and asymptotically anytime-valid confidence sequences.

title: Time-uniform and Asymptotic Confidence Sequence of Quantile under Local Differential Privacy

abstract: Reasoning has substantially improved the performance of large language models (LLMs) on complicated tasks. Central to the current reasoning studies, Process Reward Models (PRMs) offer a fine-grained evaluation of intermediate reasoning steps and guide the reasoning process. However, extending PRMs to multimodal large language models (MLLMs) introduces challenges. Since multimodal reasoning covers a wider range of tasks compared to text-only scenarios, the resulting distribution shift from the training to testing sets is more severe, leading to greater generalization difficulty. Training a reliable multimodal PRM, therefore, demands large and diverse datasets to ensure sufficient coverage. However, current multimodal reasoning datasets suffer from a marked quality imbalance, which degrades PRM performance and highlights the need for an effective data selection strategy. To address the issues, we introduce DreamPRM, a domain-reweighted training framework for multimodal PRMs which employs bi-level optimization. In the lower-level optimization, DreamPRM performs fine-tuning on multiple datasets with domain weights, allowing the PRM to prioritize high-quality reasoning signals and alleviating the impact of dataset quality imbalance. In the upper-level optimization, the PRM is evaluated on a separate meta-learning dataset; this feedback updates the domain weights through an aggregation loss function, thereby improving the generalization capability of trained PRM. Extensive experiments on multiple multimodal reasoning benchmarks covering both mathematical and general reasoning show that test-time scaling with DreamPRM consistently improves the performance of state-of-the-art MLLMs. Further comparisons reveal that DreamPRM's domain-reweighting strategy surpasses other data selection methods and yields higher accuracy gains than existing test-time scaling approaches. Notably, DreamPRM achieves a top-1 accuracy of 85.2% on the MathVista leaderboard using the o4-mini model, demonstrating strong generalization capability in complex multimodal reasoning tasks.

title: DreamPRM: Domain-reweighted Process Reward Model for Multimodal Reasoning

abstract: Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) has emerged as a critical privacy-preserving learning paradigm, enabling collaborative model training by leveraging distributed features across clients. However, due to privacy concerns, there are few publicly available real-world datasets for evaluating VFL methods, which poses significant challenges to related research. To bridge this gap, we propose MARS-VFL, a unified benchmark for realistic VFL evaluation. It integrates data from practical applications involving collaboration across different features, maintaining compatibility with the VFL setting. Based on this, we standardize the evaluation of VFL methods from the mainstream aspects of efficiency, robustness, and security. We conduct comprehensive experiments to assess different VFL approaches, providing references for unified evaluation. Furthermore, we are the first to unify the evaluation of robustness challenges in VFL and introduce a new method for addressing robustness challenges, establishing standard baselines for future research.

Evaluating these methods realistically is difficult because privacy concerns limit the availability of public data from such collaborations. MARS-VFL addresses this evaluation gap with a benchmark built around data from practical applications involving distributed features.

The benchmark keeps those applications compatible with the vertical federated setting and standardizes evaluation along three dimensions: efficiency, robustness, and security. Bringing these dimensions into a shared framework gives researchers a common basis for comparing approaches. The authors conduct comprehensive experiments across different methods to provide reference results for that evaluation process.

The paper also unifies the evaluation of robustness challenges in vertical federated learning and introduces a method aimed at addressing them. This supplies baseline methods alongside the benchmark itself. The overall contribution is an evaluation resource and protocol: it connects practical collaboration settings with consistent assessments of computational behavior, resilience, and security, creating a clearer foundation for subsequent methodological comparisons.
summary.tldr: MARS-VFL standardizes realistic evaluation of vertical federated learning across efficiency, robustness, and security.

title: MARS-VFL: A Unified Benchmark for Vertical Federated Learning with Realistic Evaluation

abstract: We study value-iteration (VI) algorithms for solving general (a.k.a. multichain) Markov decision processes (MDPs) under the average-reward criterion, a fundamental but theoretically challenging setting. Beyond the difficulties inherent to all average-reward problems posed by the lack of contractivity and non-uniqueness of solutions to the Bellman operator, in the multichain setting an optimal policy must solve the navigation subproblem of steering towards the best connected component, in addition to optimizing long-run performance within each component. We develop algorithms which better solve this navigational subproblem in order to achieve faster convergence for multichain MDPs, obtaining improved rates of convergence and sharper measures of complexity relative to prior work. Many key components of our results are of potential independent interest, including novel connections between average-reward and discounted problems, optimal fixed-point methods for discounted VI which extend to general Banach spaces, new sublinear convergence rates for the discounted value error, and refined suboptimality decompositions for multichain MDPs. Overall our results yield faster convergence rates for discounted and average-reward problems and expand the theoretical foundations of VI approaches.

paragraphs: This paper studies value iteration for decision problems where the objective is long-run average reward. In general multichain Markov decision processes, good decisions require both strong performance within a connected component and navigation toward the best component. The navigation requirement adds difficulty to an already challenging setting where the Bellman operator lacks contractivity and solutions need not be unique.

The authors develop algorithms that handle this navigation subproblem more effectively. Their analysis gives faster convergence rates and sharper complexity measures than prior work. A central contribution is to treat progress toward a favorable component as an explicit part of understanding how quickly value iteration approaches a good solution.

The work also establishes new links between average-reward and discounted problems. Its supporting results include optimal fixed-point methods for discounted value iteration extending to general Banach spaces, new sublinear rates for discounted value error, and refined decompositions of multichain suboptimality. Together, these results strengthen the theoretical basis for faster value iteration in both reward settings.
summary.tldr: Improved handling of navigation between components yields faster value-iteration methods for general average-reward decision processes.

title: Faster Fixed-Point Methods for Multichain MDPs

abstract: In the big data era, the computer vision field benefits from large-scale datasets such as LAION-2B, LAION-400M, and ImageNet-21K, Kinetics, on which popular models like the ViT and ConvNeXt series have been pre-trained, acquiring substantial knowledge. However, numerous downstream tasks in specialized and data-limited scientific domains continue to pose significant challenges. In this paper, we propose a novel Cluster Attention Adapter (CLAdapter), which refines and adapts the rich representations learned from large-scale data to various data-limited downstream tasks. Specifically, CLAdapter introduces attention mechanisms and cluster centers to personalize the enhancement of transformed features through distribution correlation and transformation matrices. This enables models fine-tuned with CLAdapter to learn distinct representations tailored to different feature sets, facilitating the models' adaptation from rich pre-trained features to various downstream scenarios effectively. In addition, CLAdapter's unified interface design allows for seamless integration with multiple model architectures, including CNNs and Transformers, in both 2D and 3D contexts. Through extensive experiments on 10 datasets spanning domains such as generic, multimedia, biological, medical, industrial, agricultural, environmental, geographical, materials science, out-of-distribution (OOD), and 3D analysis, CLAdapter achieves state-of-the-art performance across diverse data-limited scientific domains, demonstrating its effectiveness in unleashing the potential of foundation vision models via adaptive transfer. Code is available at https://github.com/qklee-lz/CLAdapter.

summary.tldr: CLAdapter uses cluster-guided attention to adapt pretrained vision features across diverse scientific tasks with limited training data.

abstract: Linear Autoencoders (LAEs) have shown strong performance in state-of-the-art recommender systems. However, this success remains largely empirical, with limited theoretical understanding. In this paper, we investigate the generalizability -- a theoretical measure of model performance in statistical learning -- of multivariate linear regression and LAEs. We first propose a PAC-Bayes bound for multivariate linear regression, extending the earlier bound for single-output linear regression by Shalaeva et al., and establish sufficient conditions for its convergence. We then show that LAEs, when evaluated under a relaxed mean squared error, can be interpreted as constrained multivariate linear regression models on bounded data, to which our bound adapts. Furthermore, we develop theoretical methods to improve the computational efficiency of optimizing the LAE bound, enabling its practical evaluation on large models and real-world datasets. Experimental results demonstrate that our bound is tight and correlates well with practical ranking metrics such as Recall@K and NDCG@K.

This paper studies their ability to generalize through PAC-Bayes bounds. It begins with the broader problem of multivariate linear regression, where a linear model predicts several outputs, extending an earlier bound for the single-output case.

They then connect linear autoencoders to this analysis: on bounded data and under a relaxed mean squared error, these autoencoders can be viewed as constrained multivariate linear regression models. This gives the theory practical relevance beyond the reconstruction criterion used in its formulation. The result links a generalization analysis under specified modeling and evaluation conditions with ranking quality observed in recommendation experiments.
summary.tldr: The paper develops practical PAC-Bayes generalization bounds for multi-output linear regression and, under stated conditions, linear autoencoders.

title: PAC-Bayes Bounds for Multivariate Linear Regression and Linear Autoencoders

abstract: Statistical models with constrained probability distributions are abundant in machine learning. Some examples include regression models with norm constraints (e.g., Lasso), probit models, many copula models, and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) models. Bayesian inference involving probability distributions confined to constrained domains could be quite challenging for commonly used sampling algorithms. For such problems, we propose a novel Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) method that provides a general and computationally efficient framework for handling boundary conditions. Our method first maps the D-dimensional constrained domain of parameters to the unit ball \bf B_0^D(1), then augments it to the D-dimensional sphere \bf S^D such that the original boundary corresponds to the equator of \bf S^D. This way, our method handles the constraints implicitly by moving freely on sphere generating proposals that remain within boundaries when mapped back to the original space. To improve the computational efficiency of our algorithm, we divide the dynamics into several parts such that the resulting split dynamics has a partial analytical solution as a geodesic flow on the sphere. We apply our method to several examples including truncated Gaussian, Bayesian Lasso, Bayesian bridge regression, and a copula model for identifying synchrony among multiple neurons. Our results show that the proposed method can provide a natural and efficient framework for handling several types of constraints on target distributions.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference becomes challenging when parameters must remain inside a constrained domain. This paper proposes a Markov chain Monte Carlo framework that handles such boundaries through a geometric transformation. The aim is to generate valid sampling proposals efficiently without treating each encounter with a boundary as a separate obstacle.

The method first maps the constrained parameter domain to a unit ball, then augments that ball to a sphere. The original boundary corresponds to the sphere's equator. Movement can proceed freely on the sphere, and mapping the proposals back places them within the original constraints. The geometry therefore incorporates the boundary conditions into the sampling construction.

For computational efficiency, the authors split the dynamics into parts, one of which has an analytical solution as geodesic motion on the sphere. They evaluate the approach on truncated Gaussian distributions, Bayesian Lasso, Bayesian bridge regression, and a copula model of neuronal synchrony. The results show that this construction can provide an efficient framework for several kinds of constrained target distributions.
summary.tldr: Mapping constrained parameters onto a sphere lets Hamiltonian Monte Carlo handle boundaries implicitly and efficiently in the reported examples.

title: Spherical Hamiltonian Monte Carlo for Constrained Target Distributions

abstract: We introduce a method for regularizing linearly parameterized functions using general derivative-based penalties, which relies on sampling as well as finite-difference approximations of the relevant derivatives. We call this approach sample-based approximate regularization (SAR). We provide theoretical guarantees on the fidelity of such regularizers, compared to those they approximate, and prove that the approximations converge efficiently. We also examine the empirical performance of SAR on several datasets.

We call this approach sample-based approximate regularization (SAR). We provide theoretical guarantees on the fidelity of such regularizers, compared to those they approximate, and prove that the approximations converge efficiently. We also examine the empirical performance of SAR on several datasets.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to apply derivative-based regularization to functions that are linear in their parameters. Such penalties constrain a function through its derivatives, making the behavior of the function part of the learning objective. The proposed method, sample-based approximate regularization, offers a way to approximate these penalties using sampled information.

The construction combines sampling with finite-difference approximations of the relevant derivatives. Finite differences use changes in function values to approximate derivative information, while sampling supplies the information used to build the approximate regularizer. The method targets general derivative-based penalties within the stated class of linearly parameterized functions, rather than a single named penalty.

The authors provide theoretical guarantees comparing the approximate regularizers with the original ones and prove efficient convergence of the approximations. This comparison matters because computationally approximating a penalty should preserve its intended effect closely enough to remain meaningful. They also examine empirical performance on several datasets. The abstract establishes approximation fidelity and convergence as the main theoretical findings, alongside that empirical investigation.
summary.tldr: Sample-based approximate regularization combines sampling and finite differences to approximate derivative penalties with fidelity and convergence guarantees.

title: Sample-based approximate regularization

abstract: We develop a learning principle and an efficient algorithm for batch learning from logged bandit feedback. This learning setting is ubiquitous in online systems (e.g., ad placement, web search, recommendation), where an algorithm makes a prediction (e.g., ad ranking) for a given input (e.g., query) and observes bandit feedback (e.g., user clicks on presented ads). We first address the counterfactual nature of the learning problem through propensity scoring. Next, we prove generalization error bounds that account for the variance of the propensity-weighted empirical risk estimator. These constructive bounds give rise to the Counterfactual Risk Minimization (CRM) principle. We show how CRM can be used to derive a new learning method – called Policy Optimizer for Exponential Models (POEM) – for learning stochastic linear rules for structured output prediction. We present a decomposition of the POEM objective that enables efficient stochastic gradient optimization. POEM is evaluated on several multi-label classification problems showing substantially improved robustness and generalization performance compared to the state-of-the-art.

Learning a new decision rule from those records is counterfactual: the records do not directly show what would have happened under alternative choices. This paper develops a principle and algorithm for learning from such logged bandit feedback.

The approach uses propensity scoring to address how the original system selected its actions. It then derives generalization bounds that explicitly account for the variance of the resulting weighted empirical-risk estimate. These bounds motivate Counterfactual Risk Minimization, connecting the learning objective to both estimated performance and uncertainty in that estimate.

The authors instantiate the principle as POEM, a method for learning stochastic linear rules with structured outputs. A decomposition of its objective supports efficient stochastic-gradient optimization. Evaluations on several multilabel classification problems show substantially improved robustness and generalization relative to the compared state-of-the-art methods. The findings support variance-aware learning from logged feedback in those experiments.
summary.tldr: Counterfactual Risk Minimization combines propensity weighting with variance-aware bounds to learn more robust decision rules from logged feedback.

title: Counterfactual Risk Minimization: Learning from Logged Bandit Feedback

abstract: Partition functions of probability distributions are important quantities for model evaluation and comparisons. We present a new method to compute partition functions of complex and multimodal distributions. Such distributions are often sampled using simulated tempering, which augments the target space with an auxiliary inverse temperature variable. Our method exploits the multinomial probability law of the inverse temperatures, and provides estimates of the partition function in terms of a simple quotient of Rao-Blackwellized marginal inverse temperature probability estimates, which are updated while sampling. We show that the method has interesting connections with several alternative popular methods, and offers some significant advantages. In particular, we empirically find that the new method provides more accurate estimates than Annealed Importance Sampling when calculating partition functions of large Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBM); moreover, the method is sufficiently accurate to track training and validation log-likelihoods during learning of RBMs, at minimal computational cost.

paragraphs: Partition functions are needed to evaluate and compare probabilistic models, but computing them for complex distributions can be difficult. This paper targets distributions with multiple modes and builds on simulated tempering, a sampling approach that augments the model with an auxiliary inverse-temperature variable.

The proposed estimator uses the probability law of that temperature variable. During sampling, it updates Rao-Blackwellized estimates of the marginal probabilities of inverse temperatures, then expresses the partition-function estimate as a simple quotient of those quantities. This turns information already associated with the tempering process into a mechanism for estimating the model's normalizing quantity.

The authors establish connections with other popular methods and report empirical advantages on large Restricted Boltzmann Machines. In those experiments, their estimates are more accurate than those from Annealed Importance Sampling. They are also accurate enough to track training and validation log-likelihoods during learning at minimal computational cost. That makes the method useful for monitoring a model as it changes, as well as for evaluating a finished model.
summary.tldr: A tempered-sampling estimator uses inverse-temperature probabilities to estimate partition functions accurately and monitor RBM training.

title: Partition Functions from Rao-Blackwellized Tempered Sampling

abstract: Recent work suggests that controlling the entire distribution of Jacobian singular values is an important design consideration in deep learning. Motivated by this, we study the distribution of singular values of the Jacobian of the generator in Generative Adversarial Networks. We find that this Jacobian generally becomes ill-conditioned at the beginning of training. Moreover, we find that the average (across the latent space) conditioning of the generator is highly predictive of two other ad-hoc metrics for measuring the “quality” of trained GANs: the Inception Score and the Frechet Inception Distance. We then test the hypothesis that this relationship is causal by proposing a “regularization” technique (called Jacobian Clamping) that softly penalizes the condition number of the generator Jacobian. Jacobian Clamping improves the mean score for nearly all datasets on which we tested it. It also greatly reduces inter-run variance of the aforementioned scores, addressing (at least partially) one of the main criticisms of GANs.

paragraphs: The paper investigates whether the mathematical conditioning of a GAN generator helps explain its performance. It studies the singular values of the generator's Jacobian, which describe how changes in latent inputs translate into changes in generated outputs. The authors find that this Jacobian generally becomes poorly conditioned early in training.

They also find that conditioning averaged across latent space strongly predicts Inception Score and Frechet Inception Distance, two measures used to assess trained GANs. To investigate whether the relationship is causal, they introduce Jacobian Clamping. This regularization technique applies a soft penalty to the Jacobian's condition number, deliberately intervening on the property linked to the scores.

Jacobian Clamping improves mean scores on nearly all tested datasets and substantially reduces score variation between training runs. Those results provide intervention-based evidence relevant to the causal hypothesis, without establishing a universal relationship between conditioning and generated quality. The reduction in run-to-run variability also partially addresses the inconsistency of GAN results highlighted by the authors.
summary.tldr: Jacobian Clamping tests the role of generator conditioning and improves average GAN scores and consistency across most tested datasets.

title: Is Generator Conditioning Causally Related to GAN Performance?

abstract: We present an environment, benchmark, and deep learning driven automated theorem prover for higher-order logic. Higher-order interactive theorem provers enable the formalization of arbitrary mathematical theories and thereby present an interesting challenge for deep learning. We provide an open-source framework based on the HOL Light theorem prover that can be used as a reinforcement learning environment. HOL Light comes with a broad coverage of basic mathematical theorems on calculus and the formal proof of the Kepler conjecture, from which we derive a challenging benchmark for automated reasoning approaches. We also present a deep reinforcement learning driven automated theorem prover, DeepHOL, that gives strong initial results on this benchmark.

paragraphs: The paper introduces infrastructure for studying automated mathematical reasoning in higher-order logic. Interactive theorem provers in this setting can formalize arbitrary mathematical theories, creating a substantial challenge for learning systems. The contribution includes an environment, a benchmark, and an initial automated prover, giving researchers both a place to train methods and a task collection for evaluating them.

The open-source environment builds on HOL Light and can be used for reinforcement learning. Its benchmark draws from HOL Light’s mathematical coverage, including basic calculus theorems and the formal proof of the Kepler conjecture. This grounds the challenge in existing formal mathematics rather than defining an unrelated collection of reasoning exercises.

The authors also introduce DeepHOL, an automated theorem prover driven by deep reinforcement learning. It delivers strong initial results on the benchmark. Those results accompany the broader infrastructure contribution: the environment and benchmark make this demanding form of mathematical reasoning available as a concrete machine learning research problem.
summary.tldr: HOList provides a reinforcement learning environment and formal mathematics benchmark, alongside a deep learning prover with strong initial results.

title: HOList: An Environment for Machine Learning of Higher Order Logic Theorem Proving

abstract: Deep unsupervised domain adaptation (Deep UDA) methods successfully leverage rich labeled data in a source domain to boost the performance on related but unlabeled data in a target domain. However, algorithm comparison is cumbersome in Deep UDA due to the absence of accurate and standardized model selection method, posing an obstacle to further advances in the field. Existing model selection methods for Deep UDA are either highly biased, restricted, unstable, or even controversial (requiring labeled target data). To this end, we propose Deep Embedded Validation (DEV), which embeds adapted feature representation into the validation procedure to obtain unbiased estimation of the target risk with bounded variance. The variance is further reduced by the technique of control variate. The efficacy of the method has been justified both theoretically and empirically.

paragraphs: Deep unsupervised domain adaptation uses labeled source data to improve predictions on related target data without target labels. Choosing between trained models is difficult in this setting because ordinary target-domain validation is unavailable. Existing selection procedures can be biased, unstable, restricted, or dependent on labeled target data that conflicts with the intended setup.

Deep Embedded Validation incorporates the adapted feature representation into the validation procedure. The authors establish an unbiased estimate of target risk with bounded variance. This directly addresses the quantity needed for model selection: how well a candidate is expected to perform in the target domain, despite the absence of target labels.

The method further reduces variance using a control variate, a technique for stabilizing an estimator. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results support its effectiveness. The contribution concerns evaluating and selecting adaptation models, an essential part of making algorithm comparisons reliable. By treating validation as a dedicated problem, the paper provides a more principled basis for comparing models intended for an unlabeled target domain.
summary.tldr: Deep Embedded Validation uses adapted features to estimate target risk without bias and controls variance for unsupervised domain-adaptation model selection.

title: Towards Accurate Model Selection in Deep Unsupervised Domain Adaptation

abstract: With the rapid adoption of machine learning systems in sensitive applications, there is an increasing need to make black-box models explainable. Often we want to identify an influential group of training samples in a particular test prediction for a given machine learning model. Existing influence functions tackle this problem by using first-order approximations of the effect of removing a sample from the training set on model parameters. To compute the influence of a group of training samples (rather than an individual point) in model predictions, the change in optimal model parameters after removing that group from the training set can be large. Thus, in such cases, the first-order approximation can be loose. In this paper, we address this issue and propose second-order influence functions for identifying influential groups in test-time predictions. For linear models, across different sizes and types of groups, we show that using the proposed second-order influence function improves the correlation between the computed influence values and the ground truth ones. We also show that second-order influence functions could be used with optimization techniques to improve the selection of the most influential group for a test-sample.

paragraphs: Understanding a prediction can involve asking which group of training examples most influenced it. Influence functions approximate how removing training data would change the fitted model. Existing first-order methods can be inaccurate for groups because removing several examples may cause a substantial change in the optimal parameters, beyond what a first-order approximation captures well.

The paper proposes second-order influence functions for this group-level problem. The aim is to improve estimates of how a group's removal affects a particular test prediction. This shifts attention from the influence of isolated examples to the combined effect of a set, where the larger parameter change motivates a richer approximation.

For linear models, the authors examine groups of different sizes and types and report improved correlation between estimated influence and ground-truth influence. They also show that the second-order functions could be combined with optimization techniques to improve the selection of influential groups. The demonstrated improvement is specifically stated for linear models, while the broader motivation concerns explaining predictions through their training-data dependencies.
summary.tldr: Second-order influence functions better estimate group influence for linear models and could improve searches for influential training groups.

title: On Second-Order Group Influence Functions for Black-Box Predictions

abstract: Despite their success, kernel methods suffer from a massive computational cost in practice. In this paper, in lieu of commonly used kernel expansion with respect to $N$ inputs, we develop a novel optimal design maximizing the entropy among kernel features. This procedure results in a kernel expansion with respect to entropic optimal features (EOF), improving the data representation dramatically due to features dissimilarity. Under mild technical assumptions, our generalization bound shows that with only $O(N^{\frac{1}{4}})$ features (disregarding logarithmic factors), we can achieve the optimal statistical accuracy (i.e., $O(1/\sqrt{N})$). The salient feature of our design is its sparsity that significantly reduces the time and space costs. Our numerical experiments on benchmark datasets verify the superiority of EOF over the state-of-the-art in kernel approximation.

paragraphs: Kernel methods can be computationally expensive because their usual representation expands in terms of the training inputs. This paper proposes a different representation built from selected kernel features. The selection procedure maximizes entropy among those features, producing what the authors call entropic optimal features, or EOF.

The design emphasizes dissimilarity between features, which the authors identify as a reason for the improved data representation. Its sparsity also reduces time and memory costs. The theoretical question is whether such a compact expansion can retain the statistical accuracy associated with a much larger representation.

Under mild technical assumptions, the generalization analysis shows that roughly N to the one-quarter features suffice for optimal statistical accuracy of order one over the square root of N, disregarding logarithmic factors in the feature count. Here N denotes the number of inputs. Benchmark experiments report superiority over state-of-the-art kernel approximation methods. Together, the bound and experiments support entropy-based feature design as a way to reduce computation while preserving strong statistical performance under the stated assumptions.
summary.tldr: Entropy-designed sparse kernel features retain optimal statistical accuracy under mild assumptions while reducing computational and memory costs.

title: Generalization Guarantees for Sparse Kernel Approximation with Entropic Optimal Features

abstract: In this paper, we study inexact high-order Tensor Methods for solving convex optimization problems with composite objective. At every step of such methods, we use approximate solution of the auxiliary problem, defined by the bound for the residual in function value. We propose two dynamic strategies for choosing the inner accuracy: the first one is decreasing as $1/k^{p + 1}$, where $p \geq 1$ is the order of the method and $k$ is the iteration counter, and the second approach is using for the inner accuracy the last progress in the target objective. We show that inexact Tensor Methods with these strategies achieve the same global convergence rate as in the error-free case. For the second approach we also establish local superlinear rates (for $p \geq 2$), and propose the accelerated scheme. Lastly, we present computational results on a variety of machine learning problems for several methods and different accuracy policies.

paragraphs: High-order tensor methods for convex optimization solve an auxiliary problem at each iteration. This paper studies what happens when those inner problems are solved approximately for composite objectives. The approximation is controlled through a bound on the remaining error in the auxiliary function value, making inner accuracy an explicit algorithmic choice.

The authors propose two ways to adjust that accuracy during optimization. The first reduces the allowed error according to one over k to the power p plus one, where k is the iteration number and p is the method's order. The second sets inner accuracy using the most recent progress in the main objective.

Both strategies preserve the global convergence rate of the corresponding error-free tensor methods. For the progress-based strategy, the authors also establish local superlinear convergence when the method order is at least two and propose an accelerated scheme. Computational results cover several machine-learning problems, methods, and accuracy policies. The main significance is that carefully controlled approximate inner solutions can retain strong outer convergence guarantees.
summary.tldr: Two dynamic inner-accuracy policies let inexact tensor optimization methods preserve exact-method global convergence rates.

title: Inexact Tensor Methods with Dynamic Accuracies

abstract: Despite substantial progress in signal source separation, results for richly structured data continue to contain perceptible artifacts. In contrast, recent deep generative models can produce authentic samples in a variety of domains that are indistinguishable from samples of the data distribution. This paper introduces a Bayesian approach to source separation that uses deep generative models as priors over the components of a mixture of sources, and noise-annealed Langevin dynamics to sample from the posterior distribution of sources given a mixture. This decouples the source separation problem from generative modeling, enabling us to directly use cutting-edge generative models as priors. The method achieves state-of-the-art performance for MNIST digit separation. We introduce new methodology for evaluating separation quality on richer datasets, providing quantitative evaluation and qualitative discussion of results for CIFAR-10 image separation. We also provide qualitative results on LSUN.

paragraphs: Source separation tries to recover the components that were combined into an observed mixture. For richly structured signals, separated outputs can still contain visible artifacts. This paper uses deep generative models to describe plausible individual sources, bringing their ability to represent realistic data into a Bayesian separation procedure.

The generative models serve as priors over the mixture’s components. Given a mixture, the method samples from the posterior distribution of possible sources using noise-annealed Langevin dynamics. This separates the task of building a good generative model from the task of recovering sources, allowing advances in generative modeling to be used directly as priors.

The method achieves state-of-the-art performance on MNIST digit separation. For richer image data, the authors introduce evaluation methodology and provide quantitative evaluation and qualitative discussion on CIFAR-10, along with qualitative results on LSUN. The evidence therefore has different forms across datasets: the abstract’s explicit state-of-the-art claim concerns MNIST, while the richer datasets support a broader examination of separation quality.
summary.tldr: The method separates mixtures by using deep generative priors and posterior sampling, achieving state-of-the-art MNIST separation results.

title: Source Separation with Deep Generative Priors

abstract: Polyak momentum (PM), also known as the heavy-ball method, is a widely used optimization method that enjoys an asymptotic optimal worst-case complexity on quadratic objectives. However, its remarkable empirical success is not fully explained by this optimality, as the worst-case analysis –contrary to the average-case– is not representative of the expected complexity of an algorithm. In this work we establish a novel link between PM and the average-case analysis. Our main contribution is to prove that any optimal average-case method converges in the number of iterations to PM, under mild assumptions. This brings a new perspective on this classical method, showing that PM is asymptotically both worst-case and average-case optimal.
