paragraphs: Polyak momentum, also called the heavy-ball method, already has an asymptotically optimal worst-case complexity result for quadratic objectives. This paper asks how that classical guarantee relates to expected performance. Worst-case analysis describes the hardest situations, while average-case analysis addresses a different question about the complexity an algorithm is expected to encounter.

The main result establishes a connection between optimal average-case methods and Polyak momentum. Under mild assumptions, any optimal average-case method converges toward Polyak momentum as the iteration count grows. The convergence here describes the optimization method’s asymptotic behavior, providing a link between average-case optimality and the form of this familiar algorithm.

Together with the existing worst-case result, the theorem gives Polyak momentum an asymptotically optimal status from both perspectives in the analyzed setting. This offers an additional theoretical perspective on its empirical success. The qualification that the result is asymptotic and depends on assumptions is central: the contribution concerns the limiting relationship between optimal methods and momentum as optimization proceeds.
summary.tldr: Under mild assumptions, optimal average-case optimization methods approach Polyak momentum as iterations grow, establishing its asymptotic average-case optimality.

title: Universal Average-Case Optimality of Polyak Momentum

abstract: The top-$k$ error is often employed to evaluate performance for challenging classification tasks in computer vision as it is designed to compensate for ambiguity in ground truth labels. This practical success motivates our theoretical analysis of consistent top-$k$ classification. To this end, we provide a characterization of Bayes optimality by defining a top-$k$ preserving property, which is new and fixes a non-uniqueness gap in prior work. Then, we define top-$k$ calibration and show it is necessary and sufficient for consistency. Based on the top-$k$ calibration analysis, we propose a rich class of top-$k$ calibrated Bregman divergence surrogates. Our analysis continues by showing previously proposed hinge-like top-$k$ surrogate losses are not top-$k$ calibrated and thus inconsistent. On the other hand, we propose two new hinge-like losses, one which is similarly inconsistent, and one which is consistent. Our empirical results highlight theoretical claims, confirming our analysis of the consistency of these losses.

paragraphs: Top-k classification evaluates whether the correct class appears among a model’s k leading choices, making it useful when labels are ambiguous. Models are often trained using a surrogate loss rather than this error directly. The paper studies when optimizing such a surrogate is theoretically consistent with achieving optimal top-k classification.

The authors introduce a top-k preserving property to characterize Bayes-optimal predictions and resolve a non-uniqueness gap in previous analysis. They then define top-k calibration and prove that it is both necessary and sufficient for consistency. This provides a criterion for determining whether a surrogate loss aligns with the classification objective it is meant to support.

Using that criterion, the paper develops a broad family of calibrated surrogates based on Bregman divergences. It also shows that previously proposed hinge-like top-k losses are inconsistent. Of two newly proposed hinge-like losses, one is consistent and the other is not. Experiments illustrate the theoretical distinctions, showing why superficially similar training losses can have different consistency properties.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes top-k consistency through calibration and uses it to distinguish valid surrogate losses from inconsistent alternatives.

title: On the consistency of top-k surrogate losses

abstract: Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS) and its Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) extensions are state-of-the-art methods for estimating normalizing constants of probability distributions. We propose here a novel Monte Carlo algorithm, Annealed Flow Transport (AFT), that builds upon AIS and SMC and combines them with normalizing flows (NFs) for improved performance. This method transports a set of particles using not only importance sampling (IS), Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and resampling steps - as in SMC, but also relies on NFs which are learned sequentially to push particles towards the successive annealed targets. We provide limit theorems for the resulting Monte Carlo estimates of the normalizing constant and expectations with respect to the target distribution. Additionally, we show that a continuous-time scaling limit of the population version of AFT is given by a Feynman–Kac measure which simplifies to the law of a controlled diffusion for expressive NFs. We demonstrate experimentally the benefits and limitations of our methodology on a variety of applications.
originalAbstract: Annealed Importance Sampling (AIS) and its Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) extensions are state-of-the-art methods for estimating normalizing constants of probability distributions. We propose here a novel Monte Carlo algorithm, Annealed Flow Transport (AFT), that builds upon AIS and SMC and combines them with normalizing flows (NFs) for improved performance. This method transports a set of particles using not only importance sampling (IS), Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) and resampling steps - as in SMC, but also relies on NFs which are learned sequentially to push particles towards the successive annealed targets. We provide limit theorems for the resulting Monte Carlo estimates of the normalizing constant and expectations with respect to the target distribution. Additionally, we show that a continuous-time scaling limit of the population version of AFT is given by a Feynman–Kac measure which simplifies to the law of a controlled diffusion for expressive NFs. We demonstrate experimentally the benefits and limitations of our methodology on a variety of applications.

paragraphs: Estimating a distribution's normalizing constant and its expected quantities is a central sampling problem. Annealed Importance Sampling and Sequential Monte Carlo approach it through successive intermediate distributions. This paper introduces Annealed Flow Transport, which adds learned transformations to this process to help move samples toward each successive target.

The algorithm maintains a collection of particles and combines importance weighting, Markov chain Monte Carlo, and resampling with normalizing flows. These flows are learned sequentially, so their role is to transport particles toward the next intermediate distribution. The approach therefore combines learned movement with the sampling and correction operations already used in Sequential Monte Carlo.

The authors establish limit theorems for estimates of both normalizing constants and target expectations. They also characterize a continuous-time limit of the population formulation through a Feynman–Kac measure; with expressive flows, this simplifies to a controlled diffusion. Experiments across several applications demonstrate both benefits and limitations, supporting the method as a promising combination rather than an unconditional improvement in every setting.
summary.tldr: Annealed Flow Transport adds sequentially learned normalizing flows to Monte Carlo sampling, with limit theory and experiments examining its benefits and limitations.

title: Annealed Flow Transport Monte Carlo

abstract: We study the problem of differentially private (DP) matrix completion under user-level privacy. We design a joint differentially private variant of the popular Alternating-Least-Squares (ALS) method that achieves: i) (nearly) optimal sample complexity for matrix completion (in terms of number of items, users), and ii) the best known privacy/utility trade-off both theoretically, as well as on benchmark data sets. In particular, we provide the first global convergence analysis of ALS with noise introduced to ensure DP, and show that, in comparison to the best known alternative (the Private Frank-Wolfe algorithm by Jain et al. (2018)), our error bounds scale significantly better with respect to the number of items and users, which is critical in practical problems. Extensive validation on standard benchmarks demonstrate that the algorithm, in combination with carefully designed sampling procedures, is significantly more accurate than existing techniques, thus promising to be the first practical DP embedding model.

This paper studies that task with user-level privacy and develops a jointly differentially private version of alternating least squares. The goal is to preserve useful predictions while accounting for the noise introduced to protect users.

These dependencies matter because the size of the user and item populations is central to practical matrix-completion problems.

The paper reports the best known privacy–utility trade-off both theoretically and empirically. These results motivate the authors’ description of the method as a promising practical private embedding model, while keeping that practical claim tied to the presented analysis and benchmark evidence.
summary.tldr: A private alternating least-squares method improves theoretical error scaling and benchmark accuracy for matrix completion with user-level privacy.

title: Private Alternating Least Squares: Practical Private Matrix Completion with Tighter Rates

abstract: We propose a distributed cubic regularization of the Newton method for solving (constrained) empirical risk minimization problems over a network of agents, modeled as undirected graph. The algorithm employs an inexact, preconditioned Newton step at each agent’s side: the gradient of the centralized loss is iteratively estimated via a gradient-tracking consensus mechanism and the Hessian is subsampled over the local data sets. No Hessian matrices are exchanged over the network. We derive global complexity bounds for convex and strongly convex losses. Our analysis reveals an interesting interplay between sample and iteration/communication complexity: statistically accurate solutions are achievable in roughly the same number of iterations of the centralized cubic Newton, with a communication cost per iteration of the order of $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(1/\sqrt{1-\rho}\big)$, where $\rho$ characterizes the connectivity of the network. This represents a significant improvement with respect to existing, statistically oblivious, distributed Newton-based methods over networks.

paragraphs: Distributed empirical risk minimization fits a model using data held across a network of agents. Newton methods use curvature information to accelerate optimization, but coordinating that information can be expensive. This paper develops a distributed cubic-regularized Newton method for constrained problems on an undirected communication network.

Each agent takes an inexact, preconditioned Newton step. A gradient-tracking consensus procedure estimates the gradient of the centralized loss, while the Hessian is subsampled from local data. The agents do not exchange Hessian matrices. The design therefore combines local curvature estimates with communication that coordinates the gradient estimate across the network.

Reaching statistical precision requires roughly as many iterations as centralized cubic Newton, with per-iteration communication scaling as approximately 1/sqrt(1-rho), up to the suppressed factors in the stated bound. Here rho describes network connectivity. The result improves on distributed Newton analyses that do not account for statistical precision, making the target estimation accuracy central to the computational guarantee.
summary.tldr: A distributed Newton method reaches statistical precision in roughly centralized iteration counts without exchanging Hessian matrices.

title: Newton Method over Networks is Fast up to the Statistical Precision

abstract: Decentralized learning enables a group of collaborative agents to learn models using a distributed dataset without the need for a central parameter server. Recently, decentralized learning algorithms have demonstrated state-of-the-art results on benchmark data sets, comparable with centralized algorithms. However, the key assumption to achieve competitive performance is that the data is independently and identically distributed (IID) among the agents which, in real-life applications, is often not applicable. Inspired by ideas from continual learning, we propose Cross-Gradient Aggregation (CGA), a novel decentralized learning algorithm where (i) each agent aggregates cross-gradient information, i.e., derivatives of its model with respect to its neighbors’ datasets, and (ii) updates its model using a projected gradient based on quadratic programming (QP). We theoretically analyze the convergence characteristics of CGA and demonstrate its efficiency on non-IID data distributions sampled from the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. Our empirical comparisons show superior learning performance of CGA over existing state-of-the-art decentralized learning algorithms, as well as maintaining the improved performance under information compression to reduce peer-to-peer communication overhead. The code is available here on GitHub.

paragraphs: Decentralized learning lets multiple agents train collaboratively without a central parameter server. Strong performance can depend on the agents receiving statistically similar data, an assumption that often fails in practice. This paper addresses the resulting problem: local learning updates must account for differences between agents’ datasets if collaboration is to remain effective.

Cross-Gradient Aggregation gives each agent information about how its own model behaves on neighboring agents’ data. These cross-gradients describe changes to that model’s parameters evaluated against the neighbors’ datasets. The agent aggregates this information and uses a quadratic programming problem to construct a projected gradient for its update. Inspired by continual learning, the approach makes neighboring data directly relevant to the local update direction.

The authors analyze convergence and evaluate the method on non-IID versions of MNIST and CIFAR-10. Their comparisons report better learning performance than existing leading decentralized algorithms. The improvement also persists when exchanged information is compressed, indicating that the tested benefits can coexist with reduced communication between peers.
summary.tldr: Cross-Gradient Aggregation uses neighboring datasets to guide local updates and improves decentralized learning on tested non-IID data, including with compressed communication.

title: Cross-Gradient Aggregation for Decentralized Learning from Non-IID Data

abstract: Neural networks trained via gradient descent with random initialization and without any regularization enjoy good generalization performance in practice despite being highly overparametrized. A promising direction to explain this phenomenon is to study how initialization and overparametrization affect convergence and implicit bias of training algorithms. In this paper, we present a novel analysis of single-hidden-layer linear networks trained under gradient flow, which connects initialization, optimization, and overparametrization. Firstly, we show that the squared loss converges exponentially to its optimum at a rate that depends on the level of imbalance of the initialization. Secondly, we show that proper initialization constrains the dynamics of the network parameters to lie within an invariant set. In turn, minimizing the loss over this set leads to the min-norm solution. Finally, we show that large hidden layer width, together with (properly scaled) random initialization, ensures proximity to such an invariant set during training, allowing us to derive a novel non-asymptotic upper-bound on the distance between the trained network and the min-norm solution.

This paper studies that issue in single-hidden-layer linear networks trained by gradient flow. A sufficiently large hidden layer keeps training near the relevant invariant set, allowing a non-asymptotic upper bound on the distance between the trained network and the minimum-norm solution. The result gives a quantitative account of initialization's influence within the stated linear-network and gradient-flow setting.
summary.tldr: For single-hidden-layer linear networks under gradient flow, initialization controls convergence speed and proximity to minimum-norm solutions.

title: On the Explicit Role of Initialization on the Convergence and Implicit Bias of Overparametrized Linear Networks

abstract: To achieve sample efficiency in reinforcement learning (RL), it necessitates to efficiently explore the underlying environment. Under the offline setting, addressing the exploration challenge lies in collecting an offline dataset with sufficient coverage. Motivated by such a challenge, we study the reward-free RL problem, where an agent aims to thoroughly explore the environment without any pre-specified reward function. Then, given any extrinsic reward, the agent computes the optimal policy via offline RL with data collected in the exploration stage. Moreover, we tackle this problem under the context of function approximation, leveraging powerful function approximators. Specifically, we propose to explore via an optimistic variant of the value-iteration algorithm incorporating kernel and neural function approximations, where we adopt the associated exploration bonus as the exploration reward. Moreover, we design exploration and planning algorithms for both single-agent MDPs and zero-sum Markov games and prove that our methods can achieve $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(1 /\varepsilon^2)$ sample complexity for generating a $\varepsilon$-suboptimal policy or $\varepsilon$-approximate Nash equilibrium when given an arbitrary extrinsic reward. To the best of our knowledge, we establish the first provably efficient reward-free RL algorithm with kernel and neural function approximators.

paragraphs: Reward-free reinforcement learning separates exploring an environment from deciding which task to solve. An agent first gathers data without a prespecified external reward. Once a reward is supplied, it uses that stored experience for offline planning. The challenge is collecting data with enough coverage to support different later objectives.

The authors develop exploration and planning algorithms using kernel and neural function approximators. Exploration follows an optimistic variant of value iteration, with an exploration bonus serving as the temporary reward. This gives the agent a learning objective before the eventual task reward is known. The approach covers both single-agent Markov decision processes and two-player zero-sum Markov games.

The paper proves sample-complexity bounds proportional to one over the squared accuracy tolerance, with logarithmic factors suppressed. The resulting guarantees concern an approximately optimal policy or an approximate Nash equilibrium for an arbitrary supplied reward in the analyzed settings. The contribution brings formal sample-efficiency guarantees to reward-free exploration with these function approximators, connecting broad data collection with later task-specific planning.
summary.tldr: Optimistic reward-free exploration with kernel and neural approximators supports provably sample-efficient later planning in single-agent problems and zero-sum games.

title: On Reward-Free RL with Kernel and Neural Function Approximations: Single-Agent MDP and Markov Game

abstract: Lossy compression algorithms are typically designed to achieve the lowest possible distortion at a given bit rate. However, recent studies show that pursuing high perceptual quality would lead to increase of the lowest achievable distortion (e.g., MSE). This paper provides nontrivial results theoretically revealing that, 1) the cost of achieving perfect perception quality is exactly a doubling of the lowest achievable MSE distortion, 2) an optimal encoder for the “classic” rate-distortion problem is also optimal for the perceptual compression problem, 3) distortion loss is unnecessary for training a perceptual decoder. Further, we propose a novel training framework to achieve the lowest MSE distortion under perfect perception constraint at a given bit rate. This framework uses a GAN with discriminator conditioned on an MSE-optimized encoder, which is superior over the traditional framework using distortion plus adversarial loss. Experiments are provided to verify the theoretical finding and demonstrate the superiority of the proposed training framework.

paragraphs: Lossy compression usually seeks the smallest reconstruction error at a fixed bit rate. This paper examines what happens when reconstruction must also satisfy perfect perceptual quality. In its theoretical formulation, imposing that constraint exactly doubles the lowest achievable mean squared error, quantifying a tradeoff between perceptual quality and numerical distortion.

The analysis also shows that an encoder optimal for the classical rate–distortion problem remains optimal for the perceptual compression problem. Furthermore, a perceptual decoder can be trained without a distortion loss. These findings separate the roles of encoding and decoding: the perceptual requirement does not require abandoning the theoretically optimal classical encoder.

The proposed training framework uses a GAN whose discriminator is conditioned on an encoder optimized for mean squared error. It aims to attain the lowest MSE permitted by perfect perception at a given bit rate. Experiments support the theoretical findings and show advantages over the traditional combination of distortion and adversarial losses. The exact doubling result concerns the stated perfect-perception constraint, rather than every possible perceptual-quality objective.
summary.tldr: The paper quantifies perfect perception’s MSE cost and derives a perceptual compression framework using an MSE-optimal encoder.

title: On Perceptual Lossy Compression: The Cost of Perceptual Reconstruction and An Optimal Training Framework

abstract: Several practical applications of reinforcement learning involve an agent learning from past data without the possibility of further exploration. Often these applications require us to 1) identify a near optimal policy or to 2) estimate the value of a target policy. For both tasks we derive exponential information-theoretic lower bounds in discounted infinite horizon MDPs with a linear function representation for the action value function even if 1) realizability holds, 2) the batch algorithm observes the exact reward and transition functions, and 3) the batch algorithm is given the best a priori data distribution for the problem class. Our work introduces a new ‘oracle + batch algorithm’ framework to prove lower bounds that hold for every distribution. The work shows an exponential separation between batch and online reinforcement learning.

Our work introduces a new ‘oracle + batch algorithm’ framework to prove lower bounds that hold for every distribution. The work shows an exponential separation between batch and online reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Batch reinforcement learning uses previously collected data without further exploration. The paper studies two central tasks in that setting: finding a nearly optimal policy and estimating the value of a specified policy. It asks how difficult these tasks can remain even when the learning algorithm receives unusually favorable information.

The authors establish exponential information-theoretic lower bounds for discounted, infinite-horizon Markov decision processes with linear representations of action values. Their bounds persist when realizability holds, meaning the representation can express the relevant action-value function. They also persist with exact reward and transition information in the batch observations and with the best data distribution chosen in advance for the problem class.

A new framework combining an oracle with a batch algorithm allows the lower-bound argument to cover every data distribution. The resulting separation shows that batch learning can be exponentially harder than online learning in the analyzed setting. This is a statement about fundamental information requirements, so improving the optimization procedure alone cannot eliminate the demonstrated difficulty.
summary.tldr: The paper proves that batch reinforcement learning can require exponentially more information than online learning, even under favorable representation and data conditions.

title: Exponential Lower Bounds for Batch Reinforcement Learning: Batch RL can be Exponentially Harder than Online RL

abstract: Recent empirical evidence has driven conventional wisdom to believe that gradient-based meta-learning (GBML) methods perform well at few-shot learning because they learn an expressive data representation that is shared across tasks. However, the mechanics of GBML have remained largely mysterious from a theoretical perspective. In this paper, we prove that two well-known GBML methods, MAML and ANIL, as well as their first-order approximations, are capable of learning common representation among a set of given tasks. Specifically, in the well-known multi-task linear representation learning setting, they are able to recover the ground-truth representation at an exponentially fast rate. Moreover, our analysis illuminates that the driving force causing MAML and ANIL to recover the underlying representation is that they adapt the final layer of their model, which harnesses the underlying task diversity to improve the representation in all directions of interest. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first results to show that MAML and/or ANIL learn expressive representations and to rigorously explain why they do so.

paragraphs: Gradient-based meta-learning methods are often thought to succeed at learning from few examples because they acquire representations shared across tasks. This paper gives a theoretical account of that explanation for MAML, ANIL, and their first-order approximations. It investigates both whether these methods recover a shared representation and what drives that recovery.

The proof applies in a multi-task linear representation learning setting. Within that setting, the methods recover the ground-truth representation at an exponentially fast rate. This establishes a concrete representation-learning capability for the analyzed algorithms, giving mathematical support to an explanation previously motivated by empirical evidence.

The analysis identifies adaptation of the final model layer as the driving mechanism. That adaptation uses diversity across tasks to improve the representation in all relevant directions. The result connects task-specific adjustment to shared learning: adapting the final layer helps expose information needed to recover the common representation. Its theoretical scope is the stated linear setting, where the authors rigorously characterize this mechanism.
summary.tldr: In a multi-task linear setting, MAML and ANIL provably recover shared representations through final-layer adaptation that exploits task diversity.

title: MAML and ANIL Provably Learn Representations

abstract: In this paper, we study gap-dependent regret guarantees for risk-sensitive reinforcement learning based on the entropic risk measure. We propose a novel definition of sub-optimality gaps, which we call cascaded gaps, and we discuss their key components that adapt to underlying structures of the problem. Based on the cascaded gaps, we derive non-asymptotic and logarithmic regret bounds for two model-free algorithms under episodic Markov decision processes. We show that, in appropriate settings, these bounds feature exponential improvement over existing ones that are independent of gaps. We also prove gap-dependent lower bounds, which certify the near optimality of the upper bounds.

Based on the cascaded gaps, we derive non-asymptotic and logarithmic regret bounds for two model-free algorithms under episodic Markov decision processes. paragraphs: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning evaluates decisions using a criterion that accounts for risk. This paper studies the entropic risk measure and asks how quickly learning algorithms can reduce the accumulated cost of making suboptimal decisions. Its focus is on regret guarantees that reflect how clearly inferior choices are separated from better ones.

The authors introduce a definition of suboptimality called cascaded gaps. These gaps incorporate components that adapt to the underlying problem structure. Using them, the paper derives logarithmic regret bounds for two model-free algorithms in episodic Markov decision processes. The guarantees are non-asymptotic, meaning they apply at finite learning durations rather than describing only eventual behavior.

In appropriate settings, the new bounds improve exponentially over existing guarantees that do not depend on gaps. The authors also prove gap-dependent lower bounds, which show that the upper bounds are nearly optimal. Together, these results explain how incorporating problem-specific separation between choices can yield substantially sharper guarantees for risk-sensitive learning, with the improvement qualified by the setting in which those gaps arise.
summary.tldr: Cascaded gaps yield nearly optimal logarithmic regret guarantees for two risk-sensitive reinforcement learning algorithms, with exponential improvements in appropriate settings.

title: Cascaded Gaps: Towards Logarithmic Regret for Risk-Sensitive Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Uncertainty estimates must be calibrated (i.e., accurate) and sharp (i.e., informative) in order to be useful. This has motivated a variety of methods for recalibration , which use held-out data to turn an uncalibrated model into a calibrated model. However, the applicability of existing methods is limited due to their assumption that the original model is also a probabilistic model. We introduce a versatile class of algorithms for recalibration in regression that we call modular conformal calibration (MCC). This framework allows one to transform any regression model into a calibrated probabilistic model. The modular design of MCC allows us to make simple adjustments to existing algorithms that enable well-behaved distribution predictions. We also provide finite-sample calibration guarantees for MCC algorithms. Our framework recovers isotonic recalibration, conformal calibration, and conformal interval prediction, implying that our theoretical results apply to those methods as well. Finally, we conduct an empirical study of MCC on 17 regression datasets. Our results show that new algorithms designed in our framework achieve near-perfect calibration and improve sharpness relative to existing methods.

paragraphs: Useful uncertainty estimates should be accurate about uncertainty and precise enough to inform decisions. Recalibration uses held-out data to improve those estimates, but many methods require the starting model to already produce probabilities. Modular conformal calibration, or MCC, extends this approach to any regression model by turning it into a calibrated probabilistic predictor.

The framework is modular, allowing adjustments to existing algorithms that produce well-behaved predictive distributions. It also unifies isotonic recalibration, conformal calibration, and conformal interval prediction as instances of the same framework. This connection lets the authors apply their finite-sample calibration guarantees to those established methods as well as to newly designed MCC algorithms.

An empirical study on 17 regression datasets finds that the new algorithms achieve nearly perfect calibration and sharper predictions than existing methods. Sharpness matters because uncertainty predictions must remain informative as well as accurate. The paper therefore contributes both broader access to probabilistic prediction and a common theoretical structure for studying calibration methods, with empirical evidence that useful precision can improve.
summary.tldr: Modular conformal calibration converts regression models into calibrated probabilistic predictors with finite-sample guarantees and improved empirical sharpness.

title: Modular Conformal Calibration

abstract: Social networks are often modeled using signed graphs, where vertices correspond to users and edges have a sign that indicates whether an interaction between users was positive or negative. The arising signed graphs typically contain a clear community structure in the sense that the graph can be partitioned into a small number of polarized communities, each defining a sparse cut and indivisible into smaller polarized sub-communities. We provide a local clustering oracle for signed graphs with such a clear community structure, that can answer membership queries, i.e., “Given a vertex $v$, which community does $v$ belong to?”, in sublinear time by reading only a small portion of the graph. Formally, when the graph has bounded maximum degree and the number of communities is at most $O(\log n)$, then with $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n}\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon))$ preprocessing time, our oracle can answer each membership query in $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{n}\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon))$ time, and it correctly classifies a $(1-\varepsilon)$-fraction of vertices w.r.t. a set of hidden planted ground-truth communities. Our oracle is desirable in applications where the clustering information is needed for only a small number of vertices. Previously, such local clustering oracles were only known for unsigned graphs; our generalization to signed graphs requires a number of new ideas and gives a novel spectral analysis of the behavior of random walks with signs. We evaluate our algorithm for constructing such an oracle and answering membership queries on both synthetic and real-world datasets, validating its performance in practice.

paragraphs: Signed graphs represent relationships as positive or negative, as in a network of social interactions. This paper studies graphs with a clear structure of polarized communities and asks how to identify an individual vertex’s community without processing the entire graph. summary.tldr: A local oracle answers signed-graph community queries in sublinear time with accuracy guarantees under explicit structural assumptions.

title: Sublinear-Time Clustering Oracle for Signed Graphs

abstract: We present an approach that incorporates expert knowledge for time-series representation learning. Our method employs expert features to replace the commonly used data transformations in previous contrastive learning approaches. We do this since time-series data frequently stems from the industrial or medical field where expert features are often available from domain experts, while transformations are generally elusive for time-series data. We start by proposing two properties that useful time-series representations should fulfill and show that current representation learning approaches do not ensure these properties. We therefore devise ExpCLR, a novel contrastive learning approach built on an objective that utilizes expert features to encourage both properties for the learned representation. Finally, we demonstrate on three real-world time-series datasets that ExpCLR surpasses several state-of-the-art methods for both unsupervised and semi-supervised representation learning.

Domain experts may already have useful features for these signals, creating another source of guidance for representation learning.

The paper introduces ExpCLR, which uses expert features in place of the transformations commonly used by earlier contrastive methods. The authors first propose two desirable properties for time-series representations and show that existing approaches do not ensure them. They then construct an objective that uses expert features to encourage both properties in the learned representation.

Evaluations on three real-world time-series datasets show ExpCLR outperforming several state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised and semi-supervised representation learning. The findings support incorporating available domain knowledge directly into the learning objective. The approach matters because it offers a route to useful representations when meaningful transformations are elusive, while making expert-designed signal descriptions part of the learning process.
summary.tldr: ExpCLR uses expert features to guide contrastive time-series learning and outperforms several existing methods on three real-world datasets.

title: Utilizing Expert Features for Contrastive Learning of Time-Series Representations

abstract: Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) has been shown to generalize well in many deep learning applications. In practice, one often runs SGD with a geometrically decaying stepsize, i.e., a constant initial stepsize followed by multiple geometric stepsize decay, and uses the last iterate as the output. This kind of SGD is known to be nearly minimax optimal for classical finite-dimensional linear regression problems (Ge et al., 2019). However, a sharp analysis for the last iterate of SGD in the overparameterized setting is still open. In this paper, we provide a problem-dependent analysis on the last iterate risk bounds of SGD with decaying stepsize, for (overparameterized) linear regression problems. In particular, for last iterate SGD with (tail) geometrically decaying stepsize, we prove nearly matching upper and lower bounds on the excess risk. Moreover, we provide an excess risk lower bound for last iterate SGD with polynomially decaying stepsize and demonstrate the advantage of geometrically decaying stepsize in an instance-wise manner, which complements the minimax rate comparison made in prior work.

paragraphs: A common training procedure runs SGD with an initially constant learning rate, reduces it geometrically in stages, and returns the final parameter estimate. Although this procedure is well understood for classical linear regression, its final output had lacked a sharp analysis in overparameterized settings. This paper studies that final output directly through problem-dependent excess-risk bounds.

For a schedule with geometric decay in its later stages, the authors prove upper and lower bounds that nearly match. Upper bounds describe how large the excess risk can be, while lower bounds establish how far such guarantees can be improved. Their close agreement gives a sharper characterization of the final iterate’s statistical performance for the regression problems considered.

The paper also derives an excess-risk lower bound for polynomially decaying learning rates. This supports an instance-wise advantage for geometric decay, complementing earlier comparisons based on worst-case minimax rates. The distinction matters because a problem-dependent analysis examines how schedules behave for particular regression instances, adding detail beyond a single worst-case assessment across a problem class.
summary.tldr: Nearly matching risk bounds characterize final-iterate SGD with geometric learning-rate decay in overparameterized linear regression and support instance-wise advantages over polynomial decay.

title: Last Iterate Risk Bounds of SGD with Decaying Stepsize for Overparameterized Linear Regression

abstract: We study the use of amortized optimization to predict optimal transport (OT) maps from the input measures, which we call Meta OT. This helps repeatedly solve similar OT problems between different measures by leveraging the knowledge and information present from past problems to rapidly predict and solve new problems. Otherwise, standard methods ignore the knowledge of the past solutions and suboptimally re-solve each problem from scratch. We instantiate Meta OT models in discrete and continuous settings between grayscale images, spherical data, classification labels, and color palettes and use them to improve the computational time of standard OT solvers. Our source code is available at http://github.com/facebookresearch/meta-ot

paragraphs: Optimal transport problems ask how to map one measure to another according to a transport objective. Applications often require solving many related instances with different input measures. This paper investigates how experience from earlier instances can help solve later ones, instead of treating every new pair of measures as an entirely separate optimization problem.

The proposed approach, Meta OT, uses amortized optimization to predict transport maps directly from the input measures. Information gathered across past problems is captured in a predictive model, allowing it to rapidly predict and help solve new problems. The key idea is to reuse structure shared by similar transport tasks, making learning part of the repeated-solving process.

The authors instantiate this approach in both discrete and continuous settings, covering grayscale images, spherical data, classification labels, and color palettes. They report improvements in the computational time of standard optimal transport solvers. These demonstrations establish the approach across several kinds of transport inputs. The central benefit concerns repeated related problems, where earlier solutions provide information that a solver starting afresh would leave unused.
summary.tldr: Meta OT learns from previous transport problems to predict maps for new inputs and accelerate repeated optimal transport solving.

title: Meta Optimal Transport

abstract: Aligning language models with preferences can be posed as approximating a target distribution representing some desired behavior. Existing approaches differ both in the functional form of the target distribution and the algorithm used to approximate it. For instance, Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) corresponds to minimizing a reverse KL from an implicit target distribution arising from a KL penalty in the objective. On the other hand, Generative Distributional Control (GDC) has an explicit target distribution and minimizes a forward KL from it using the Distributional Policy Gradient (DPG) algorithm. In this paper, we propose a new approach, $f$-DPG, which allows the use of any $f$-divergence to approximate any target distribution that can be evaluated. $f$-DPG unifies both frameworks (RLHF, GDC) and the approximation methods (DPG, RL with KL penalties). We show the practical benefits of various choices of divergence objectives and demonstrate that there is no universally optimal objective but that different divergences present different alignment and diversity trade-offs. We show that Jensen-Shannon divergence strikes a good balance between these objectives, and frequently outperforms forward KL divergence by a wide margin, leading to significant improvements over prior work. These distinguishing characteristics between divergences persist as the model size increases, highlighting the importance of selecting appropriate divergence objectives.

paragraphs: This paper views language-model alignment as matching a distribution of outputs that represents desired behavior. Existing methods differ in how they define that target and how they measure the gap between the model and the target. Under this view, RLHF uses reverse KL divergence from an implicit target, while Generative Distributional Control uses forward KL with an explicit target.

The proposed f-DPG framework allows any f-divergence to be used with any target distribution that can be evaluated. It brings these alignment approaches and their optimization methods into a shared framework. That makes the choice of discrepancy measure an explicit part of designing alignment, rather than something fixed by the chosen method.

The experiments show that different divergences produce different trade-offs between preference alignment and output diversity. No objective is universally best. Jensen-Shannon divergence often gives a favorable balance and frequently improves substantially over forward KL. These differences persist as model size increases, suggesting that scaling the model does not remove the importance of choosing an appropriate alignment objective.
summary.tldr: f-DPG unifies distribution-based alignment methods and shows that divergence choice shapes the trade-off between alignment and diversity.

title: Aligning Language Models with Preferences through $f$-divergence Minimization

abstract: Exploration in environments which differ across episodes has received increasing attention in recent years. Current methods use some combination of global novelty bonuses, computed using the agent’s entire training experience, and episodic novelty bonuses, computed using only experience from the current episode. However, the use of these two types of bonuses has been ad-hoc and poorly understood. In this work, we shed light on the behavior of these two types of bonuses through controlled experiments on easily interpretable tasks as well as challenging pixel-based settings. We find that the two types of bonuses succeed in different settings, with episodic bonuses being most effective when there is little shared structure across episodes and global bonuses being effective when more structure is shared. We develop a conceptual framework which makes this notion of shared structure precise by considering the variance of the value function across contexts, and which provides a unifying explanation of our empirical results. We furthermore find that combining the two bonuses can lead to more robust performance across different degrees of shared structure, and investigate different algorithmic choices for defining and combining global and episodic bonuses based on function approximation. This results in an algorithm which sets a new state of the art across 16 tasks from the MiniHack suite used in prior work, and also performs robustly on Habitat and Montezuma’s Revenge.

paragraphs: An exploration bonus rewards an agent for encountering something unfamiliar. But unfamiliarity can be measured against its entire training history or only its current episode. When environments change between episodes, these two definitions can encourage different behavior. This paper investigates when each is useful through controlled, interpretable tasks and more challenging settings using pixel observations.

The experiments find that episodic bonuses are most effective when episodes share little structure, whereas global bonuses work well when more structure carries across episodes. The authors develop a conceptual explanation using variation in the value function across contexts. This connects the meaning of shared structure to how much the expected usefulness of states changes between environments.

Combining the bonuses can make performance more robust across different amounts of shared structure. The paper explores ways to define and combine them using function approximation, producing an algorithm that establishes a new state of the art on 16 previously used MiniHack tasks. It also performs robustly on Habitat and Montezuma’s Revenge, supporting the practical value of the combined approach.
summary.tldr: Experiments explain when global or episodic exploration bonuses work best and show that combining them can improve robustness across changing environments.

title: A Study of Global and Episodic Bonuses for Exploration in Contextual MDPs

abstract: There is extensive interest in metric learning methods for image retrieval. Many metric learning loss functions focus on learning a correct ranking of training samples, but strongly overfit semantically inconsistent labels and require a large amount of data. To address these shortcomings, we propose a new metric learning method, called contextual loss, which optimizes contextual similarity in addition to cosine similarity. Our contextual loss implicitly enforces semantic consistency among neighbors while converging to the correct ranking. We empirically show that the proposed loss is more robust to label noise, and is less prone to overfitting even when a large portion of train data is withheld. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves a new state-of-the-art across four image retrieval benchmarks and multiple different evaluation settings. Code is available at: https://github.com/Chris210634/metric-learning-using-contextual-similarity

paragraphs: Metric learning for image retrieval aims to arrange representations so that relevant images rank ahead of irrelevant ones. Many training losses focus on matching the labeled ranking, but semantically inconsistent labels can encourage overfitting. These methods can also depend on having a large amount of training data.

The paper introduces contextual loss, which optimizes contextual similarity together with cosine similarity. It implicitly encourages semantic consistency among neighboring samples while converging toward the correct ranking. The approach makes the relationships around an example part of the learning objective, supplementing the direct similarity information used to order individual samples.

Experiments show greater robustness to label noise and less tendency to overfit when a large portion of the training set is withheld. The method also reaches a new state of the art across four image retrieval benchmarks and multiple evaluation settings. These findings support neighborhood consistency as a useful training signal when labels are imperfect or data is limited, while retaining the central retrieval goal of learning an effective ranking.
summary.tldr: Contextual loss adds neighborhood consistency to image retrieval training, improving measured robustness to noisy labels and reduced training data.

title: Supervised Metric Learning to Rank for Retrieval via Contextual Similarity Optimization

abstract: Aiming to produce reinforcement learning (RL) policies that are human-interpretable and can generalize better to novel scenarios, Trivedi et al. (2021) present a method (LEAPS) that first learns a program embedding space to continuously parameterize diverse programs from a pre-generated program dataset, and then searches for a task-solving program in the learned program embedding space when given a task. Despite the encouraging results, the program policies that LEAPS can produce are limited by the distribution of the program dataset. Furthermore, during searching, LEAPS evaluates each candidate program solely based on its return, failing to precisely reward correct parts of programs and penalize incorrect parts. To address these issues, we propose to learn a meta-policy that composes a series of programs sampled from the learned program embedding space. By learning to compose programs, our proposed hierarchical programmatic reinforcement learning (HPRL) framework can produce program policies that describe out-of-distributionally complex behaviors and directly assign credits to programs that induce desired behaviors. The experimental results in the Karel domain show that our proposed framework outperforms baselines. The ablation studies confirm the limitations of LEAPS and justify our design choices.

paragraphs: Programmatic reinforcement learning represents behavior through programs, aiming for policies that people can interpret and that generalize to new situations. The earlier LEAPS approach searches a learned embedding space of programs. Its available policies are constrained by the program dataset, and judging each candidate only by its total return makes it difficult to credit useful parts.

HPRL introduces a meta-policy that composes a sequence of programs sampled from that embedding space. Learning how to combine programs lets the resulting policy express behaviors more complex than those represented in the original program distribution. It also allows credit to be assigned directly to programs that produce desired behavior.

The authors evaluate the framework in the Karel domain and report improvements over the tested baselines. Ablation studies support both their diagnosis of LEAPS’s limitations and their design choices. The central idea is to expand what learned program components can accomplish through composition while giving the learning process more specific feedback about which components help.
summary.tldr: HPRL learns to compose program components into more complex policies while assigning credit to components that produce useful behavior.

title: Hierarchical Programmatic Reinforcement Learning via Learning to Compose Programs

abstract: Existing theoretical studies on offline reinforcement learning (RL) mostly consider a dataset sampled directly from the target task. In practice, however, data often come from several heterogeneous but related sources. Motivated by this gap, this work aims at rigorously understanding offline RL with multiple datasets that are collected from randomly perturbed versions of the target task instead of from itself. An information-theoretic lower bound is derived, which reveals a necessary requirement on the number of involved sources in addition to that on the number of data samples. Then, a novel HetPEVI algorithm is proposed, which simultaneously considers the sample uncertainties from a finite number of data samples per data source and the source uncertainties due to a finite number of available data sources. Theoretical analyses demonstrate that HetPEVI can solve the target task as long as the data sources collectively provide a good data coverage. Moreover, HetPEVI is demonstrated to be optimal up to a polynomial factor of the horizon length. Finally, the study is extended to offline Markov games and offline robust RL, which demonstrates the generality of the proposed designs and theoretical analyses.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning often assumes its dataset comes directly from the task the agent will eventually solve. This paper instead studies multiple datasets collected from randomly perturbed versions of that target task. The setting reflects a distinction between having many observations and having enough different related sources to learn reliably about the target.

An information-theoretic lower bound establishes requirements on both the number of samples and the number of sources. The proposed HetPEVI algorithm explicitly accounts for both uncertainties: limited observations within each source and a limited collection of sources overall. Treating these separately is central to how the method handles heterogeneous data.

The analysis shows that HetPEVI can solve the target task when the sources collectively provide good data coverage. Its optimality guarantee is qualified by a polynomial factor in the horizon length. Extensions to offline Markov games and robust offline reinforcement learning demonstrate that the same design ideas and analysis can apply beyond the initial setting.
summary.tldr: HetPEVI accounts for both sample and source uncertainty when learning offline from randomly perturbed versions of a target task.

title: Provably Efficient Offline Reinforcement Learning with Perturbed Data Sources

abstract: We formalize the problem of machine unlearning as design of efficient unlearning algorithms corresponding to learning algorithms which perform a selection of adaptive queries from structured query classes. We give efficient unlearning algorithms for linear and prefix-sum query classes. As applications, we show that unlearning in many problems, in particular, stochastic convex optimization (SCO), can be reduced to the above, yielding improved guarantees for the problem. In particular, for smooth Lipschitz losses and any $\rho>0$, our results yield an unlearning algorithm with excess population risk of $\tilde O\big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n\rho}\big)$ with unlearning query (gradient) complexity $\tilde O(\rho \cdot \text{Retraining Complexity})$, where $d$ is the model dimensionality and $n$ is the initial number of samples. For non-smooth Lipschitz losses, we give an unlearning algorithm with excess population risk $\tilde O\big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}+\big(\frac{\sqrt{d}}{n\rho}\big)^{1/2}\big)$ with the same unlearning query (gradient) complexity. Furthermore, in the special case of Generalized Linear Models (GLMs), such as those in linear and logistic regression, we get dimension-independent rates of $\tilde O\big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} +\frac{1}{(n\rho)^{2/3}}\big)$ and $\tilde O\big(\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} +\frac{1}{(n\rho)^{1/3}}\big)$ for smooth Lipschitz and non-smooth Lipschitz losses respectively. Finally, we give generalizations of the above from one unlearning request to dynamic streams consisting of insertions and deletions.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning seeks efficient ways to remove the influence of data from a learning procedure. This paper approaches the problem by representing learning algorithms as sequences of adaptive queries from structured classes. It develops efficient unlearning algorithms for linear and prefix-sum queries, then uses reductions to apply them to broader learning problems.

For stochastic convex optimization, the guarantees expose a tradeoff controlled by a positive parameter ρ. Unlearning uses roughly ρ times the gradient-query cost of retraining, up to logarithmic factors. For smooth Lipschitz losses, the excess population-risk bound combines a 1/√n term with √d/(nρ), where n is the original sample size and d is model dimension. For nonsmooth losses, the second contribution becomes the square root of that ratio.

For generalized linear models, including linear and logistic regression, the paper obtains dimension-independent rates, with different exponents for smooth and nonsmooth losses. It also extends the framework beyond one deletion request to streams containing insertions and deletions. The contribution is a reusable query-based route to unlearning guarantees that explicitly relate computational savings to statistical accuracy.
summary.tldr: A structured adaptive-query framework yields efficient unlearning algorithms with explicit computation–accuracy tradeoffs and extensions to dynamic data streams.

title: From Adaptive Query Release to Machine Unlearning

abstract: We propose Rockmate to control the memory requirements when training PyTorch DNN models. Rockmate is an automatic tool that starts from the model code and generates an equivalent model, using a predefined amount of memory for activations, at the cost of a few re-computations. Rockmate automatically detects the structure of computational and data dependencies and rewrites the initial model as a sequence of complex blocks. We show that such a structure is widespread and can be found in many models in the literature (Transformer based models, ResNet, RegNets,...). This structure allows us to solve the problem in a fast and efficient way, using an adaptation of Checkmate (too slow on the whole model but general) at the level of individual blocks and an adaptation of Rotor (fast but limited to sequential models) at the level of the sequence itself. We show through experiments on many models that Rockmate is as fast as Rotor and as efficient as Checkmate, and that it allows in many cases to obtain a significantly lower memory consumption for activations (by a factor of 2 to 5) for a rather negligible overhead (of the order of 10% to 20%). Rockmate is open source and available at https://github.com/topal-team/rockmate.

paragraphs: Training neural networks requires memory for intermediate activations. Rockmate automatically transforms PyTorch model code into an equivalent model that respects a specified activation-memory budget by recomputing some intermediate results. This gives users a way to trade additional computation for reduced memory use without manually organizing the recomputation strategy.

The tool detects computational and data dependencies and represents the model as a sequence of complex blocks. It adapts Checkmate within individual blocks and Rotor across the sequence. This division combines an approach that handles general dependencies with one that is fast for sequential structures. The authors identify this block structure in several model families, including Transformers, ResNet, and RegNets.

Experiments across many models find Rockmate as fast as Rotor and as efficient as Checkmate. In many cases, activation memory falls by a factor of two to five, with overhead around 10% to 20%. These are measured trade-offs rather than universal savings. The results show how recognizing model structure can make automatic recomputation both efficient to plan and useful during training.
summary.tldr: Rockmate automatically plans activation recomputation in PyTorch, substantially reducing memory with modest overhead in many tested models.

title: Rockmate: an Efficient, Fast, Automatic and Generic Tool for Re-materialization in PyTorch

abstract: Recent studies have shown that high disparities in effective learning rates (ELRs) across layers in deep neural networks can negatively affect trainability. We formalize how these disparities evolve over time by modeling weight dynamics (evolution of expected gradient and weight norms) of networks with normalization layers, predicting the evolution of layer-wise ELR ratios. We prove that when training with any constant learning rate, ELR ratios converge to 1, despite initial gradient explosion. We identify a "critical learning rate" beyond which ELR disparities widen, which only depends on current ELRs. To validate our findings, we devise a hyper-parameter-free warm-up method that successfully minimizes ELR spread quickly in theory and practice. Our experiments link ELR spread with trainability, a relationship that is most evident in very deep networks with significant gradient magnitude excursions.

Our experiments link ELR spread with trainability, a relationship that is most evident in very deep networks with significant gradient magnitude excursions.

paragraphs: Different layers of a normalized neural network can experience very different effective learning rates, even during the same training run. Large disparities can make training difficult. This paper models the evolution of expected gradient norms and weight norms to explain how those layerwise differences change over time.

Within this analysis, the authors prove that effective-learning-rate ratios converge to one under any constant learning rate, even when gradients initially explode. They also identify a critical learning rate, determined only by current effective learning rates, above which disparities widen. These statements describe different aspects of the dynamics: eventual equalization can coexist with an initial period in which differences become larger.

The authors turn the analysis into a warm-up method that requires no hyperparameters and quickly reduces the spread of effective learning rates in theory and practice. Experiments connect that spread to trainability, with the relationship clearest in very deep networks experiencing large changes in gradient magnitude. The work thus provides both an account of layer imbalance and a practical way to reduce it early in training.
summary.tldr: The paper explains layerwise effective-learning-rate dynamics and derives a hyperparameter-free warm-up that rapidly reduces their disparities.

title: On the Weight Dynamics of Deep Normalized Networks

abstract: Recent research in the field of graph neural network (GNN) has identified a critical issue known as "over-squashing," resulting from the bottleneck phenomenon in graph structures, which impedes the propagation of long-range information. Prior works have proposed a variety of graph rewiring concepts that aim at optimizing the spatial or spectral properties of graphs to promote the signal propagation. However, such approaches inevitably deteriorate the original graph topology, which may lead to a distortion of information flow. To address this, we introduce an expanded width-aware (PANDA) message passing, a new message passing paradigm where nodes with high centrality, a potential source of over-squashing, are selectively expanded in width to encapsulate the growing influx of signals from distant nodes. Experimental results show that our method outperforms existing rewiring methods, suggesting that selectively expanding the hidden state of nodes can be a compelling alternative to graph rewiring for addressing the over-squashing.

This problem is called over-squashing. Existing approaches often change graph connections to improve information propagation, but those changes alter the original topology and may distort how information flows.

PANDA takes a different architectural approach by selectively increasing the width of node representations. It targets nodes with high centrality, which can be potential sources of over-squashing. Giving these nodes larger hidden states lets them hold more of the information arriving from distant parts of the graph as message passing proceeds.

Experiments show PANDA outperforming existing graph-rewiring methods in the reported evaluations. The findings suggest that increasing representation capacity at selected nodes can be a compelling alternative to modifying graph connectivity. The central contribution is to connect where information accumulates with how much representational space a node receives, addressing the bottleneck through node capacity while respecting the graph’s original structure.
summary.tldr: PANDA mitigates graph information bottlenecks by widening selected node representations and outperforms rewiring methods in reported experiments.

title: PANDA: Expanded Width-Aware Message Passing Beyond Rewiring

abstract: Schrödinger bridge (SB) has emerged as the go-to method for optimizing transportation plans in diffusion models. However, SB requires estimating the intractable forward score functions, inevitably resulting in the (costly) implicit training loss based on simulated trajectories. To improve the scalability while preserving efficient transportation plans, we leverage variational inference to linearize the forward score functions (variational scores) of SB and restore simulation-free properties in training backward scores. We propose the variational Schrödinger diffusion model (VSDM), where the forward process is a multivariate diffusion and the variational scores are adaptively optimized for efficient transport. Theoretically, we use stochastic approximation to prove the convergence of the variational scores and show the convergence of the adaptively generated samples based on the optimal variational scores. Empirically, we test the algorithm in simulated examples and observe that VSDM is efficient in generations of anisotropic shapes and yields straighter sample trajectories compared to the single-variate diffusion. We also verify the scalability of the algorithm in real-world data and achieve competitive unconditional generation performance in CIFAR10 and conditional generation in time series modeling. Notably, VSDM no longer depends on warm-up initializations required by SB.

title: Variational Schrödinger Diffusion Models

abstract: The Bures-Wasserstein (BW) gradient descent method has gained considerable attention in various domains, including Gaussian barycenter, matrix recovery and variational inference problems, due to its alignment with the Wasserstein geometry of normal distributions. Despite its popularity, existing convergence analysis are often contingent upon specific loss functions, and the exploration of constrained settings within this framework remains limited. In this work, we make an attempt to bridge this gap by providing a general convergence rate guarantee for BW gradient descent when the Euclidean strong convexity of the loss and the constraints is assumed. In an effort to advance practical implementations, we also derive a closed-form solution for the projection onto BW distance-constrained sets, which enables the fast implementation of projected BW gradient descent for problems that arise in the constrained barycenter and distributionally robust optimization literature. Experimental results demonstrate significant improvements in computational efficiency and convergence speed, underscoring the efficacy of our method in practical scenarios.

paragraphs: Bures-Wasserstein gradient descent uses a geometry suited to normal distributions and appears in problems involving Gaussian barycenters, matrix recovery, and variational inference. Existing convergence analyses often depend on particular loss functions. This paper seeks a more general guarantee, while also addressing optimization problems that impose constraints.

The authors establish a convergence-rate guarantee under stated Euclidean strong-convexity assumptions on the loss and constraints. The result connects assumptions expressed in Euclidean terms with the behavior of an algorithm operating in Bures-Wasserstein geometry. Its scope therefore depends on those assumptions, rather than covering every objective for which the method might be used.

For practical implementation, the paper derives a closed-form projection onto sets defined by Bures-Wasserstein distance constraints. This enables fast projected updates in constrained barycenter and distributionally robust optimization problems. Experiments report substantial gains in computational efficiency and convergence speed. Together, the analysis and projection formula address two complementary needs: understanding when the method converges and making its constrained version efficient to execute.
summary.tldr: The paper gives conditional convergence guarantees and a closed-form projection for efficient constrained Bures-Wasserstein gradient descent.

title: On the Convergence of Projected Bures-Wasserstein Gradient Descent under Euclidean Strong Convexity

abstract: The Partial Credit Model (PCM) of Andrich (1978) and Masters (1982) is a fundamental model within the psychometric literature with wide-ranging modern applications. It models the integer-valued response that a subject gives to an item where there is a natural notion of monotonic progress between consecutive response values, such as partial scores on a test and customer ratings of a product. In this paper, we introduce a novel, time-efficient and accurate statistical spectral algorithm for inference under the PCM model. We complement our algorithmic contribution with in-depth non-asymptotic statistical analysis, the first of its kind in the literature. We show that the spectral algorithm enjoys the optimal error guarantee under three different metrics, all under reasonable sampling assumptions. We leverage the efficiency of the spectral algorithm to propose a novel EM-based algorithm for learning mixtures of PCMs. We perform comprehensive experiments on synthetic and real-life datasets covering education testing, recommendation systems, and financial investment applications. We show that the proposed spectral algorithm is competitive with previously introduced algorithms in terms of accuracy while being orders of magnitude faster.

This paper introduces a spectral algorithm for statistical inference under that model. Its goal is to combine accurate parameter estimation with substantially faster computation, making the model easier to use across different application settings.

Under sampling assumptions, the algorithm achieves optimal error guarantees according to three different metrics. Together, these findings connect a finite-sample theoretical guarantee with a practical speed advantage, and show how a faster inference component can support learning mixtures as well as individual models.
summary.tldr: A spectral Partial Credit Model estimator combines optimal finite-sample error guarantees under sampling assumptions with large empirical speed gains.

title: Novel Spectral Algorithms for the Partial Credit Model

abstract: The development of deep learning architectures is a resource-demanding process, due to a vast design space, long prototyping times, and high compute costs associated with at-scale model training and evaluation. We set out to simplify this process by grounding it in an end-to-end mechanistic architecture design (MAD) pipeline, encompassing small-scale capability unit tests predictive of scaling laws. Through a suite of synthetic token manipulation tasks such as compression and recall, designed to probe capabilities, we identify and test new hybrid architectures constructed from a variety of computational primitives. We experimentally validate the resulting architectures via an extensive compute-optimal and a new state-optimal scaling law analysis, training over 500 language models between 70M to 7B parameters. Surprisingly, we find MAD synthetics to correlate with compute-optimal perplexity, enabling accurate evaluation of new architectures via isolated proxy tasks. The new architectures found via MAD, based on simple ideas such as hybridization and sparsity, outperform state-of-the-art Transformer, convolutional, and recurrent architectures (Transformer++, Hyena, Mamba) in scaling, both at compute-optimal budgets and in overtrained regimes. Overall, these results provide evidence that performance on curated synthetic tasks can be predictive of scaling laws, and that an optimal architecture should leverage specialized layers via a hybrid topology.

paragraphs: Designing neural architectures is expensive because there are many possibilities and large training runs take substantial resources. The mechanistic architecture design pipeline, or MAD, uses small synthetic capability tests to guide this search. Tasks such as token compression and recall probe particular abilities before full-scale language-model evaluation.

The authors use these tests to identify hybrid architectures built from different computational primitives. They validate the designs by training more than 500 language models ranging from 70 million to 7 billion parameters. Their analysis examines compute-optimal scaling and introduces state-optimal scaling, connecting the small tests to behavior across model sizes and resource regimes.

Architectures found through MAD outperform the named Transformer, convolutional, and recurrent alternatives in both compute-optimal and overtrained regimes. These findings support curated synthetic tasks as useful predictors of scaling behavior and favor combining specialized layers. The evidence establishes a promising design strategy rather than a universal guarantee for every proxy task.
summary.tldr: Small synthetic capability tests guide hybrid architecture design and predict language-model scaling performance in extensive experiments.

title: Mechanistic Design and Scaling of Hybrid Architectures

abstract: We investigate the generalization error of statistical learning models in a Federated Learning (FL) setting. Specifically, we study the evolution of the generalization error with the number of communication rounds $R$ between $K$ clients and a parameter server (PS), i.e. the effect on the generalization error of how often the clients’ local models are aggregated at PS. In our setup, the more the clients communicate with PS the less data they use for local training in each round, such that the amount of training data per client is identical for distinct values of $R$. We establish PAC-Bayes and rate-distortion theoretic bounds on the generalization error that account explicitly for the effect of the number of rounds $R$, in addition to the number of participating devices $K$ and individual datasets size $n$. The bounds, which apply to a large class of loss functions and learning algorithms, appear to be the first of their kind for the FL setting. Furthermore, we apply our bounds to FL-type Support Vector Machines (FSVM); and derive (more) explicit bounds in this case. In particular, we show that the generalization bound of FSVM increases with $R$, suggesting that more frequent communication with PS diminishes the generalization power. This implies that the population risk decreases less fast with $R$ than does the empirical risk. Moreover, our bound suggests that the generalization error of FSVM decreases faster than that of centralized learning by a factor of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\log(K)/K})$. Finally, we provide experimental results obtained using neural networks (ResNet-56) which show evidence that not only may our observations for FSVM hold more generally but also that the population risk may even start to increase beyond some value of $R$.

The comparison holds each client's total training-data amount fixed: increasing the number of communication rounds means using less local training data in each round.

The authors derive PAC-Bayes and rate-distortion bounds that explicitly include communication rounds, client count, and dataset size. For federated support vector machines, a more explicit generalization bound grows with the number of rounds. The analysis also suggests a generalization-error advantage over centralized learning involving a factor of O(sqrt(log(K)/K)). Experiments with ResNet-56 provide evidence that the support-vector-machine observations may extend more broadly and that population risk may eventually rise with additional rounds. The findings challenge the expectation that more communication necessarily improves generalization under the paper's fixed-data setup.
summary.tldr: With total client data fixed, theoretical bounds and experiments suggest that more federated communication can worsen generalization.

title: Lessons from Generalization Error Analysis of Federated Learning: You May Communicate Less Often!

abstract: The burgeoning field of algorithms with predictions studies the problem of using possibly imperfect machine learning predictions to improve online algorithm performance. While nearly all existing algorithms in this framework make no assumptions on prediction quality, a number of methods providing uncertainty quantification (UQ) on machine learning models have been developed in recent years, which could enable additional information about prediction quality at decision time. In this work, we investigate the problem of optimally utilizing uncertainty-quantified predictions in the design of online algorithms. In particular, we study two classic online problems, ski rental and online search, where the decision-maker is provided predictions augmented with UQ describing the likelihood of the ground truth falling within a particular range of values. We demonstrate that non-trivial modifications to algorithm design are needed to fully leverage the UQ predictions. Moreover, we consider how to utilize more general forms of UQ, proposing an online learning framework that learns to exploit UQ to make decisions in multi-instance settings.
