paragraphs: Online algorithms must make decisions before all relevant information is available. Predictions can help, but their reliability matters. This paper studies how algorithms should use predictions accompanied by uncertainty information, specifically a stated likelihood that the true value lies within a particular range. The objective is to use that additional information effectively at decision time.

The authors investigate two classic online problems, ski rental and online search. Their results show that fully exploiting uncertainty-quantified predictions requires substantial changes to algorithm design. Providing an uncertainty range is therefore only part of the solution; the decision rule must be designed to make use of what that range says about possible outcomes.

The paper also considers more general forms of uncertainty quantification through an online learning framework for repeated problem instances. This framework learns how to use uncertainty information when making decisions across instances. The contribution connects predictive uncertainty with online decision-making at two levels: algorithms for particular problems and a learning approach that can adapt its use of uncertainty over repeated decisions.
summary.tldr: Online algorithms can use quantified predictive uncertainty, but doing so effectively requires redesigned decision rules and, across repeated instances, learning how to exploit it.

title: Online Algorithms with Uncertainty-Quantified Predictions

abstract: Recent text and image foundation models are incredibly impressive, and these models are attracting an ever-increasing portion of research resources. In this position piece we aim to shift the ML research community's priorities ever so slightly to a different modality: tabular data. Tabular data is the dominant modality in many fields, yet it is given hardly any research attention and significantly lags behind in terms of scale and power. **We believe the time is now to start developing tabular foundation models**, or what we coin a _Large Tabular Model_ (LTM). LTMs could revolutionise the way science and ML use tabular data: not as single datasets that are analyzed in a vacuum, but contextualized with respect to related datasets. The potential impact is far-reaching: from few-shot tabular models to automating data science; from out-of-distribution synthetic data to empowering multidisciplinary scientific discovery. We intend to excite reflections on the modalities we study, and convince some researchers to study Large Tabular Models.

paragraphs: This position paper argues that machine learning research should devote more attention to foundation models for tabular data. The authors see an imbalance: text and image models attract increasing resources, while tables remain central to many fields but receive comparatively little attention and lag in model scale and capability.

They propose prioritizing Large Tabular Models, or LTMs. The central vision is to analyze a table in the context of related datasets instead of treating each dataset as an isolated problem. This shifts the ambition from building a separate model around each table toward models that can draw useful context from a broader collection of tabular information.

The authors describe potential benefits including learning from few examples, automating parts of data science, generating out-of-distribution synthetic data, and supporting discovery across disciplines. These are proposed opportunities, rather than demonstrated outcomes of a new system. The paper's contribution is a research agenda and an argument about resource allocation: tabular foundation models could have broad scientific and practical impact if developed successfully.
summary.tldr: This position paper calls for Large Tabular Models that contextualize individual tables using related datasets.

title: Position: Why Tabular Foundation Models Should Be a Research Priority

abstract: The random feature (RF) approach is a well-established and efficient tool for scalable kernel methods, but existing literature has primarily focused on kernel ridge regression with random features (KRR-RF), which has limitations in handling heterogeneous data with heavy-tailed noises. This paper presents a generalization study of kernel quantile regression with random features (KQR-RF), which accounts for the non-smoothness of the check loss in KQR-RF by introducing a refined error decomposition and establishing a novel connection between KQR-RF and KRR-RF. Our study establishes the capacity-dependent learning rates for KQR-RF under mild conditions on the number of RFs, which are minimax optimal up to some logarithmic factors. Importantly, our theoretical results, utilizing a data-dependent sampling strategy, can be extended to cover the agnostic setting where the target quantile function may not precisely align with the assumed kernel space. By slightly modifying our assumptions, the capacity-dependent error analysis can also be applied to cases with Lipschitz continuous losses, enabling broader applications in the machine learning community. To validate our theoretical findings, simulated experiments and a real data application are conducted.

paragraphs: Random features make kernel methods more scalable, but much of their theory concerns ridge regression. This paper studies kernel quantile regression with random features, motivated by heterogeneous data and heavy-tailed noise. Quantile learning targets positions within an outcome distribution, making its statistical objective different from the ridge-regression setting that dominates existing analysis.

A central technical obstacle is the nonsmooth check loss used for quantile regression. The authors develop a refined error decomposition and connect the quantile estimator to kernel ridge regression with random features. Under mild conditions on the feature count, they establish learning rates that depend on the kernel space's capacity and are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors.

With data-dependent feature sampling, the theory also covers an agnostic setting in which the target quantile function need not belong exactly to the assumed kernel space. Simulations and a real-data application support the theoretical findings, connecting scalable approximation to statistical guarantees beyond the usual ridge-regression objective.
summary.tldr: Kernel quantile regression with random features achieves capacity-dependent rates that are minimax optimal up to logarithmic factors under the stated conditions.

title: Optimal Kernel Quantile Learning with Random Features

abstract: While Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning is vital in many real-world scenarios, its application to graph data still remains under-explored. We unveil that a critical challenge for PU learning on graph lies on the edge heterophily, which directly violates the $\textit{irreducibility assumption}$ for $\textit{Class-Prior Estimation}$ (class prior is essential for building PU learning algorithms) and degenerates the latent label inference on unlabeled nodes during classifier training. In response to this challenge, we introduce a new method, named $\textit{$\underline{G}$raph $\underline{P}$U Learning with $\underline{L}$abel Propagation Loss}$ (GPL). Specifically, GPL considers learning from PU nodes along with an intermediate heterophily reduction, which helps mitigate the negative impact of the heterophilic structure. We formulate this procedure as a bilevel optimization that reduces heterophily in the inner loop and efficiently learns a classifier in the outer loop. Extensive experiments across a variety of datasets have shown that GPL significantly outperforms baseline methods, confirming its effectiveness and superiority.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning uses known positive examples alongside examples whose labels are unknown. On graphs, connections between nodes add information but can also undermine learning. This paper identifies edge heterophily, where connected nodes have different labels, as a central difficulty for this setting.

The analysis finds that heterophily violates the irreducibility assumption used in estimating the class prior, a quantity needed for building positive-unlabeled learning algorithms. It also degrades inference of hidden labels on unlabeled nodes during classifier training. The issue therefore affects both estimating the class balance and using graph relationships to learn predictions.

The proposed GPL method incorporates an intermediate heterophily-reduction step into learning from positive and unlabeled nodes. It expresses the process as bilevel optimization: an inner loop reduces heterophily, while an outer loop trains the classifier. Experiments across varied datasets show significant gains over baseline methods. These findings support explicitly addressing graph structure when adapting positive-unlabeled learning, because problematic connections can interfere with multiple parts of the learning pipeline.
summary.tldr: GPL improves graph positive-unlabeled learning by reducing heterophily within a bilevel classifier-training procedure.

title: Unraveling the Impact of Heterophilic Structures on Graph Positive-Unlabeled Learning

abstract: Text data has become extremely valuable due to the emergence of machine learning algorithms that learn from it. A lot of high-quality text data generated in the real world is private and therefore cannot be shared or used freely due to privacy concerns. Generating synthetic replicas of private text data with a formal privacy guarantee, i.e., differential privacy (DP), offers a promising and scalable solution. However, existing methods necessitate DP finetuning of large language models (LLMs) on private data to generate DP synthetic data. This approach is not viable for proprietary LLMs (e.g., GPT-3.5) and also demands considerable computational resources for open-source LLMs. Lin et al. (2024) recently introduced the Private Evolution (PE) algorithm to generate DP synthetic images with only API access to diffusion models. In this work, we propose an augmented PE algorithm, named Aug-PE, that applies to the complex setting of text. We use API access to an LLM and generate DP synthetic text without any model training. We conduct comprehensive experiments on three benchmark datasets. Our results demonstrate that Aug-PE produces DP synthetic text that yields competitive utility with the SOTA DP finetuning baselines. This underscores the feasibility of relying solely on API access of LLMs to produce high-quality DP synthetic texts, thereby facilitating more accessible routes to privacy-preserving LLM applications.

However, existing methods necessitate DP finetuning of large language models (LLMs) on private data to generate DP synthetic data. This approach is not viable for proprietary LLMs (e.g., GPT-3.5) and also demands considerable computational resources for open-source LLMs. Lin et al. paragraphs: Private text can be valuable for machine learning while remaining difficult to share. Synthetic text with a differential privacy guarantee offers one route to making its information useful. Existing approaches described in this paper require privately fine-tuning a language model, which demands substantial computation and is unavailable when a proprietary model can only be accessed through an API.

The authors introduce Aug-PE, an extension of the Private Evolution approach previously developed for synthetic images. Aug-PE adapts that approach to text and uses language-model API access to generate differentially private synthetic data. Crucially, the process requires no model training, removing fine-tuning as a prerequisite for this form of private text generation.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets find that the synthetic text provides utility competitive with state-of-the-art private fine-tuning methods. The result supports the feasibility of obtaining useful, formally private synthetic text through API access alone. It establishes an alternative workflow for privacy-preserving language-model applications without claiming that API access by itself supplies the privacy guarantee.
summary.tldr: Aug-PE generates differentially private synthetic text using only language-model APIs, with utility competitive with private fine-tuning in the reported benchmarks.

title: Differentially Private Synthetic Data via Foundation Model APIs 2: Text

abstract: Image fusion integrates essential information from multiple images into a single composite, enhancing structures, textures, and refining imperfections. Existing methods predominantly focus on pixel-level and semantic visual features for recognition, but often overlook the deeper text-level semantic information beyond vision. Therefore, we introduce a novel fusion paradigm named image Fusion via vIsion-Language Model (FILM), for the first time, utilizing explicit textual information from source images to guide the fusion process. Specifically, FILM generates semantic prompts from images and inputs them into ChatGPT for comprehensive textual descriptions. These descriptions are fused within the textual domain and guide the visual information fusion, enhancing feature extraction and contextual understanding, directed by textual semantic information via cross-attention. FILM has shown promising results in four image fusion tasks: infrared-visible, medical, multi-exposure, and multi-focus image fusion. We also propose a vision-language dataset containing ChatGPT-generated paragraph descriptions for the eight image fusion datasets across four fusion tasks, facilitating future research in vision-language model-based image fusion. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/Zhaozixiang1228/IF-FILM.

paragraphs: Image fusion combines useful information from multiple images into one composite. FILM introduces explicit textual descriptions into that process, extending approaches centered on pixels and visual recognition features. Its premise is that language can supply semantic context that helps determine how information from the source images should be combined.

The pipeline first produces semantic prompts from the images and sends them to ChatGPT to obtain fuller descriptions. It combines those descriptions in the textual domain, then uses the resulting semantic information to guide visual fusion through cross-attention. It also introduces a vision-language dataset with ChatGPT-generated paragraph descriptions for eight image-fusion datasets spanning those four tasks. The contribution includes both a method for using language during fusion and a descriptive data resource that supports further research on this approach across several kinds of source imagery.
summary.tldr: FILM combines textual descriptions of source images and uses them to guide visual fusion through cross-attention.

title: Image Fusion via Vision-Language Model

abstract: Effective modelling of large-scale spatio-temporal datasets is essential for many domains, yet existing approaches often impose rigid constraints on the input data, such as requiring them to lie on fixed-resolution grids. With the rise of foundation models, the ability to process diverse, heterogeneous data structures is becoming increasingly important. Neural processes (NPs), particularly transformer neural processes (TNPs), offer a promising framework for such tasks, but struggle to scale to large spatio-temporal datasets due to the lack of an efficient attention mechanism. To address this, we introduce gridded pseudo-token TNPs which employ specialised encoders and decoders to handle unstructured data and utilise a processor comprising gridded pseudo-tokens with efficient attention mechanisms. Furthermore, we develop equivariant gridded TNPs for applications where exact or approximate translation equivariance is a useful inductive bias, improving accuracy and training efficiency. Our method consistently outperforms a range of strong baselines in various synthetic and real-world regression tasks involving large-scale data, while maintaining competitive computational efficiency. Experiments with weather data highlight the potential of gridded TNPs and serve as just one example of a domain where they can have a significant impact.

paragraphs: Large datasets spanning space and time often contain observations that do not fit a fixed-resolution grid. Transformer neural processes offer a way to model such data, but their attention mechanisms can become difficult to scale. This paper introduces gridded pseudo-token transformer neural processes to combine flexible handling of observations with more efficient internal computation.

Specialized encoders and decoders handle unstructured data, while the central processor operates on pseudo-tokens arranged on a grid. This separates the organization of the input observations from the structure used for efficient attention. The authors also develop versions with exact or approximate translation equivariance, a property that makes spatial shifts produce corresponding shifts in model behavior when that bias suits the application.

Across the reported synthetic and real-world regression tasks, the method consistently outperforms strong baselines while retaining competitive computational efficiency. The equivariant versions improve accuracy and training efficiency in suitable applications. Weather experiments provide a concrete demonstration of the approach’s potential for large-scale spatial and temporal modeling.
summary.tldr: Gridded internal tokens make transformer neural processes scalable while preserving support for unstructured spatial and temporal observations.

title: Gridded Transformer Neural Processes for Spatio-Temporal Data

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have exhibited exceptional performance across a spectrum of natural language processing tasks. However, their substantial sizes pose considerable challenges, particularly in computational demands and inference speed, due to their quadratic complexity. In this work, we have identified a key pattern: certain seemingly meaningless separator tokens (i.e., punctuations) contribute disproportionately to attention scores compared to semantically meaningful tokens. This observation suggests that information of the segments between these separator tokens can be effectively condensed into the separator tokens themselves without significant information loss. Guided by this insight, we introduce SepLLM, a plug-and-play framework that accelerates inference by compressing these segments and eliminating redundant tokens. Additionally, we implement efficient kernels for training acceleration. Experimental results across training-free, training-from-scratch, and post-training settings demonstrate SepLLM’s effectiveness. Notably, using the Llama-3-8B backbone, SepLLM achieves over 50% reduction in KV cache on the GSM8K-CoT benchmark while maintaining comparable performance. Furthermore, in streaming settings, SepLLM effectively processes sequences of up to 4 million tokens or more while maintaining consistent language modeling capabilities.

paragraphs: Language model attention can become computationally expensive as sequences grow. This paper identifies an unexpected pattern: separator tokens, including punctuation, can receive disproportionately high attention compared with tokens carrying more obvious semantic content. The observation suggests that separators can hold information from the segments between them.

SepLLM uses that pattern to compress segments into separator tokens and remove redundant tokens. It is designed as a plug-and-play inference framework, and the authors also implement efficient kernels to accelerate training. They evaluate the approach without additional training, when training from scratch, and after training, examining its usefulness across several ways of deploying a model.

With a Llama-3-8B backbone on GSM8K-CoT, SepLLM reduces the key-value cache by more than 50% while maintaining comparable performance. In streaming experiments, it processes sequences of four million tokens or more with consistent language modeling capabilities. The results support separator-based compression as a practical way to reduce retained token information, with the stated performance evidence tied to the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SepLLM compresses text segments into separator tokens, reducing inference storage while maintaining comparable performance in reported evaluations.

title: SepLLM: Accelerate Large Language Models by Compressing One Segment into One Separator

abstract: We consider the branch-length estimation problem on a bifurcating tree: a character evolves along the edges of a binary tree according to a two-state symmetric Markov process, and we seek to recover the edge transition probabilities from repeated observations at the leaves. This problem arises in phylogenetics, and is related to latent tree graphical model inference. In general, the log-likelihood function is non-concave and may admit many critical points. Nevertheless, simple coordinate maximization has been known to perform well in practice, defying the complexity of the likelihood landscape. In this work, we provide the first theoretical guarantee as to why this might be the case. We show that deep inside the Kesten-Stigum reconstruction regime, provided with polynomially many $m$ samples (assuming the tree is balanced), there exists a universal parameter regime (independent of the size of the tree) where the log-likelihood function is strongly concave and smooth with high probability. On this high-probability likelihood landscape event, we show that the standard coordinate maximization algorithm converges exponentially fast to the maximum likelihood estimator, which is within $O(1/\sqrt{m})$ from the true parameter, provided a sufficiently close initial point.

title: Sample Complexity of Branch-length Estimation by Maximum Likelihood

abstract: Poisson Surface Reconstruction is a widely-used algorithm for reconstructing a surface from an oriented point cloud. To facilitate applications where only partial surface information is available, or scanning is performed sequentially, a recent line of work proposes to incorporate uncertainty into the reconstructed surface via Gaussian process models. The resulting algorithms first perform Gaussian process interpolation, then solve a set of volumetric partial differential equations globally in space, resulting in a computationally expensive two-stage procedure. In this work, we apply recently-developed techniques from geometric Gaussian processes to combine interpolation and surface reconstruction into a single stage, requiring only one linear solve per sample. The resulting reconstructed surface samples can be queried locally in space, without the use of problem-dependent volumetric meshes or grids. These capabilities enable one to (a) perform probabilistic collision detection locally around the region of interest, (b) perform ray casting without evaluating points not on the ray’s trajectory, and (c) perform next-view planning on a per-ray basis. They also do not requiring one to approximate kernel matrix inverses with diagonal matrices as part of intermediate computations, unlike prior methods. Results show that our approach provides a cleaner, more-principled, and more-flexible stochastic surface reconstruction pipeline.

paragraphs: Reconstructing a surface from oriented points becomes more complicated when scans are incomplete or arrive sequentially. Gaussian-process approaches represent uncertainty in the reconstructed surface, but earlier pipelines first interpolate the data and then solve volumetric equations across space. That two-stage procedure can be computationally expensive even when an application only needs information in a small region.

These capabilities connect uncertainty-aware reconstruction to the particular geometry a downstream task needs. The reported results support a more flexible and principled pipeline, with reconstruction and querying organized around a single-stage formulation.
summary.tldr: Geometric Gaussian processes combine uncertain surface interpolation and reconstruction into one solve per sample while enabling local queries.

title: Stochastic Poisson Surface Reconstruction with One Solve using Geometric Gaussian Processes

abstract: We study the problem of efficiently aggregating the preferences of items from multiple information sources (oracles) and infer the ranking under both the weak stochastic transitivity (WST) and the strong stochastic transitivity (SST) conditions. When the underlying preference model satisfies the WST condition, we propose an algorithm named RMO-WST, which has a bi-level design: at the higher level, it actively allocates comparison budgets to all undetermined pairs until the full ranking is recovered; at the lower level, it attempts to compare the pair of items and selects the more accurate oracles simultaneously. We prove that the sample complexity of RMO-WST is $ \tilde O( N\sum_{i=2}^{N}H_{\sigma^{-1}(i),{\sigma^{-1}(i-1)}} )$, where $N$ is the number of items to rank, $H$ is a problem-dependent hardness factor, and $\sigma^{-1}(i)$ represents the $i$-th best item. We also provide a tight lower bound that matches the upper bound of approximate ranking under the WST condition, answering a previously open problem. In addition, when the SST condition is satisfied, we propose an algorithm named RMO-SST, which can achieve an $\tilde{O}(\sum_{i=1}^{N} H_i \log(N))$ sample complexity. This outperforms the best-known sample complexity by a factor of $\log(N)$. The theoretical advantages of our algorithms are verified by empirical experiments in a simulated environment.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to rank items efficiently when comparisons come from multiple information sources, called oracles. It considers two assumptions about the consistency of noisy preferences: weak and strong stochastic transitivity. The central challenge is to allocate comparisons effectively while also learning which sources provide more accurate information about the items being compared.

Under weak stochastic transitivity, RMO-WST uses two levels of decision-making. The upper level assigns comparison budgets to unresolved pairs until the ranking is recovered. The lower level compares a chosen pair while selecting more accurate oracles. The authors derive a sample complexity bound involving item count and problem-dependent hardness, and establish a matching lower bound for approximate ranking under this condition.

Under strong stochastic transitivity, RMO-SST improves the best-known sample complexity by a factor of log(N), where N is the number of items. Simulated experiments support the algorithms’ theoretical advantages. The separate results show how stronger consistency assumptions permit greater comparison efficiency, while the weak-condition lower bound resolves a previously open question about approximate ranking.
summary.tldr: Two algorithms efficiently rank items using multiple noisy oracles, with theoretical guarantees under weak and strong stochastic transitivity.

title: Ranking with Multiple Oracles: From Weak to Strong Stochastic Transitivity

abstract: Existing reward shaping techniques for sparse-reward reinforcement learning generally fall into two categories: novelty-based exploration bonuses and significance-based hidden state values. The former promotes exploration but can lead to distraction from task objectives, while the latter facilitates stable convergence but often lacks sufficient early exploration. To address these limitations, we propose Dual Random Networks Distillation (DuRND), a novel reward shaping framework that efficiently balances exploration and exploitation in a unified mechanism. DuRND leverages two lightweight random network modules to simultaneously compute two complementary rewards: a novelty reward to encourage directed exploration and a contribution reward to assess progress toward task completion. With low computational overhead, DuRND excels in high-dimensional environments with challenging sparse rewards, such as Atari, VizDoom, and MiniWorld, outperforming several benchmarks.

To address these limitations, we propose Dual Random Networks Distillation (DuRND), a novel reward shaping framework that efficiently balances exploration and exploitation in a unified mechanism. paragraphs: Sparse rewards make reinforcement learning difficult because an agent receives little feedback about whether its actions are useful. Reward shaping adds feedback between those infrequent task rewards. The paper identifies a tension between rewarding novelty, which encourages exploration but can distract from the objective, and rewarding significant states, which supports stable convergence but can leave early exploration weak.

Dual Random Networks Distillation, or DuRND, combines these aims within one framework. Two lightweight random network modules produce complementary signals: a novelty reward for directed exploration and a contribution reward for progress toward completing the task. This gives the agent feedback about both encountering something new and moving toward its objective.

The authors report low computational overhead and strong performance in high-dimensional environments with sparse rewards, including Atari, VizDoom, and MiniWorld. DuRND outperforms several benchmarks in these evaluations. The findings support the value of coordinating exploration and task progress through a shared reward-shaping mechanism, rather than leaving either signal to carry the full learning problem.
summary.tldr: DuRND uses two lightweight random networks to reward both novelty and task progress, improving learning in evaluated sparse-reward environments.

title: Catching Two Birds with One Stone: Reward Shaping with Dual Random Networks for Balancing Exploration and Exploitation

abstract: Little is known about the training dynamics of equivariant neural networks, in particular how it compares to data augmented training of their non-equivariant counterparts. Recently, neural tangent kernels (NTKs) have emerged as a powerful tool to analytically study the training dynamics of wide neural networks. In this work, we take an important step towards a theoretical understanding of training dynamics of equivariant models by deriving neural tangent kernels for a broad class of equivariant architectures based on group convolutions. As a demonstration of the capabilities of our framework, we show an interesting relationship between data augmentation and group convolutional networks. Specifically, we prove that they share the same expected prediction over initializations at all training times and even off the data manifold. In this sense, they have the same training dynamics. We demonstrate in numerical experiments that this still holds approximately for finite-width ensembles. By implementing equivariant NTKs for roto-translations in the plane ($G=C_{n}\ltimes\mathbb{R}^{2}$) and 3d rotations ($G=\mathrm{SO}(3)$), we show that equivariant NTKs outperform their non-equivariant counterparts as kernel predictors for histological image classification and quantum mechanical property prediction.

paragraphs: Equivariant networks build transformations such as rotations into their architecture, while data augmentation exposes a model to transformed examples. This paper studies how the training dynamics of these approaches relate. It derives neural tangent kernels for a broad class of equivariant architectures based on group convolutions, creating a mathematical framework for analyzing wide networks.

Within that framework, the authors prove that group convolutional networks and the corresponding data-augmentation approach have the same predictions when averaged over initializations, at every training time. The equality also applies away from the data manifold. This is a statement about expected predictions, rather than identical behavior for every individual initialized model.

Numerical experiments show approximate agreement for finite-width ensembles as well. The authors implement kernels for planar rotations and translations and for three-dimensional rotations. As kernel predictors, these equivariant versions outperform non-equivariant counterparts on histological image classification and quantum mechanical property prediction. The work therefore connects an analytical comparison of training dynamics with practical evaluations of symmetry-aware kernels.
summary.tldr: Equivariant neural tangent kernels establish an expected-prediction equivalence with data augmentation and improve prediction in two evaluated domains.

title: Equivariant Neural Tangent Kernels

abstract: While the activations of neurons in deep neural networks usually do not have a simple human-understandable interpretation, sparse autoencoders (SAEs) can be used to transform these activations into a higher-dimensional latent space which can be more easily interpretable. However, SAEs can have millions of distinct latents, making it infeasible for humans to manually interpret each one. In this work, we build an open-source automated pipeline to generate and evaluate natural language interpretations for SAE latents using LLMs. We test our framework on SAEs of varying sizes, activation functions, and losses, trained on two different open-weight LLMs. We introduce five new techniques to score the quality of interpretations that are cheaper to run than the previous state of the art. One of these techniques, intervention scoring, evaluates the interpretability of the effects of intervening on a latent, which we find explains latents that are not recalled by existing methods. We propose guidelines for generating better interpretations that remain valid for a broader set of activating contexts, and discuss pitfalls with existing scoring techniques. Our code is available at https://github.com/EleutherAI/delphi.

paragraphs: Individual neural activations are often difficult to explain in human terms. Sparse autoencoders transform them into a larger collection of latent features that can be more interpretable, but this can create millions of features to examine. The paper addresses that scale problem with an open-source pipeline that uses language models to generate and evaluate natural-language explanations.

The authors test the pipeline on sparse autoencoders with different sizes, activation functions, and training losses, built on two open-weight language models. They introduce five ways to score explanations that cost less to run than the previous state of the art. This makes evaluating interpretations part of the automated workflow, alongside producing them.

One method, intervention scoring, examines whether an explanation captures the effects of intervening on a latent feature. The authors find that this reveals interpretable latents missed by existing methods. They also offer guidance for explanations that hold across a broader range of activating contexts and identify pitfalls in scoring. The contribution therefore concerns both scalable explanation and how to assess its reliability.
summary.tldr: An automated pipeline generates and evaluates explanations for sparse-autoencoder features, including through the effects of interventions.

title: Automatically Interpreting Millions of Features in Large Language Models

abstract: Secure Aggregation (SA) is a cornerstone of Federated Learning (FL), ensuring that user updates remain hidden from servers. The advanced Flamingo (S&P’23) has realized multi-round aggregation and improved efficiency. However, it still faces several key challenges: scalability issues with dynamic user participation, a lack of verifiability for server-side aggregation results, and vulnerability to Model Inconsistency Attacks (MIA) caused by a malicious server distributing inconsistent models. To address these issues, we propose $\textit{Janus}$, a generic SA scheme based on dual-server architecture. Janus ensures security against up to $n-2$ colluding clients (where $n$ is the total client count), which prevents privacy breaches for non-colluders. Additionally, Janus is model-independent, ensuring applicability across any FL model without specific adaptations. Furthermore, Janus introduces a new cryptographic primitive, Separable Homomorphic Commitment, which enables clients to efficiently verify the correctness of aggregation. Finally, extensive experiments show that Janus not only significantly enhances security but also reduces per-client communication and computation overhead from logarithmic to constant scale, with a tolerable impact on model performance.
originalAbstract: Secure Aggregation (SA) is a cornerstone of Federated Learning (FL), ensuring that user updates remain hidden from servers. The advanced Flamingo (S&P’23) has realized multi-round aggregation and improved efficiency. However, it still faces several key challenges: scalability issues with dynamic user participation, a lack of verifiability for server-side aggregation results, and vulnerability to Model Inconsistency Attacks (MIA) caused by a malicious server distributing inconsistent models. To address these issues, we propose $\textit{Janus}$, a generic SA scheme based on dual-server architecture. Janus ensures security against up to $n-2$ colluding clients (where $n$ is the total client count), which prevents privacy breaches for non-colluders. Additionally, Janus is model-independent, ensuring applicability across any FL model without specific adaptations. Furthermore, Janus introduces a new cryptographic primitive, Separable Homomorphic Commitment, which enables clients to efficiently verify the correctness of aggregation. Finally, extensive experiments show that Janus not only significantly enhances security but also reduces per-client communication and computation overhead from logarithmic to constant scale, with a tolerable impact on model performance.

paragraphs: Federated learning relies on secure aggregation to combine client updates while keeping individual updates hidden from servers. Existing multi-round aggregation still faces challenges when participation changes, when clients need to verify an aggregate, and when a malicious server distributes inconsistent models. Janus proposes a dual-server aggregation scheme to address these issues.

The scheme provides security against collusion by as many as n−2 clients, where n is the total number of clients, protecting the updates of those who do not collude. Its design is independent of the particular federated learning model. Janus also introduces Separable Homomorphic Commitment, a cryptographic component that lets clients efficiently check whether aggregation was performed correctly.

Experiments show security improvements and a reduction in per-client communication and computation overhead from logarithmic to constant scale, with an impact on model performance described as tolerable. This connects privacy and verification with the practical cost of participation. The paper’s contribution is a reusable aggregation design that makes checking server results part of the protocol while reducing the burden placed on each client.
summary.tldr: Janus combines dual-server secure aggregation with client verification and constant-scale per-client overhead for federated learning.

title: Janus: Dual-Server Multi-Round Secure Aggregation with Verifiability for Federated Learning

abstract: Modern language models represent probability distributions over character strings as distributions over (shorter) token strings derived via a deterministic tokenizer, such as byte-pair encoding. While this approach is highly effective at scaling up language models to large corpora, its current incarnations have a concerning property: the model assigns nonzero probability mass to an exponential number of noncanonical token encodings of each character string—these are token strings that decode to valid character strings but are impossible under the deterministic tokenizer (i.e., they will never be seen in any training corpus, no matter how large). This misallocation is both erroneous, as noncanonical strings never appear in training data, and wasteful, diverting probability mass away from plausible outputs. These are avoidable mistakes! In this work, we propose methods to enforce canonicality in token-level language models, ensuring that only canonical token strings are assigned positive probability. We present two approaches: (1) canonicality by conditioning, leveraging test-time inference strategies without additional training, and (2) canonicality by construction, a model parameterization that guarantees canonical outputs but requires training. We demonstrate that fixing canonicality mistakes improves the likelihood of held-out data for several models and corpora.

paragraphs: A deterministic tokenizer assigns a particular token sequence to a character string. Yet a token-level language model can assign probability to other sequences that decode to the same text. These noncanonical sequences never arise from that tokenizer in training, but the paper identifies exponentially many such encodings for each character string.

The authors propose restricting positive probability to canonical sequences. One approach enforces the restriction through conditioning at inference time, without additional training. The other builds it into the model's parameterization, guaranteeing canonical outputs but requiring training. These provide two different ways to align the model's output space with the tokenizer's actual behavior.

Across several models and corpora, correcting canonicality mistakes improves held-out data likelihood. The result shows that tokenization consistency has a measurable consequence for probability allocation. By eliminating token sequences that the deterministic encoding process would never produce, the methods redirect probability toward the canonical representation used by the data, with empirical benefits for the evaluated language models.
summary.tldr: Enforcing canonical token encodings prevents probability allocation to tokenizer-impossible sequences and improves held-out likelihood in the reported evaluations.

title: Language Models over Canonical Byte-Pair Encodings

abstract: We introduce Knowledge Swapping, a novel task designed to selectively regulate knowledge of a pretrained model by enabling the forgetting of user-specified information, retaining essential knowledge, and acquiring new knowledge simultaneously. By delving into the analysis of knock-on feature hierarchy, we find that incremental learning typically progresses from low-level representations to higher-level semantics, whereas forgetting tends to occur in the opposite direction—starting from high-level semantics and moving down to low-level features. Building upon this, we propose to benchmark the knowledge swapping task with the strategy of Learning Before Forgetting. Comprehensive experiments on various tasks like image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation validate the effectiveness of the proposed strategy. The source code is available at https://github.com/xingmingyu123456/KnowledgeSwapping.

paragraphs: Knowledge Swapping defines a model-update task with three simultaneous goals: remove user-specified information, preserve essential knowledge, and learn something new. This makes successful updating depend on more than either learning or forgetting alone. A pretrained model must change selectively while retaining the information that should remain useful.

The authors study how learning and forgetting affect the hierarchy of features inside a model. Their analysis finds that incremental learning typically moves from lower-level representations toward higher-level meanings. Forgetting tends to follow the reverse direction, affecting higher-level semantics before lower-level features. These different patterns motivate a strategy called Learning Before Forgetting.

The strategy gives knowledge acquisition priority before carrying out the forgetting stage within the broader swapping task. Experiments on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation validate its effectiveness. The paper’s contribution is both the combined task definition and an ordering strategy informed by observed feature dynamics, offering a way to study acquiring, retaining, and removing knowledge together.
summary.tldr: Knowledge Swapping combines selective learning, retention, and forgetting, with experiments supporting a strategy that learns before it forgets.

title: Knowledge Swapping via Learning and Unlearning

abstract: Automatic evaluation methods based on large language models (LLMs) are emerging as the standard tool for assessing the instruction-following abilities of LLM-based agents. The most common method in this paradigm, pairwise comparisons with a baseline model, critically depends on the assumption of transitive preferences. However, the validity of this assumption remains largely unexplored. In this study, we investigate the presence of non-transitivity within the AlpacaEval framework and analyze its effects on model rankings. We find that LLM judges exhibit non-transitive preferences, leading to rankings that are sensitive to the choice of the baseline model. To mitigate this issue, we show that round-robin tournaments combined with Bradley-Terry models of preference can produce more reliable rankings. Notably, our method increases both the Spearman correlation and the Kendall correlation with Chatbot Arena (95.0% $\rightarrow$ 96.4% and 82.1% $\rightarrow$ 86.3% respectively). To address the computational cost of round-robin tournaments, we propose Swiss-Wise Iterative Matchmaking (Swim) tournaments, using a dynamic matching strategy to capture the benefits of round-robin tournaments while maintaining computational efficiency.

paragraphs: Using a language model to judge pairs of answers can produce rankings of instruction-following systems. But comparisons against a single baseline depend critically on preferences behaving transitively: if one system is preferred to a second and that second to a third, the ordering should remain consistent. This paper investigates that assumption within AlpacaEval.

The authors find non-transitive preferences in LLM judges and show that model rankings can change with the selected baseline. They mitigate this by combining round-robin comparisons with Bradley-Terry preference models. Comparing systems across a broader set of opponents gives the ranking process more information than comparisons centered on one baseline.

The resulting rankings align more closely with Chatbot Arena: Spearman correlation rises from 95.0% to 96.4%, and Kendall correlation from 82.1% to 86.3%. Because round-robin evaluation is computationally costly, the authors also propose Swim tournaments. Their dynamic matchmaking strategy aims to retain the benefits of broader comparisons while making the evaluation process more efficient.
summary.tldr: LLM judges exhibit non-transitive preferences, and tournament-based comparisons produce rankings less dependent on a single baseline.

title: Investigating Non-Transitivity in LLM-as-a-Judge

abstract: Simplicity is a powerful inductive bias. In reinforcement learning, regularization is used for simpler policies, data augmentation for simpler representations, and sparse reward functions for simpler objectives, all that, with the underlying motivation to increase generalizability and robustness by focusing on the essentials. Supplementary to these techniques, we investigate how to promote simple behavior throughout the episode. To that end, we introduce a modification of the reinforcement learning problem that additionally maximizes the total correlation within the induced trajectories. We propose a practical algorithm that optimizes all models, including policy and state representation, based on a lower-bound approximation. In simulated robot environments, our method naturally generates policies that induce periodic and compressible trajectories, and that exhibit superior robustness to noise and changes in dynamics compared to baseline methods, while also improving performance in the original tasks.

paragraphs: This paper investigates how to encourage a reinforcement learning agent to behave simply across an entire episode. Existing approaches can favor simpler policies, simpler representations of observations, or simpler objectives. The authors explore a complementary target: the structure of the sequence of states and actions produced as the agent performs its task.

Their approach modifies the learning problem to also maximize total correlation within these trajectories. Total correlation measures statistical dependence among variables; here, it provides a way to encourage structure across a trajectory. The motivation is that simplicity in an agent’s overall behavior could help it focus on patterns that remain useful when conditions change.

To make this objective practical, the authors propose an algorithm based on a lower-bound approximation. It optimizes the policy and the state representation along with the other models. This connects how the agent represents its situation and chooses its actions to the structure of the resulting behavior.

In simulated robot environments, the method produces periodic trajectories with patterns that repeat, as well as trajectories that are compressible. The resulting policies show greater robustness to noise and changes in dynamics than the baseline methods, while also improving performance on the original tasks. These findings support trajectory structure as a useful additional target for learning in the environments studied.
summary.tldr: Encouraging statistical dependence within an agent’s trajectories produces periodic, compressible behavior and improves task performance and robustness in simulated robot environments.

title: Maximum Total Correlation Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Many real-world graphs support multiple predictive tasks over the same underlying structure, creating an opportunity to reuse supervision across node classification (NC) and link prediction (LP). However, existing evaluations often rely on incompatible splits, observed-graph assumptions, and negative sampling rules, making conclusions about same-graph cross-task transfer unreliable. We formalize same-graph NC–LP transfer and propose a leakage-free protocol that fixes node and edge splits, uses a shared message-passing graph that excludes evaluated edges, and employs fixed negatives for LP. Across three backbones (GCN, GraphSAGE, GPS), we find transfer is strongly directional and predictable: NC$\to$LP is consistently beneficial on homophilic graphs, while LP$\to$NC is fragile and can even degrade accuracy under naive representation reuse. LP$\to$NC becomes reliably positive mainly in a structure-dominant regime where LP is easy but NC is unsaturated, suggesting LP acts as structural pretraining. Finally, we introduce CoTask Score (CTS) to summarize joint NC+LP utility when a shared encoder must serve both tasks, and show that simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can guide mechanism choice and help avoid negative transfer.

paragraphs: A graph can support both node classification and link prediction, creating opportunities to reuse what a model learns between tasks. This paper argues that such transfer is hard to assess when evaluations use incompatible splits, different observed graphs, or changing negative examples. It introduces a leakage-free protocol with fixed node and edge splits, a shared message-passing graph excluding evaluated edges, and fixed link-prediction negatives.

Across GCN, GraphSAGE, and GPS, transfer depends strongly on direction. Node classification consistently helps link prediction on homophilic graphs. The reverse direction is fragile: simply reusing link-prediction representations can reduce classification accuracy. It becomes reliably helpful mainly when structure dominates, link prediction is easy, and node classification still has room to improve.

These results suggest that link prediction can serve as structural pretraining under suitable conditions. The authors also introduce CoTask Score to summarize joint utility when one encoder serves both tasks. Simple dataset statistics, especially homophily, can help select transfer mechanisms and avoid harmful reuse.
summary.tldr: A controlled graph-transfer protocol reveals directional benefits and identifies conditions under which sharing representations helps or harms.

title: Same Graph Cross-Task Transfer in GNNs: Protocols and Predictors

abstract: We provide evidence of performative chain-of-thought (CoT) in reasoning models, where a model becomes strongly confident in its final answer, but continues generating tokens without revealing its internal belief. Our analysis compares activation probing, early forced answering, and a CoT monitor across two large models (DeepSeek-R1 671B & GPT-OSS 120B) and find task difficulty-specific differences: The model’s final answer is decodable from activations far earlier in CoT than a monitor is able to say, especially for easy recall-based MMLU questions. We contrast this with genuine reasoning in difficult multihop GPQA-Diamond questions. Despite this, inflection points (e.g., backtracking, ‘aha’ moments) occur almost exclusively in responses where probes show large belief shifts, suggesting these behaviors track genuine uncertainty rather than learned “reasoning theater." Finally, probe-guided early exit reduces tokens by up to 80% on MMLU and 30% on GPQA-Diamond with similar accuracy, positioning attention probing as an efficient tool for detecting performative reasoning and enabling adaptive computation.

paragraphs: A long written reasoning trace does not necessarily show when a model settled on its answer. This paper compares three ways of examining that timing: probing internal activations, forcing an early answer, and monitoring the visible chain of thought. The analysis covers DeepSeek-R1 671B and GPT-OSS 120B.

For easy recall-oriented MMLU questions, the eventual answer can be decoded from activations well before a monitor can identify it from the reasoning text. The authors interpret this as evidence of performative reasoning: generation continues after strong internal confidence has developed. Difficult multihop GPQA-Diamond questions show a contrasting pattern of genuine reasoning. Backtracking and apparent breakthroughs occur almost exclusively when probes detect large belief changes, suggesting these visible events often reflect real uncertainty.

The authors use probe signals to stop generation early, reducing token use by up to 80% on MMLU and 30% on GPQA-Diamond while maintaining similar accuracy. The findings support adapting computation to the question and internal state, rather than assuming all visible reasoning tokens contribute equally.
summary.tldr: Internal probes reveal that some reasoning continues after answers are already decodable, enabling substantial token savings through early stopping.

title: Reasoning Theater: Disentangling Model Beliefs from Chain-of-Thought

abstract: Tool-use agents that address day-to-day digital tasks such as ordering groceries must not only operate applications, but also interact with the user, e.g., to ask clarification questions, prompt for confirmation, and inform the user when the instruction is infeasible. However, current benchmarks for evaluating agent-user interactions do not capture the diversity of such interactions. Further, they operate in small environments with few, often non-state-changing, APIs. To address this gap, we introduce AppWorld-UL, a “user-in-the-loop” benchmark of 516 challenging tasks requiring diverse agent-user interactions. Building upon the AppWorld framework with 9 popular simulated apps like Amazon and Spotify, we systematically modify original tasks to introduce ambiguities and constraints that necessitate various types of agent-user interaction. User behavior is simulated by an LLM prompted to respond with carefully designed knowledge boundaries, offering more reliable simulation than the unconstrained or overly rigid alternatives used in prior work. Our evaluation reveals that a state-of-the-art LLM, Claude Opus 4.7, achieves only 48.6% success on AppWorld-UL, and only 35.7% on the harder, compositional subset. On the stricter, scenario-level metric, compositional task performance drops to only 21.3%. Our analysis reveals that correct user-interaction is crucial for success. This demonstrates the benchmark’s difficulty and its potential to advance research on user-in-the-loop tool-use agents.

It may need to clarify an ambiguous request, obtain confirmation, or explain why an instruction cannot be completed. AppWorld-UL evaluates these interactions in a richer application environment than benchmarks built around a few mostly non-state-changing interfaces.

summary.tldr: AppWorld-UL tests whether tool-use agents can handle the clarifications, confirmations, and constraints required by realistic user interactions.

title: AppWorld-UL: Benchmarking Diverse Agent-User Interactions for Tool-Use

abstract: Open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation is a core capability for robotics and AR/VR, but prior methods trade one bottleneck for another: multi-stage 2D+3D pipelines aggregate foundation-model outputs at hundreds of seconds per scene, while pseudo-labeled end-to-end approaches rely on fragmented masks and external region proposals. We present SpaCeFormer, a proposal-free space-curve transformer that runs in 0.12–0.30 seconds per scene across standard benchmarks, 2–3 orders of magnitude faster than multi-stage 2D+3D pipelines. We pair it with SpaCeFormer-3M, the largest open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation dataset (3.0M multi-view-consistent captions over 604K instances from 7.4K scenes) built through multi-view mask clustering and multi-view VLM captioning; it reaches 21$\times$ higher mask recall than prior single-view pipelines (54.3% vs 2.5% at IoU$>$0.5). SpaCeFormer combines spatial window attention with Morton-curve serialization for spatially coherent features, and uses a RoPE-enhanced decoder to predict instance masks directly from learned queries without external proposals. On ScanNet200 we achieve 11.1 zero-shot mAP, a 2.8$\times$ improvement over the prior best proposal-free method; on ScanNet++ and Replica, we reach 22.9 and 24.1 mAP, surpassing all prior methods including those using multi-view 2D inputs.

paragraphs: Open-vocabulary 3D instance segmentation identifies individual objects in scenes using flexible language descriptions. Existing approaches can be slow or depend on external proposals for candidate object regions. SpaCeFormer predicts instance masks directly from learned queries, aiming to remove that proposal dependency while accelerating scene processing.

The model combines spatial window attention with Morton-curve serialization, which arranges scene information to preserve spatial coherence. Its decoder adds rotary positional encoding. The authors also build SpaCeFormer-3M using multi-view mask clustering and vision-language captioning, producing 3.0 million captions over 604,000 instances from 7,400 scenes. Its reported mask recall is 54.3%, compared with 2.5% for prior single-view pipelines at the stated overlap threshold.

SpaCeFormer runs in 0.12–0.30 seconds per scene across the evaluated benchmarks. It achieves 11.1 zero-shot mAP on ScanNet200, 2.8 times the prior best proposal-free result, and reports 22.9 and 24.1 mAP on ScanNet++ and Replica. The findings combine a faster direct-prediction architecture with training data that better consolidates objects across views.
summary.tldr: SpaCeFormer combines direct 3D mask prediction and multi-view captioned training data to deliver fast, improved open-vocabulary instance segmentation.

title: SpaCeFormer: Fast Proposal-Free Open-Vocabulary 3D Instance Segmentation

abstract: Planning with a generative model aims to estimate the value of a state using as few simulator calls as possible. SmoothCruiser achieves problem-independent complexity $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-4})$ by exploiting the smoothness of the entropy-regularized Bellman backup, but its estimator is only first-order. We show that the sample-complexity exponent of SmoothCruiser-type planners is governed by the order $\beta$ of the local Taylor remainder, giving oracle complexity $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-(2+2/(\beta-1))})$: the first-order case $\beta=2$ recovers SmoothCruiser, while a second-order/cubic remainder $\beta=3$ yields $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$. We reach this regime with an optimal-transport-smoothed Bellman backup over action distributions, which has a closed form, a policy gradient, and a Lipschitz Hessian, and whose quadratic correction admits an unbiased cross-product estimator. The resulting SecondOrderSmoothCruiser achieves $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-3})$ oracle complexity for fixed OT parameters, and we relate the OT, entropy-regularized, and unregularized objectives through explicit regularization-bias bounds.

paragraphs: Planning with a simulator requires estimating state values while limiting simulator calls. This paper studies how the local smoothness used by a planning estimator controls that cost. It shows that, for SmoothCruiser-type planners, the sample-complexity exponent depends on the order β of the local Taylor remainder, yielding complexity proportional to ε^−(2+2/(β−1)), up to logarithmic factors.

A first-order estimator with a quadratic remainder recovers the existing ε^−4 dependence. A second-order estimator with a cubic remainder improves it to ε^−3. To achieve this regime, the authors smooth the Bellman backup over action distributions using optimal transport. The resulting backup has a closed form, a policy gradient, and a Lipschitz Hessian; its quadratic correction admits an unbiased cross-product estimator.

The resulting SecondOrderSmoothCruiser achieves ε^−3 oracle complexity, up to logarithmic factors, for fixed optimal-transport parameters. The paper also provides explicit bounds on the bias separating optimal-transport-smoothed, entropy-regularized, and unregularized objectives. Those bounds matter because the computational guarantee applies to a smoothed planning objective, and smoothing changes the value being estimated.
summary.tldr: Optimal-transport smoothing enables a second-order planner with ε^−3 oracle complexity for fixed smoothing parameters, improving the earlier ε^−4 dependence.

title: Second-Order Smooth Planning with Optimal-Transport Bellman Smoothing

abstract: 3D Scene Graph Generation (3DSGG) aims to create a structured representation of 3D environment by identifying objects as nodes and their relations as edges. Existing 3DSGG methods based on RGB-D sequences typically put much focus on the adaption of neural networks to robust node and edge feature extraction in complex 3D scenes, yet ignoring the inherent intra-class diversity within each class and inter-class similarity between different categories associated with nodes and edges. In this work, we develop GMPSSG, a novel Gaussian Mixture-distributed Prototype mining framework for 3DSGG. Specifically, we model different categories with independent Gaussian Mixture-distributed Prototype to effectively mitigate inter-class similarity, while employing multiple Gaussian components within each prototype to capture intra-class diversity. Moreover, Prototype-anchored Representation Learning is introduced to construct a well-structured and mutually independent category space; Topology-aware Prototype Interaction is devised to capture implicit co-occurrence priors within the scene, and leverage them to calibrate prototype distributions, thereby ensuring the plausibility of node-edge matching. Experiments on 3DSSG dataset demonstrate GMPSSG outperforms various top-leading methods. Our code is available at GMPSSG.
originalAbstract: 3D Scene Graph Generation (3DSGG) aims to create a structured representation of 3D environment by identifying objects as nodes and their relations as edges. Existing 3DSGG methods based on RGB-D sequences typically put much focus on the adaption of neural networks to robust node and edge feature extraction in complex 3D scenes, yet ignoring the inherent intra-class diversity within each class and inter-class similarity between different categories associated with nodes and edges. In this work, we develop GMPSSG, a novel Gaussian Mixture-distributed Prototype mining framework for 3DSGG. Specifically, we model different categories with independent Gaussian Mixture-distributed Prototype to effectively mitigate inter-class similarity, while employing multiple Gaussian components within each prototype to capture intra-class diversity. Moreover, Prototype-anchored Representation Learning is introduced to construct a well-structured and mutually independent category space; Topology-aware Prototype Interaction is devised to capture implicit co-occurrence priors within the scene, and leverage them to calibrate prototype distributions, thereby ensuring the plausibility of node-edge matching. Experiments on 3DSSG dataset demonstrate GMPSSG outperforms various top-leading methods. Our code is available at GMPSSG.

paragraphs: A 3D scene graph represents objects as nodes and their relationships as edges. Generating these graphs from RGB-D sequences requires distinguishing categories that can look similar while accommodating substantial variation within each category. GMPSSG addresses these category-level issues alongside the extraction of object and relationship features.

The framework assigns each category its own prototype represented by a Gaussian mixture. Separate category prototypes help reduce confusion between categories, while multiple components within a prototype represent diversity inside one category. Prototype-anchored representation learning organizes the feature space around these category structures, aiming to make the categories distinct and internally expressive.

A topology-aware interaction mechanism then uses implicit co-occurrence patterns in the scene to adjust prototype distributions. This helps align object and relationship predictions into plausible node-edge combinations. On the 3DSSG dataset, GMPSSG outperforms several leading methods. The findings support combining flexible category representations with scene-level relational information, so predictions account for both what an individual feature resembles and how it fits the surrounding graph.
summary.tldr: GMPSSG uses Gaussian-mixture category prototypes and scene co-occurrence patterns to improve 3D object-and-relation graph generation.

title: Learning Gaussian Mixture-distributed Prototypes for 3D Scene Graph Generation from RGB-D Sequences

abstract: Developing reliable machine translation (MT) systems hinges on our ability to distinguish superior translations from inferior ones. However, existing evaluation paradigms, whether limited to coarse overall rankings or misaligned with human preferences, fail to deliver interpretable, fine-grained feedback in reference-free settings. We present a Fine-Grained Ranking Evaluation method (FiRE) that leverages off-the-shelf large language models to perform criterion-driven pairwise comparison across three complementary dimensions: faithfulness, fluency, and consistency of style, instead of producing a single holistic judgment. To enable rigorous meta-evaluation of evaluation paradigms in the absence of any suitable testbed, we construct the first human-annotated, reference-free benchmark for fine-grained ranking evaluation, achieving substantial inter-annotator agreement. Through meta-evaluation on this benchmark and existing MQM datasets, FiRE demonstrably outperforms regression-based and error-analysis metrics in aligning with human comparative judgments, while providing more informative insights into translation quality. Finally, our examination of LLM evaluator biases (position and self-enhancement) and their handling of tied cases offers guidance for more nuanced MT evaluation. Code and benchmark resources are available at https://github.com/wygao8/FiRE-MT.

paragraphs: Translation evaluation is more useful when it explains why one translation is preferable to another. FiRE addresses reference-free evaluation, where a reference translation is unavailable. Instead of asking for one overall judgment, it uses existing language models to compare translation pairs separately for faithfulness, fluency, and consistency of style.

Separating these criteria makes the judgment more interpretable: a comparison can identify which aspect of quality favors each candidate. To evaluate this approach, the authors construct a human-annotated benchmark for fine-grained, reference-free ranking. They report substantial agreement among annotators, providing support for using these judgments to assess automated evaluators.

On that benchmark and existing MQM datasets, FiRE aligns more closely with human comparative judgments than regression-based and error-analysis metrics. It also provides more detailed feedback about translation quality. The paper examines position bias, evaluators’ tendency to favor their own outputs, and handling of ties. These analyses help explain how language-model comparisons should be interpreted alongside the reported gains in agreement with human rankings.
summary.tldr: FiRE compares translations by faithfulness, fluency, and style, producing rankings that better match human judgments in the reported evaluations.

title: FiRE: Fine-grained Ranking Evaluation for Machine Translation

abstract: Visuomotor policies aim to learn complex manipulation tasks from expert demonstrations. However, generating smooth and coherent trajectories remains challenging, as it requires balancing proximal precision with distal foresight. Existing approaches typically focus on optimizing intra-chunk action distributions, often neglecting the inter-chunk coherence. Consequently, inter-chunk discontinuities significantly impede the learning of coherent long-horizon actions. To overcome this limitation and achieve a synergetic balance between precision and foresight, we propose FocalPolicy, a foresight-aware visuomotor policy that combines Frequency-Optimized Chunking with Locally Anchored flow matching. We introduce a foresight composite objective that supervises time-domain alignment within the proximal actions while regularizing frequency-domain structure over multiple future action chunks to improve cross-chunk coherence. To efficiently learn complex action distributions, we design locally anchored sampling to enhance target signal propagation efficiency during consistency flow matching training. Extensive experiments demonstrate that FocalPolicy outperforms existing approaches and confirm the generalizability of our modules to other baselines. Project website: https://focalpolicy.github.io/

paragraphs: Robot policies often generate actions in chunks, but individually plausible chunks do not necessarily join into a smooth trajectory. FocalPolicy targets these transitions while balancing precision in the immediate future with planning farther ahead. The paper identifies discontinuities between chunks as a significant obstacle to learning coherent long-horizon manipulation.

Its training objective treats near-term and longer-term behavior differently. It supervises the timing and alignment of nearby actions directly, while regularizing frequency structure across several future chunks. This gives training a way to account for broader patterns of motion spanning chunk boundaries, rather than evaluating only the action distribution inside each separate chunk.

The policy also introduces locally anchored sampling during consistency flow-matching training to improve how efficiently target signals propagate. Experiments report stronger performance than existing approaches and show that the proposed modules also benefit other baselines. Together, the results support addressing cross-chunk coherence explicitly and pairing that objective with a training mechanism for learning complex action distributions efficiently.
summary.tldr: FocalPolicy combines near-term action alignment, longer-range frequency regularization, and locally anchored flow matching to improve motion coherence.

title: FocalPolicy: Frequency-Optimized Chunking and Locally Anchored Flow Matching for Coherent Visuomotor Policy

abstract: Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering (KB-VQA) remains a challenging task, particularly when queries require precise identification and grounding of fine-grained entities within large-scale knowledge base. Existing methods often treat visual and textual signals in isolation and rely heavily on image-centric retrieval, which makes them sensitive to visual ambiguities. To address these limitations, we propose EntRAG, an entity-centric retrieval-augmented generation framework. Our approach first introduces EntBind to align query representations with multimodal entity embeddings by explicitly binding entity tokens to latent visual features, retrieving a set of relevant candidate entities. A reranking mechanism is applied to these candidate entities to select the most informative context by combining entity-level alignment with overall contextual relevance. The selected evidence is incorporated into context-aware generation module to produce final answer. By explicitly operating at the entity level, EntRAG achieves more consistent and reliable results. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EntRAG consistently outperforms prior methods, achieving scores of 46.1 on E-VQA and 44.5 on InfoSeek.

paragraphs: Knowledge-based visual question answering requires connecting an image and question to relevant external knowledge. Fine-grained entity identification makes this difficult: visual ambiguity can send retrieval toward the wrong knowledge, particularly when image and text signals are handled separately. EntRAG organizes retrieval around entities to make this connection more explicit.

Its EntBind component binds entity tokens to latent visual features and aligns the query with multimodal entity representations. This produces candidate entities that reflect both visual information and the question. A reranker then selects useful context by considering entity-level alignment alongside relevance to the overall query. The selected evidence feeds a context-aware answer generator.

The approach matters because identifying the right entity and choosing useful evidence are treated as connected steps before answer generation. Experiments report consistently stronger results than prior methods, including scores of 46.1 on E-VQA and 44.5 on InfoSeek. These findings support entity-centered retrieval as a way to obtain more consistent and reliable answers when precise visual grounding is required.
summary.tldr: EntRAG connects visual features to entities, reranks their evidence, and uses the selected context to improve knowledge-based visual question answering.

title: EntRAG: Entity-Centric Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering

abstract: Time-Dependent Differential Equations (TDDEs) model dynamical processes across science and engineering, but time-critical applications require solvers that deliver high-fidelity trajectories under stringent latency constraints. Most existing TDDE solvers are limited by time discretization, forcing a latency-accuracy trade-off where smaller step sizes capture high-fidelity trajectories but incur prohibitive runtime, while larger steps meet real-time budgets at the cost of trajectory distortion. Dynamical System Machines (DSMs) offer a promising alternative by computing through continuous physical evolution, yet existing DSMs struggle to capture the spatiotemporal complexity of TDDEs. This work introduces DS-TS, a novel TDDE solver that is both accurate and efficient by leveraging the unique computational advantages of DSMs. DS-TS integrates three key innovations: (1) Excitatory-Inhibitory Inspired Coupling to better model complex spatial interactions; (2) State-aware Dynamic Nonlinearity to enable dynamic spatiotemporal correlations; and (3) Hierarchical Temporal Integration to capture high-order temporal dependencies. Experiments demonstrate that DS-TS achieves high-fidelity solutions while delivering orders-of-magnitude improvements in speed ($\sim 10^3\times$) and energy efficiency ($\sim 10^5\times$) compared to baseline solvers.
