paragraphs: Solving time-dependent differential equations quickly often requires a compromise: small time steps improve trajectory fidelity but increase runtime, while large steps can distort the solution. Dynamical System Machines offer another computational route through continuous physical evolution. This paper develops DS-TS to help such machines represent the complex spatial and temporal interactions these equations require.

DS-TS introduces three mechanisms. Excitatory–inhibitory inspired coupling models complex spatial interactions. State-aware dynamic nonlinearity supports correlations that change with the system’s state. Hierarchical temporal integration captures higher-order dependencies over time. These components address different aspects of the same problem: representing a system whose behavior depends jointly on spatial relationships and temporal evolution.

Experiments report high-fidelity solutions alongside approximately a thousandfold speed improvement and a hundred-thousandfold energy-efficiency improvement relative to baseline solvers. These are reported experimental comparisons rather than universal speed guarantees. The results suggest that improving the representational capabilities of physical dynamical computation can make it useful for time-critical equation solving, where both accurate trajectories and low latency are central requirements.
summary.tldr: DS-TS equips physical dynamical computation with spatial and temporal mechanisms for fast, energy-efficient differential-equation solving.

title: Solving Time-Dependent Differential Equations with Physical Dynamical Systems

abstract: Classical dynamic programming algorithms such as Smith-Waterman, edit distance, and constituency parsing solve structured combinatorial problems using hard constraints. Soft relaxations replace hard $\max$ or $\min$ operators with differentiable probabilistic models whose gradients correspond to alignment or parsing marginals, but existing approaches typically treat the DP algorithm itself as fixed, relying on hand-tuned gap penalties, edit costs, span penalties, and temperatures. We show how to learn these parameters directly from data: the marginals these algorithms produce are themselves first-order derivatives, so learning them is inherently a second-order problem. We derive efficient Hessian-vector products and cross-Jacobians for twelve dynamic programming algorithms spanning alignment, edit distance, and parsing; both derivative families admit closed-form covariance expressions under the induced Gibbs distribution. We implement these operators as fused CUDA kernels in d$^2$p, achieving $100$-$20{,}000\times$ speedups over standard PyTorch and making end-to-end parameter learning practical at modern scales. We then demonstrate that learning these parameters is critical in practice. In protein structure alignment, freezing gap penalties collapses performance from $0.74$ to $0.32$ $F_1$ (and to $0.13$ at lower encoder capacity), while jointly learning them recovers biologically meaningful gap regimes and reaches $0.75$ $F_1$ and $0.445$ lDDT, $91$% of the TM-align lDDT ceiling. The same machinery transfers to constituency parsing, where a structured CKY CRF matches dense per-span supervision to within $0.003$ $F_1$ on English with no direct parse-tree structural supervision.

Differentiable versions soften hard choices into probability distributions, but their penalties and temperatures are often fixed manually. This paper makes those settings learnable, allowing the structure of the algorithm itself to adapt alongside the model supplying its inputs.

The technical difficulty is that alignment and parsing probabilities already arise as first derivatives. Training through them therefore requires second-order information. The authors derive efficient Hessian-vector products and cross-Jacobians for twelve algorithms, expressing both through covariances under their probabilistic models. Fused CUDA implementations in d²p deliver reported speedups of 100–20,000 times over standard PyTorch.

In protein alignment, fixing gap penalties lowers F1 from 0.74 to 0.32, with a further drop at lower encoder capacity; jointly learned settings reach 0.75 F1 and 0.445 lDDT. In English constituency parsing, a structured CKY model comes within 0.003 F1 of dense span supervision without direct parse-tree structural supervision. The contribution combines practical differentiation machinery with evidence that learned structural choices materially affect performance.
summary.tldr: d²p makes structural dynamic-programming parameters learnable through efficient second-order derivatives, improving alignment and parsing.

title: d$^2$p: Structured Soft Attention Is All You Need

abstract: Despite considerable progress in the development of machine-text detectors, the ease with which machine-text can be manipulated to evade detection has led to suggestions that the problem is inherently intractable. In this work, we investigate the limits of such evasion strategies. We demonstrate that while current attacks, ranging from prompt engineering to detector-guided optimization can effectively degrade performance of standard detectors, they fail to erase the underlying stylistic "fingerprints" of machine text. We show that few-shot detectors that utilize the stylistic feature space are robust to these evasion attempts, reliably detecting samples even from models explicitly tuned to prevent detection. This raises the question: does style represent a universal defense against machine-detection attacks? We demonstrate that the answer is "no" by introducing a novel paraphrasing approach that simultaneously optimizes for undetectability and adherence to specific human styles. We show that unlike prior methods, this attack effectively evades all considered detectors, including those that utilize writing style. However, we find that this evasion is not absolute: as the number of documents available for analysis grows, the human and machine distributions become distinguishable again. Overall, our findings suggest that reliable machine-text detection requires moving beyond single-document analysis to multi-document analysis.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether successful attacks on machine-text detectors actually remove the signals that distinguish generated writing. The authors examine attacks ranging from prompt changes to detector-guided optimization. Although these approaches weaken standard detectors, the experiments show that recognizable stylistic patterns can remain in the resulting text.

Few-shot detectors operating on stylistic features remain robust to these attacks, including text from models explicitly tuned to avoid detection. However, the authors also test whether style provides a universal defense. They introduce a paraphrasing approach that jointly seeks undetectability and conformity to particular human writing styles. This approach evades every detector considered, including the style-based ones.

The successful evasion still has a boundary: as more documents become available for analysis, differences between the human and machine distributions reappear. The findings therefore distinguish hiding signals in individual documents from making collections of generated text indistinguishable. They suggest that reliable detection may require examining multiple documents together, rather than relying exclusively on judgments about isolated texts.
summary.tldr: Style-aware attacks evade the tested text detectors, but detectable differences reappear when larger document collections are analyzed.

title: Attacks on Machine-Text Detectors Retain Stylistic Fingerprints

abstract: We investigate the extent to which an LLM’s hidden-state geometry can be recovered from its behavior in psycholinguistic experiments. Across eight instruction-tuned transformer models, we run two experimental paradigms—similarity-based forced choice and free association—over a shared 5,000-word vocabulary, collecting 17.5M+ trials to build behavior-based similarity matrices. Using representational similarity analysis, we compare behavioral geometries to layerwise hidden-state similarity and benchmark against FastText, BERT, and cross-model consensus. We find that forced-choice behavior aligns substantially more with hidden-state geometry than free association. In a held-out-words regression, behavioral similarity (especially forced choice) predicts unseen hidden-state similarities beyond lexical baselines and cross-model consensus, indicating that behavior-only measurements retain recoverable information about internal semantic geometry. Finally, we discuss implications for the ability of behavioral tasks to uncover hidden cognitive states.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much a language model's observable word judgments reveal about its internal representation of meaning. The authors compare two behavioral tasks: choosing between alternatives based on similarity and freely producing associated words. Across eight instruction-tuned transformers, they collect more than 17.5 million trials over a shared vocabulary of 5,000 words.

The responses become similarity matrices describing which words the models treat as related. Representational similarity analysis then compares these behavioral patterns with similarities in hidden states at different layers. FastText, BERT, and agreement across models provide reference points for assessing how much information the behavioral measurements contain.

Forced-choice judgments align substantially more closely with hidden-state geometry than free associations do. In a regression test using held-out words, behavioral similarities also predict unseen internal similarities beyond the lexical baselines and cross-model consensus. The findings indicate that behavior contains recoverable information about internal semantic structure, especially when elicited through forced choice. They support a route to studying hidden representations through carefully selected tasks without establishing complete recovery of those representations.
summary.tldr: Forced-choice word judgments reveal more about language models' hidden semantic geometry than free association does.

title: From Associations to Activations: Comparing Behavioral and Hidden-State Semantic Geometry in LLMs

abstract: Learning-augmented algorithms have received significant attention in recent years, particularly in the context of online optimization. Motivated by the high computational cost of generating predictions, a growing line of work studies the tradeoff between performance guarantees and the number of predictions used in learning-augmented algorithms for problems such as caching and metrical task systems. In this paper, we extend this line of research to online metric matching by developing parsimonious learning-augmented algorithms and establishing lower bounds on their performance. Our approach extends the Follow-the-Prediction framework to the parsimonious setting by filling in a virtual prediction in the absence of an actual prediction, using an online metric matching algorithm that maintains good intermediate matchings throughout its execution. We complement our theoretical results with an empirical evaluation, demonstrating the practical effectiveness of our approach.

paragraphs: This paper studies online metric matching when an algorithm can receive predictions, but generating those predictions is costly. The objective is to understand how much performance can be retained while consulting predictions sparingly. It extends research on prediction budgets to matching problems, making the number of predictions part of the algorithmic tradeoff.

The approach adapts the Follow-the-Prediction framework so that it can operate even when an actual prediction is unavailable. At those moments, it constructs a virtual prediction using an online matching algorithm that maintains good intermediate matchings. This gives the prediction-following procedure a substitute input derived from its ongoing matching process, allowing it to continue without a fresh prediction each time.

The authors establish theoretical performance guarantees and lower bounds, addressing both what their algorithms achieve and limits on achievable performance. An empirical evaluation also supports the approach's practical effectiveness. The contribution is a way to reason jointly about matching quality and prediction use, rather than treating predictive advice as an unlimited resource with no computational cost.
summary.tldr: Parsimonious online matching algorithms use virtual predictions to reduce reliance on costly predictive advice while retaining performance guarantees.

title: Parsimonious Learning-Augmented Online Metric Matching

abstract: Automated red-teaming of Large Language Models (LLMs) commonly relies on attack success rates (ASR) as a proxy for real-world harm, implicitly assuming that judge-detected violations correspond to actionable risk. In practice, safety judges are imperfect, and outputs that satisfy automated criteria for harm can vary widely in their operational usefulness. In this work, we investigate whether model failure modes can be reshaped so that, when defenses fail, they preferentially produce reduced-actionability outputs rather than highly actionable harm. Inspired by honeypots in computer security, we construct responses that are frequently flagged as harmful by automated judges yet provide limited real-world operational value, and treat them as hard negatives in the safety training pipeline. Our findings show that shaping how models fail under attack can improve overall safety by reducing both the real-world impact and the frequency of harmful failures, and serves as a practical complement to ASR-based evaluations.

That count treats detected violations as a proxy for real-world harm, even though judges are imperfect and flagged responses differ in operational usefulness. This paper asks whether safety training can influence the kind of failure a model produces when an attack succeeds.

Inspired by security honeypots, the authors construct responses that automated judges frequently flag as harmful but that provide limited practical value for carrying out harm. They use these responses as hard negatives in the safety-training pipeline. The aim is to shift failures toward less actionable content while also reducing harmful behavior overall.

The reported findings show that shaping failure modes can reduce both the frequency of harmful failures and their real-world impact. This makes actionability a useful consideration alongside attack success rates. The contribution is a training approach that addresses the consequences of failed defenses, together with evidence that safety evaluation benefits from distinguishing a judge-detected violation from an operationally useful harmful response.
summary.tldr: Honeypot-inspired safety training aims to make adversarial failures less actionable while reducing the frequency of harmful responses.

title: Training with Honeypots: Reshaping How LLMs Fail Under Adversarial Attacks

abstract: High dynamic range novel view synthesis (HDR-NVS) remains challenged by geometric artifacts and radiometric distortions under multi-exposure conditions, primarily due to existing methods ignoring exposure and over-relying on color cues. Inspired by the integrated processing of color and structure of the human visual system (HVS), we propose Expo-GS, a novel framework that decomposes HDR-NVS into three interpretable components, namely, Irradiance Field Training, Geometry Field Training, and Interactive Joint Training. Central to Expo-GS is the exposure-aware signed distance function (Expo-SDF), which dynamically reweights geometric supervision via localized exposure reliability estimation, suppressing noisy gradients from unstable regions while enhancing structure learning in well-exposed areas. Building on this, we design an interactive optimization strategy that synchronizes Gaussian primitive growth and pruning with evolving Expo-SDF cues, enabling exposure-aware density control and eliminating hallucinated structures near exposure transitions. Experiments show that Expo-GS significantly outperforms prior methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets. It achieves a peak PSNR of 39.06 dB under HDR settings and up to 41.38 dB in the LDR-OE configuration, excelling in preserving high-frequency textures and maintaining structural consistency.
originalAbstract: High dynamic range novel view synthesis (HDR-NVS) remains challenged by geometric artifacts and radiometric distortions under multi-exposure conditions, primarily due to existing methods ignoring exposure and over-relying on color cues. Inspired by the integrated processing of color and structure of the human visual system (HVS), we propose Expo-GS, a novel framework that decomposes HDR-NVS into three interpretable components, namely, Irradiance Field Training, Geometry Field Training, and Interactive Joint Training. Central to Expo-GS is the exposure-aware signed distance function (Expo-SDF), which dynamically reweights geometric supervision via localized exposure reliability estimation, suppressing noisy gradients from unstable regions while enhancing structure learning in well-exposed areas. Building on this, we design an interactive optimization strategy that synchronizes Gaussian primitive growth and pruning with evolving Expo-SDF cues, enabling exposure-aware density control and eliminating hallucinated structures near exposure transitions. Experiments show that Expo-GS significantly outperforms prior methods on both synthetic and real-world datasets. It achieves a peak PSNR of 39.06 dB under HDR settings and up to 41.38 dB in the LDR-OE configuration, excelling in preserving high-frequency textures and maintaining structural consistency.

paragraphs: Expo-GS reconstructs scenes for high-dynamic-range novel-view synthesis from images with different exposures. Exposure differences can corrupt both brightness estimates and inferred geometry, particularly when reconstruction relies heavily on color. The framework separates learning into irradiance, geometry, and interactive joint training so that appearance and structure can inform each other.

Its central component is an exposure-aware signed distance function, a representation used to guide surface geometry. It estimates local exposure reliability and adjusts the strength of geometric supervision accordingly. Unstable regions contribute less noisy guidance, while well-exposed regions contribute more. Joint optimization also coordinates the growth and pruning of Gaussian primitives with this evolving geometric information.

This exposure-aware control targets hallucinated structures near exposure transitions while preserving detailed surfaces. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report significant improvements over prior methods, with peak PSNR values of 39.06 dB in HDR settings and up to 41.38 dB in the LDR-OE configuration. The reported gains include preservation of high-frequency textures and improved structural consistency.
summary.tldr: Expo-GS uses local exposure reliability to guide geometry learning and Gaussian density control for improved HDR view synthesis.

title: Expo-GS: Exposure-Aware Signed Distance Function in Gaussian Splatting for High Dynamic Range

abstract: Standard practice across domains from robotics to language is to first pretrain a policy on a large-scale demonstration dataset, and then finetune this policy, typically with reinforcement learning (RL), in order to improve performance on deployment domains. This finetuning step has proved critical in achieving human or super-human performance, yet while much attention has been given to developing more effective finetuning algorithms, little attention has been given to ensuring the pretrained policy is an effective initialization for RL finetuning. In this work we seek to understand how the pretrained policy affects finetuning performance, and how to pretrain policies in order to ensure they are effective initializations for finetuning. We first show theoretically that standard behavioral cloning (BC) can fail to ensure coverage over the demonstrator’s actions, a minimal condition necessary for effective RL finetuning. We then show that if, instead of exactly fitting the observed demonstrations, we train a policy to model the posterior distribution of the demonstrator’s behavior given the demonstration dataset, we do obtain a policy that ensures coverage over the demonstrator’s actions, enabling more effective finetuning. Furthermore, this policy achieves this while ensuring pretrained performance is no worse than that of the BC policy. We then show this approach is practically implementable with modern generative models and leads to significantly improved RL finetuning performance on both realistic robotic control benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks, as compared to standard behavioral cloning.

It significantly improves RL fine-tuning performance relative to standard behavioral cloning. The contribution is therefore a change to what pretraining learns, supported by theory and robotic experiments, that makes subsequent reinforcement learning more effective.
summary.tldr: Posterior Behavioral Cloning preserves demonstrator-action coverage during pretraining and improves subsequent reinforcement learning in robotic tasks.

title: Posterior Behavioral Cloning: Pretraining BC Policies for Efficient RL Finetuning

abstract: Transformer architectures, and their attention mechanisms in particular, form the foundation of modern large language models. While transformer models are widely believed to operate in high-dimensional hidden spaces, we show that attention outputs are confined to a surprisingly low-dimensional subspace, with an effective dimensionality of only about 60% of the full space—a phenomenon that is consistently observed across diverse model families and datasets, and arises from overlap among the output subspaces of different attention heads. Critically, we find this low-rank structure as a key factor of the prevalent dead feature problem in sparse dictionary learning, where it creates a mismatch between randomly initialized features and the intrinsic geometry of the activation space. Building on this insight, we propose a subspace-constrained training method for sparse autoencoders (SAEs), initializing feature directions into the active subspace of activations. Our approach reduces dead features from 87% to below 1% in Attention Output SAEs with 1M features, and can further extend to other sparse dictionary learning methods. Our findings provide both new insights into the geometry of attention and practical tools for improving sparse dictionary learning in large language models. Code is available at https://github.com/OpenMOSS/Llamascopium.

paragraphs: A transformer can have a large hidden representation without using every available direction in its attention outputs. This paper finds that those outputs occupy an effective subspace of about 60% of the full dimensionality across diverse model families and datasets. Overlap between the output subspaces of different attention heads produces this reduced dimensionality.

That geometry matters for sparse dictionary learning, which seeks features that explain model activations. The authors identify the low-rank structure as a key contributor to dead features: learned features that fail to become active. Random initialization can place feature directions poorly relative to the subspace the attention outputs actually occupy, creating a mismatch before useful learning develops.

The proposed remedy constrains sparse autoencoder training to the relevant subspace and initializes feature directions within it. For attention-output autoencoders containing one million features, the reported dead-feature proportion falls from 87% to below 1%. The approach can also extend to other sparse dictionary methods. The result connects a measured property of attention geometry to a concrete improvement in learning usable features.
summary.tldr: Initializing sparse autoencoder features inside attention outputs’ active subspace reduces dead features from 87% to below 1% in the reported million-feature setting.

title: Dimensional Collapse in Transformer Attention Outputs: A Challenge for Sparse Dictionary Learning

abstract: We reconceptualize Personalized Multimodal Federated Learning (PMFL) by treating missing modalities as intrinsic structural identities that constrain each client to a distinct Riemannian submanifold, rather than as deficiencies to be compensated. To reconcile the tension between identity preservation and cross-client collaboration, we cast PMFL as an identity-aware potential game and seek a geometry-consistent equilibrium instead of a monolithic full-modality optimum. We propose GeoEvo, a federated approximate solver that combines curvature-adaptive Fisher descent with manifold-lifted evolutionary search: Natural Evolution Strategies for basin escape and Particle Swarm updates anchored to a server-broadcast Fréchet prototype for cross-client transfer. A monotone selection rule guarantees surrogate descent and an $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{T})$ stationarity rate; controlled lift residuals further imply expected potential dissipation and, when vanishing, convergence toward first-order Nash equilibria. Empirically, GeoEvo improves personalization and robustness across diverse missing-modality patterns.

paragraphs: GeoEvo studies federated learning when clients have different combinations of data modalities. It treats each combination as a structural identity that places the client on its own curved mathematical space. The objective is a collaborative equilibrium compatible with those identities, allowing personalization without requiring every client to approach a single full-modality solution.

The authors formulate this objective as an identity-aware potential game. Their approximate solver combines curvature-adaptive Fisher descent with evolutionary search lifted between manifolds. Natural Evolution Strategies help escape optimization basins, while Particle Swarm updates use a server-broadcast Fréchet prototype to support transfer across clients. Together, these components connect local geometric optimization with broader search and shared information.

A monotone selection rule guarantees descent of a surrogate objective and a stationarity rate of order one over the square root of the iteration count. Further conclusions depend on lift residuals: controlled residuals imply expected potential dissipation, and vanishing residuals support convergence toward first-order Nash equilibria. Experiments report improved personalization and robustness across varied missing-modality patterns, complementing these explicitly conditional theoretical results.
summary.tldr: GeoEvo uses geometric optimization and evolutionary search to support personalized federated collaboration across clients with different available modalities.

title: GeoEvo: Identity-Aware Potential Game with Geometric Evolution for Personalized Multimodal Federated Learning

abstract: Zero-shot imitation learning requires an agent to reproduce expert behavior from a single demonstration without additional environment interaction or gradient updates at test time. We introduce Contrastive Inverse Reinforcement Learning (CIRL), a self-supervised framework for pre-training zero-shot imitation agents. Our methods rests on a key observation that many useful tasks can be summarized by a single goal state. We can thus convert the multi-task inverse RL problem into a more tractable goal-inference problem, and utilize state-of-the-art goal-conditioned RL methods to recover a policy that reaches the goal. During pre-training, CIRL jointly employs three components to learn without any rewards or demonstrations: (1) a variant of contrastive RL designed to learn maximum-entropy goal-conditioned policies, (2) an automatic goal proposal mechanism (GoalKDE) that drives exploration, and (3) a mean-field variational model that performs amortized goal inference from trajectories. We prove that this procedure consistently recovers the demonstrator’s intent by accounting for the relative difficulty of reaching different states and show how structurally similar prior work may otherwise fail to infer the correct reward. Experiments on goal-conditioned and standard reward-maximizing control tasks show that CIRL outperforms prior zero-shot imitation methods, supporting the expressiveness of goals as a compact summary of behavior.

paragraphs: Zero-shot imitation asks an agent to reproduce expert behavior from one demonstration, without further environment interaction or parameter updates at test time. CIRL approaches this by treating many tasks as attempts to reach a particular goal state. Inferring that goal can make interpreting a demonstration more tractable than recovering an unrestricted reward function.

During pretraining, the framework learns without rewards or demonstrations. It combines a contrastive method for learning maximum-entropy goal-conditioned policies, an automatic goal proposal mechanism called GoalKDE that encourages exploration, and a variational model that infers goals from trajectories. These components connect learning how to reach states with learning how to interpret observed behavior.

The theoretical result establishes consistent recovery of demonstrator intent while accounting for differences in how difficult states are to reach. The authors also explain why structurally similar approaches can infer the wrong reward. Experiments on both goal-conditioned and standard reward-maximizing control tasks outperform prior zero-shot imitation methods, supporting goal states as useful compact descriptions of behavior across the tested tasks.
summary.tldr: CIRL learns to infer goals from single demonstrations and pursue them without test-time interaction or updates, accounting for differences in goal difficulty.

title: Consistent Zero-Shot Imitation with Contrastive Goal Inference

abstract: While Bayesian inference provides a principled framework for reasoning under uncertainty, its widespread adoption is limited by the intractability of exact posterior computation, necessitating the use of approximate inference. However, existing methods are often computationally expensive, or demand costly retraining when priors change, limiting their utility, particularly in sequential inference problems such as real-time sensor fusion. To address these challenges, we introduce the Distribution Transformer—a novel architecture that can learn arbitrary distribution-to-distribution mappings. Our method can be trained to map a prior to the corresponding posterior, conditioned on some dataset—thus performing approximate Bayesian inference. Our novel architecture represents a prior distribution as a (universally-approximating) Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM), and transforms it into a GMM representation of the posterior. The components of the GMM attend to each other via self-attention, and to the datapoints via cross-attention. We demonstrate that Distribution Transformers both maintain flexibility to vary the prior, and significantly reduces computation times—from minutes to milliseconds—while achieving expected log-likelihood performance on par with or superior to existing approximate inference methods across tasks such as sequential inference, quantum system parameter inference, and Gaussian Process predictive posterior inference with hyperpriors.

paragraphs: Bayesian inference updates an initial belief, called a prior, after observing data to produce a posterior. Computing that update exactly is often impractical. Approximate methods can still be slow, and some require expensive retraining when the prior changes. This is particularly inconvenient for sequential tasks that repeatedly update uncertain beliefs.

Distribution Transformers learn mappings between distributions. For Bayesian inference, they receive a prior and data and produce an approximate posterior. Both distributions are represented as Gaussian mixtures, which combine several Gaussian components into a flexible distribution. Self-attention connects the mixture components, while cross-attention lets them incorporate information from the observed data.

The evaluated models accommodate changing priors and reduce inference times from minutes to milliseconds. Their expected log-likelihood performance matches or exceeds compared approximate methods on sequential inference, quantum parameter estimation, and Gaussian-process prediction with hyperpriors. The contribution combines speed with a flexible input representation: the prior itself is supplied to the model, allowing inference to adapt as initial beliefs change.
summary.tldr: Distribution Transformers map changing priors and observed data to approximate posteriors, delivering millisecond inference in the evaluated tasks.

title: Distribution Transformers: Fast Approximate Bayesian Inference With On-The-Fly Prior Adaptation

abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly coordinate in multi-agent systems, yet we lack an understanding of where and why cooperation fails. Many real-world coordination problems are not social dilemmas: helping others—sharing documentation, unblocking a teammate—costs the helper almost nothing while producing substantial collective benefit. Whether LLM agents cooperate in this regime, where helping is free and they are explicitly instructed to do so, remains unknown. We build a turn-based multi-agent environment that strips away all strategic complexity, making cooperation costless and trivially optimal. Across eight widely used LLMs, capability does not predict cooperation: OpenAI o3 reaches only 17% of optimal collective performance while the weaker o3-mini reaches 50%, despite identical instructions to maximize group revenue. Using a causal decomposition that automates one side of agent communication, we separate cooperation failures from competence failures, and find that several capable models actively withhold information despite gaining nothing from withholding. Targeted interventions address each mode: explicit protocols roughly double the performance of competence-limited models, while small sharing incentives unlock cooperation-limited ones. Our results suggest that scaling intelligence alone will not solve coordination in multi-agent systems, and will require deliberate cooperative design, even when helping costs nothing.

This isolates failures that cannot be explained by a useful trade-off between helping the team and protecting an agent's own payoff.

They also show why diagnosing the cause matters: clearer procedures and stronger motivation to share address different obstacles to collective performance.
summary.tldr: Even when cooperation is free and explicitly requested, capable LLM agents can withhold useful information, requiring interventions tailored to the failure mode.

title: More Capable, Less Cooperative? When LLMs Fail at Zero-Cost Collaboration

abstract: Spatial understanding remains a key challenge in vision-language models. Yet it is still unclear whether such understanding is truly acquired, and if so, through what mechanisms. We present a controllable 1D image–text testbed to probe how left–right relational understanding emerges in Transformer-based vision and text encoders trained with a CLIP-style contrastive objective. We train lightweight Transformer-based vision and text encoders end-to-end on paired descriptions of one- and two-object scenes and evaluate generalization to unseen object pairs while systematically varying label and layout diversity. We find that contrastive training learns left–right relations and that label diversity, more than layout diversity, is the primary driver of generalization in this setting. To gain the mechanistic understanding, we perform an attention decomposition and show that interactions between positional and token embeddings induce a horizontal attention gradient that breaks left–right symmetry in the encoders; ablating this contribution substantially reduces left–right discrimination. Our results provide a mechanistic insight of when and how CLIP-style models acquire relational competence.

paragraphs: This paper studies how vision–language models learn the difference between an object being on the left and being on the right. It uses a controlled one-dimensional image–text environment with scenes containing one or two objects. Lightweight vision and text Transformers are trained together with a CLIP-style contrastive objective, allowing the researchers to vary the training data systematically.

Evaluation uses object pairs absent from training, testing whether learned relations transfer to new combinations. The researchers vary both label diversity and layout diversity. They find that contrastive training acquires left–right relations and that label diversity is the stronger driver of generalization within this setting. This identifies a specific property of the training data associated with relational transfer.

This gradient breaks left–right symmetry in the encoders. Removing its contribution substantially weakens left–right discrimination. The controlled experiments therefore connect a generalization finding to an internal mechanism, explaining how directional distinctions emerge in these synthetic spatial tasks.
summary.tldr: A controlled CLIP-style testbed links left–right generalization to label diversity and a symmetry-breaking interaction between positional and token embeddings.

title: Left–Right Symmetry Breaking in CLIP-Style Vision-Language Models Trained on Synthetic Spatial-Relation Data

abstract: This paper considers decentralized optimization of convex functions with mixed affine equality constraints involving both local and global variables. Constraints on global variables may vary across different nodes in the network, while local variables are subject to coupled and node-specific constraints. Such problem formulations arise in machine learning applications, including federated learning and multi-task learning, as well as in resource allocation and distributed control. We analyze this problem under smooth and non-smooth assumptions, considering both strongly convex and general convex objective functions. Our main contribution is an optimal algorithm for the smooth, strongly convex regime, whose convergence rate matches established lower complexity bounds. We further provide optimal and near-optimal methods for the remaining cases.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization problems distributed across a network, where participants must coordinate decisions involving both shared and local variables. The constraints are affine equalities, meaning they impose linear relationships with possible constant offsets. Different nodes can impose different constraints on global variables, while local variables face both node-specific restrictions and constraints coupling them together.

That combination captures coordination requirements found in federated learning, multi-task learning, resource allocation, and distributed control. The analysis covers smooth and nonsmooth objectives, as well as strongly convex and general convex cases. These distinctions matter because they change the mathematical structure available to an algorithm and the convergence rates that can be achieved.

The main result is an optimal algorithm for smooth, strongly convex objectives: its convergence rate matches established lower complexity bounds. Here, optimality concerns the algorithm’s rate relative to those bounds in that regime. For the other regimes, the authors provide optimal or near-optimal methods, extending the treatment beyond the most favorable objective assumptions.
summary.tldr: The paper develops optimal or near-optimal decentralized optimization methods for convex problems with interacting local and global affine equality constraints.

title: Complexity of Decentralized Optimization with Mixed Affine Constraints

abstract: Upcycling, a strategy that initializes Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) by replicating pre-trained feed-forward or MoE networks to expand model capacity, has become a popular method in continual learning due to its effectiveness in mitigating catastrophic forgetting. However, existing paradigms indiscriminately expand capacity to prioritize performance at the cost of severe inefficiency, introducing severe parameter redundancy and failing to exploit structural heterogeneity. To address this, we investigate the determinants of forgetting in training dynamics using Centered Kernel Alignment (CKA) and loss landscape flatness to analyze the behavior of pre- and post-expansion MoE layers, uncovering instability in deep-layer representations and heterogeneous expert sensitivity to new tasks, thereby demonstrating the potential of selective upcycling to eliminate redundancy. Consequently, we propose a dynamic bilevel optimization framework to guide adaptive upcycling, featuring an outer loop employing a Gumbel-Softmax differentiable mask to perform Neural Architecture Search (NAS) for adaptive growth, while an inner loop optimizes weight updates via task objectives and CKA-regularized replay. Experiments on the TRACE benchmark demonstrate that our proposed method achieves better average accuracy with 80% forgetting reduction, while effectively eliminating 60% of redundant parameter expansion that standard upcycling would introduce.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-experts upcycling expands a pretrained model by replicating existing networks, helping it learn new tasks while retaining earlier knowledge. The paper argues that expanding capacity indiscriminately creates redundant parameters. It investigates where expansion is useful by studying representation similarity with Centered Kernel Alignment, or CKA, together with loss-landscape flatness.

The analysis finds unstable representations in deeper layers and differences in how sensitive individual experts are to new tasks. These observations motivate selective growth. An outer optimization loop uses a differentiable Gumbel-Softmax mask to search for an appropriate expansion pattern. An inner loop updates model weights using task objectives and replay regularized by CKA.

On the TRACE benchmark, the framework achieves better average accuracy and reports an 80% reduction in forgetting. It also removes 60% of the redundant parameter expansion that standard upcycling would introduce. The results support coordinating architectural growth with representation-preserving training, so additional capacity is allocated according to the model’s differing needs across its structure.
summary.tldr: This method selectively expands mixture-of-experts models using bilevel optimization, reducing forgetting and redundant growth on TRACE.

title: Efficient Bilevel Optimization for CKA-Guided MoE Upcycling

abstract: State abstraction plays a key role in scaling reinforcement learning to complex but structured systems. In studying such systems, a wide range of behavioral structures have been studied in reinforcement learning, including value functions, invariants, bisimulation relations, and behavioral metrics. However, a general principle for determining what structures are provably preserved under state abstraction is still lacking. In this paper, we present a unified framework for defining and analyzing behavioral structures in reinforcement learning. Our framework provides a compositional way to specify behavioral semantics based on local, one-step descriptions of system dynamics. Using this framework, we establish results showing how behavioral structures can be safely transferred between abstract and concrete systems. We further show how to construct quantitative metrics from logical behavioral semantics with soundness guarantees. Together, these results provide a principled foundation for reasoning about behaviors under state abstraction in reinforcement learning and offer reusable definition and proof principles for a broad class of behavioral structures in reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: State abstraction makes structured reinforcement learning systems easier to reason about by replacing detailed states with a simpler representation. The central question is which behavioral properties survive that simplification. Researchers study properties such as value functions, invariants, behavioral equivalence, and distances between behaviors, but the paper identifies a missing general principle for analyzing their preservation.

The authors introduce a unified framework that builds behavioral descriptions compositionally from local, one-step system dynamics. This connects small descriptions of individual transitions to larger statements about behavior. Within the framework, they establish results governing how behavioral structures can be transferred safely between a concrete system and its abstraction.

The work also explains how to construct quantitative behavioral metrics from logical descriptions, with soundness guarantees. This connects statements about behavior to numerical ways of comparing it. The contribution is a reusable theoretical foundation for definitions and proofs across a broad class of reinforcement learning structures. Its preservation results provide principled ways to justify abstraction, rather than implying that every simplification automatically preserves every property.
summary.tldr: A unified theoretical framework explains how behavioral properties and metrics can be defined and safely transferred under reinforcement learning state abstraction.

title: Compositional Behavioral Semantics for State Abstraction in Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) systems are crucial for identifying malicious activities on endpoint devices, yet existing methods struggle to efficiently model ultra-long log sequences and to provide interpretable reasoning for security analysts. We propose WatchLog, a novel framework that represents raw logs as video-structured data, enabling scalable and expressive video-language modeling of endpoint behaviors. Each event is encoded as a key–value-guided image, and the resulting images are temporally organized into a video sequence. To capture long-range dependencies, WatchLog employs a temporal cross-attention adapter that enables pixel-wise interaction across time. The adapter acts as an auxiliary temporal reasoning pathway, aligning spatial representations with relevant temporal contexts while preserving the original behavioral semantics. We adopt a two-stage pre-training strategy followed by supervised fine-tuning to generate behavior explanations grounded in event-level semantics and detection outcomes. Experiments on our newly constructed EDR8M-20R dataset and a public benchmark demonstrate that WatchLog consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods in detection accuracy and recall, while offering more interpretable reasoning traces and significantly improved inference efficiency. Extensive ablation studies further support the robustness and interpretability of the proposed method.

WatchLog converts these logs into a video-like representation so a multimodal model can reason about endpoint behavior over time. Each event becomes an image guided by its key–value fields, and events are arranged chronologically.

A temporal cross-attention adapter allows image locations to interact across time, helping the model connect events separated within the sequence. This adapter provides an auxiliary pathway for temporal reasoning while preserving event semantics. The contribution combines a new log representation with temporal reasoning and explanation training, addressing both detection performance and analysts’ ability to understand the result.
summary.tldr: WatchLog represents endpoint logs as video sequences to improve threat detection, temporal reasoning, and behavior explanations.

title: WatchLog: Efficient and Interpretable Event Reasoning for Endpoint Detection and Response Logs with Multimodal LLMs

abstract: Graph generation is a fundamental task with broad applications, such as drug discovery. Recently, discrete flow matching-based graph generation, a.k.a., graph flow model (GFM), has emerged due to its superior performance and flexible sampling. However, effectively aligning GFMs with complex human preferences or task-specific objectives remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we propose Graph-GRPO, an online reinforcement learning (RL) framework for training GFMs under verifiable rewards. Our method makes two key contributions: (1) We derive an analytical expression for the transition probability of GFMs, replacing the Monte Carlo sampling and enabling fully differentiable rollouts for RL training; (2) We propose a refinement strategy that randomly perturbs specific nodes and edges in a graph, and regenerates them, allowing for localized exploration and self-improvement of generation quality. Extensive experiments on both synthetic and real datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of Graph-GRPO. With only 50 denoising steps, our method achieves 95.0% and 97.5% Valid-Unique-Novelty scores on the planar and tree datasets, respectively. Moreover, Graph-GRPO achieves state-of-the-art performance on the molecular optimization tasks, outperforming graph-based and fragment-based RL methods as well as classic genetic algorithms. Code is available in https://github.com/Zhubaoheng/Graph-GRPO.

Graph-GRPO introduces online reinforcement learning for these models when rewards can be verified, connecting graph generation directly to measurable goals.

The method derives an analytical expression for transition probabilities, replacing Monte Carlo estimation and enabling fully differentiable rollouts for reinforcement-learning training. It also reports state-of-the-art molecular optimization performance, outperforming graph-based and fragment-based reinforcement-learning methods and classic genetic algorithms. These findings support combining tractable transition calculations with local structural exploration to optimize graph generators under verifiable rewards.
summary.tldr: Graph-GRPO combines analytical transition probabilities and local graph refinement to train graph flow models with verifiable rewards.

title: Graph-GRPO: Training Graph Flow Models with Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Preference-based alignment methods (e.g., RLHF, DPO) typically optimize a single scalar objective, implicitly averaging over heterogeneous human preferences. In practice, systematic annotator and user-group disagreement makes mean-reward maximization brittle and susceptible to proxy over-optimization. We propose Disagreement-Aware Alignment via Risk-Constrained Decoding (DARC), a retraining-free inference-time method that frames response selection as distributionally robust, risk-sensitive decision making. Given multiple preference samples or scalable disagreement proxies, DARC reranks candidates by maximizing a KL-robust (entropic) satisfaction objective, and provides simple deployment controls that cap or penalize the corresponding entropic risk premium relative to the mean, enabling explicit risk budgets without retraining. We provide theoretical characterization linking this decoding rule to principled pessimism and KL-based distributionally robust optimization. Experiments on alignment benchmarks show that DARC reduces disagreement and tail risk while maintaining competitive average quality under noisy, heterogeneous feedback.

paragraphs: People can systematically disagree about which model responses are desirable. When alignment reduces their preferences to one average reward, a response can score well overall while performing poorly for some preference patterns. DARC addresses this problem during response selection, without retraining the language model.

The method uses multiple preference samples or scalable proxies for disagreement to rerank candidate responses. Its objective incorporates a pessimistic view of satisfaction under changes to the preference distribution, formalized through KL-based distributional robustness. Deployment controls can cap or penalize an entropic risk premium relative to mean satisfaction. These controls make the acceptable level of preference-related risk an explicit part of decoding.

The paper theoretically connects its selection rule to principled pessimism and robust optimization. On alignment benchmarks with noisy, heterogeneous feedback, DARC reduces disagreement and tail risk while keeping average response quality competitive. The findings suggest that inference-time selection can account for uneven preference outcomes, provided the method has preference samples or disagreement proxies to inform that selection.
summary.tldr: DARC reranks responses using disagreement-aware risk controls, reducing tail risk while maintaining competitive average quality without retraining.

abstract: In sequence modeling, we often wish to represent complex interaction between labels, such as when performing multiple, cascaded labeling tasks on the same sequence, or when long-range dependencies exist. We present {\em dynamic conditional random fields (DCRFs)}, a generalization of linear-chain conditional random fields (CRFs) in which each time slice contains a set of state variables and edges---a distributed state representation as in dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs)---and parameters are tied across slices. Since exact inference can be intractable in such models, we perform approximate inference using several schedules for belief propagation,including tree-based reparameterization (TRP). On a natural-language chunking task, we show that a DCRF performs better than a series of linear-chain CRFs, achieving comparable performance using only half the training data.

Since exact inference can be intractable in such models, we perform approximate inference using several schedules for belief propagation,including tree-based reparameterization (TRP). paragraphs: Sequence labeling can involve several interacting labels at each position, or dependencies that extend beyond adjacent positions. The paper introduces dynamic conditional random fields to represent these relationships. They generalize linear-chain CRFs by placing a collection of state variables and connecting edges within each time slice, with parameters shared across slices.

This distributed representation resembles the organization used in dynamic Bayesian networks. It gives the model a way to express relationships among multiple labeling tasks within one probabilistic structure. The added flexibility can make exact inference intractable, so the authors use approximate belief propagation and investigate several update schedules, including tree-based reparameterization.

On a natural-language chunking task, the dynamic model outperforms a series of linear-chain CRFs. It also reaches comparable performance with only half the training data. The result suggests that representing interactions among labels can make training data more useful in this task. The evidence is task-specific, while the modeling framework is designed for more general sequence-labeling relationships.
summary.tldr: Dynamic CRFs model interacting sequence labels jointly and improve reported chunking performance, including comparable results with half the training data.

title: Dynamic conditional random fields: factorized probabilistic models for labeling and segmenting sequence data

abstract: There is a range of potential applications of Machine Learning where it would be more useful to predict the probability distribution for a variable rather than simply the most likely value for that variable. In meteorology and in finance it is often important to know the probability of a variable falling within (or outside) different ranges. In this paper we consider the prediction of surf height with the objective of predicting if it will fall within a given ‘surfable’ range. Prediction problems such as this are considerably more difficult if the distribution of the phenomenon is significantly different from a normal distribution. This is the case with the surf data we have studied. To address this we use an ensemble of mixture density networks to predict the probability density function. Our evaluation shows that this is an effective solution. We also describe a web-based application that presents these predictions in a usable manner.

Our evaluation shows that this is an effective solution. We also describe a web-based application that presents these predictions in a usable manner.

paragraphs: The paper studies surf-height prediction with a decision-oriented goal: estimating whether the height will fall within a surfable range. A single most likely height does not directly express the probability of that event. Predicting the full distribution instead supplies information about the likelihood of values falling inside or outside ranges of interest.

The surf data studied have a distribution that differs substantially from a normal distribution, making this prediction problem harder. The authors address that feature using an ensemble of mixture density networks to predict a probability density function. This makes the distribution itself the model’s output and connects the prediction to the range-based question.

The evaluation finds the approach effective for the surf-height problem studied. The paper also describes a web application that presents the resulting predictions in a usable form. Its contribution therefore spans both distribution prediction and presentation: the learning method estimates uncertainty across possible heights, and the application makes those estimates available for interpreting surf conditions.
summary.tldr: An ensemble of mixture density networks predicts surf-height distributions to estimate the probability of surfable conditions.

title: Predicting probability distributions for surf height using an ensemble of mixture density networks
Optimal kernel selection in Kernel Fisher discriminant analysis

abstract: Typically agent evaluation is done through Monte Carlo estimation. However, stochastic agent decisions and stochastic outcomes can make this approach inefficient, requiring many samples for an accurate estimate. We present a new technique that can be used to simultaneously evaluate many strategies while playing a single strategy in the context of an extensive game. This technique is based on importance sampling, but utilizes two new mechanisms for significantly reducing variance in the estimates. We demonstrate its effectiveness in the domain of poker, where stochasticity makes traditional evaluation problematic.
originalAbstract: Typically agent evaluation is done through Monte Carlo estimation. However, stochastic agent decisions and stochastic outcomes can make this approach inefficient, requiring many samples for an accurate estimate. We present a new technique that can be used to simultaneously evaluate many strategies while playing a single strategy in the context of an extensive game. This technique is based on importance sampling, but utilizes two new mechanisms for significantly reducing variance in the estimates. We demonstrate its effectiveness in the domain of poker, where stochasticity makes traditional evaluation problematic.

paragraphs: Evaluating an agent through repeated play can require many samples when both its decisions and the game's outcomes are stochastic. Ordinary Monte Carlo estimates may fluctuate substantially, making accurate comparisons expensive. This paper addresses that problem for extensive games, where evaluation must account for the unfolding sequence of decisions and outcomes.

The proposed technique evaluates many strategies simultaneously while only one strategy is played. It uses importance sampling to make the observations useful for evaluating those different strategies. The paper adds two mechanisms that significantly reduce the variance of the estimates, addressing the instability that makes straightforward sampling inefficient.

The authors demonstrate the technique in poker, a domain where stochasticity makes conventional evaluation problematic. The finding supports the practical value of sharing sampled experience across strategy evaluations while reducing estimation noise. Its significance is an improvement in how strategies can be assessed: collecting experience under one played strategy can inform several evaluations, and lower-variance estimates can make that information more useful.
summary.tldr: An importance-sampling technique evaluates multiple strategies from play under one strategy, using two variance-reduction mechanisms demonstrated in poker.

title: Strategy evaluation in extensive games with importance sampling

abstract: The central issue in representing graph-structured data instances in learning algorithms is designing features which are invariant to permuting the numbering of the vertices. We present a new system of invariant graph features which we call the skew spectrum of graphs. The skew spectrum is based on mapping the adjacency matrix to a function on the symmetric group and computing bispectral invariants. The reduced form of the skew spectrum is computable in O(n 3 ) time, and experiments show that on several benchmark datasets it can outperform state of the art graph kernels.
originalAbstract: The central issue in representing graph-structured data instances in learning algorithms is designing features which are invariant to permuting the numbering of the vertices. We present a new system of invariant graph features which we call the skew spectrum of graphs. The skew spectrum is based on mapping the adjacency matrix to a function on the symmetric group and computing bispectral invariants. The reduced form of the skew spectrum is computable in O(n 3 ) time, and experiments show that on several benchmark datasets it can outperform state of the art graph kernels.

paragraphs: A graph's vertex numbers are arbitrary, so changing those numbers should not change the features used to represent the graph. This paper addresses that requirement with a system of invariant features called the skew spectrum. The aim is to give learning algorithms a graph representation that does not depend on the chosen vertex numbering.

The construction maps the adjacency matrix to a function on the symmetric group and computes bispectral invariants from that function. This makes invariance to vertex permutations part of the mathematical representation. The authors also provide a reduced form of the skew spectrum that can be computed in O(n³) time, supplying a concrete computational bound for extracting the features.

Experiments show that the representation can outperform state-of-the-art graph kernels on several benchmark datasets. The finding supports the skew spectrum as a useful graph-learning representation in those comparisons, without implying that it is best for all graph data. The contribution combines the required invariance, an explicit construction, and empirical evidence of predictive usefulness.
summary.tldr: The skew spectrum provides graph features invariant to vertex renumbering, with a cubic-time reduced form and promising benchmark results.

title: The skew spectrum of graphs

abstract: A new procedure for learning cost-sensitive SVM classifiers is proposed. The SVM hinge loss is extended to the cost sensitive setting, and the cost-sensitive SVM is derived as the minimizer of the associated risk. The extension of the hinge loss draws on recent connections between risk minimization and probability elicitation. These connections are generalized to cost-sensitive classification, in a manner that guarantees consistency with the cost-sensitive Bayes risk, and associated Bayes decision rule. This ensures that optimal decision rules, under the new hinge loss, implement the Bayes-optimal cost-sensitive classification boundary. Minimization of the new hinge loss is shown to be a generalization of the classic SVM optimization problem, and can be solved by identical procedures. The resulting algorithm avoids the shortcomings of previous approaches to cost-sensitive SVM design, and has superior experimental performance.

This ensures that optimal decision rules, under the new hinge loss, implement the Bayes-optimal cost-sensitive classification boundary. paragraphs: This paper develops support vector machines for classification problems where different mistakes have different costs. It extends the hinge loss to reflect those costs and derives the classifier by minimizing the corresponding risk. The approach connects the training objective directly to the decision costs that the classifier is intended to respect.

The derivation generalizes connections between risk minimization and probability elicitation to cost-sensitive classification. The resulting loss is consistent with the cost-sensitive Bayes risk and decision rule. In particular, optimal decision rules under this loss produce the Bayes-optimal cost-sensitive boundary, providing a theoretical link between the surrogate objective and the desired classification decision.

The optimization problem generalizes the classic SVM formulation and can be solved using the same procedures. The authors also report superior experimental performance and avoidance of shortcomings in previous cost-sensitive SVM designs. The contribution combines a decision-theoretic justification with compatibility with established SVM optimization methods, supported by the reported empirical comparisons.
summary.tldr: A cost-sensitive hinge loss yields SVMs with Bayes-consistent optimal decisions and an optimization problem solvable by standard SVM procedures.

title: Risk minimization, probability elicitation, and cost-sensitive SVMs

abstract: The restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) is a flexible tool for modeling complex data, however there have been significant computational difficulties in using RBMs to model high-dimensional multinomial observations. In natural language processing applications, words are naturally modeled by K-ary discrete distributions, where K is determined by the vocabulary size and can easily be in the hundreds of thousands. The conventional approach to training RBMs on word observations is limited because it requires sampling the states of K-way softmax visible units during block Gibbs updates, an operation that takes time linear in K. In this work, we address this issue by employing a more general class of Markov chain Monte Carlo operators on the visible units, yielding updates with computational complexity independent of K. We demonstrate the success of our approach by training RBMs on hundreds of millions of word n-grams using larger vocabularies than previously feasible and using the learned features to improve performance on chunking and sentiment classification tasks, achieving state-of-the-art results on the latter.

paragraphs: Restricted Boltzmann machines can model complex observations, but word data create a computational bottleneck. Each word is a discrete choice from a vocabulary that may contain hundreds of thousands of entries. Conventional block Gibbs training samples from visible softmax units with a cost that grows linearly with vocabulary size.

The authors replace those visible-unit updates with a more general class of Markov chain Monte Carlo operators. The resulting update complexity is independent of vocabulary size. This targets the costly sampling operation directly, making larger vocabularies feasible without the same vocabulary-dependent cost for each such update.

The method is demonstrated by training on hundreds of millions of word n-grams with vocabularies larger than previously feasible. The learned features improve performance on chunking and sentiment classification, with state-of-the-art results reported for sentiment classification. These findings connect the computational change to useful learned representations: the approach supports larger-scale word modeling and yields features that benefit downstream language tasks.
summary.tldr: Alternative Monte Carlo updates remove vocabulary-size dependence from RBM visible-unit updates and enable useful large-scale word representations.

title: Training Restricted Boltzmann Machines on Word Observations

abstract: We suggest using the max-norm as a convex surrogate constraint for clustering. We show how this yields a better exact cluster recovery guarantee than previously suggested nuclear-norm relaxation, and study the effectiveness of our method, and other related convex relaxations, compared to other approaches.
originalAbstract: We suggest using the max-norm as a convex surrogate constraint for clustering. We show how this yields a better exact cluster recovery guarantee than previously suggested nuclear-norm relaxation, and study the effectiveness of our method, and other related convex relaxations, compared to other approaches.

paragraphs: This paper considers clustering through a constrained optimization formulation. Its main proposal is to use the max-norm as a convex surrogate constraint. A surrogate replaces a difficult constraint with one that is more amenable to optimization. The central research question is whether this particular replacement preserves enough of the clustering structure to recover the desired groups.

The main stated theoretical result is a better guarantee for exact cluster recovery than a previously proposed nuclear-norm relaxation. Exact recovery concerns identifying the clusters themselves, making the choice of convex constraint consequential for the result one can prove. The comparison shows that different convex surrogates can provide different recovery guarantees even when they serve the same broad clustering purpose.

The paper also studies the effectiveness of its method and related convex relaxations against other approaches. The abstract states the improvement in recovery guarantees, while describing the practical comparisons as an investigation. Together, these contributions position the max-norm as a theoretically motivated alternative whose practical behavior is also examined.
summary.tldr: A max-norm convex constraint gives clustering a stronger exact-recovery guarantee than an earlier nuclear-norm relaxation.

title: Clustering using Max-norm Constrained Optimization
